National Transcontinental railway-further amount required, $1,000,000.

["I wish to tell the hon. minister that my opinion is as valuable to me as his opinions are to him. This is not

the first time that he read papers prepared by his officials, and the next day swallowed them in toto. If to-morrow or the next day the minister is brought face to face with the fact that this statement which he has read is an absolute tissue of falsehood, he will say: I read the statement prepared for me in the department; I am not responsible. The minister comes here with a statement containing coarse language, a production or an essay by a gentleman in his office who has nothing to do from one end of the year to the other but write such letters. I do not propose to lecture the minister or anybody else, but I want the minister to understand that his avoirdupois or altitude is not going to make the slightest difference to me. I submit that if any member in this House makes a statement that does not agree with what an officer would consider to be right, that officer has the right to protection. He has the right to take the matter up privately with the member, to set forth the facts and to prove that the member was mistaken. It is then up to the member to say in the House that he did misrepresent the officer in question, and if the member does not do so, the minister is within his rights in saying: I am aware that my officer has brought this matter up with the member; that he has or ought to have convinced the member that he was wrong; that the member has not explained the matter, and that as the officer has not an opportunity of coming here and defending himself, the minister will do so for him. But the minister comes here with an essay for which the country has paid the equivalent of many months' salary, prepared to blackguard a member of this House and to tell him that his statements are absurd and absolutely false. That is the kind of literature the minister has been putting on ' Hansard ' to-night. So far as we in Nova Scotia are concerned we shall try to defend ourselves and see that no Cowie is going to cowe anybody on this side of the House. Mr. Oowie will find that he will experience a day of reckoning if he thinks that he is at liberty to browbeat and bulldoze hon. gentlemen of this House as long as he has a minister to read his essays at two o'clock in the morning, when there is very little opportunity of criticism.
Progress reported.

Why is this further
amount of $1,000,000 required for the National Transcontinental railway?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (acting Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext: The commission decided that the $8,000,000 in the Main Estimates was not sufficient, and thought it advisable to put another million dollars in the Supplementary Estimates in case it might be required.
Are you going to bring the grades up to the standard?

The matter of grades was thoroughly discussed here last night and on previous occasions. Prom a point 100 miles west of Cochrane to Winnipeg, there

is no complaint about the grades. Any grades west of Cochrane, in regard to which there might be any complaints, would be within 100 miles of Cochrane, on what is known as the Fauquier contract. East of Cochrane, any grades in regard to which there might be any complaints would be within 200 miles of Cochrane. From the 200 mile limit to Moncton, there are no complaints whatever about the grades. From Cochrane east for 200 miles the work has not been completed. Therefore if any sags or grades are to be brought to the proper level, as suggested by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), there is no reason why the contractors cannot complete that portion, so that the grades between Cochrane and Moncton will be of such a standard as has been mentioned. For 100 miles west of Cochrane the line is completed and ready for opera. tion, and there are a few sags, not very heavy grades, that can be remedied at very little expense.
With regard to the operation of the road, it is the desire of the Government and, I believe, of every hon. member, that the operation of the portion between Winnipeg and Moncton should take place at the earliest possible moment. As I have stated, that portion will be ready for operation this fall; and if there are a few sags in the 300 miles, the Grand Trunk Pacific, if they take over the road, can remedy them, and the work will be added to the cost according to the terms of the contract. As long as any portion of the road is in the hands of the contractors, such as is the case in regard to that portion of the road from Cochrane 200 miles east, it is impossible to have a through operation by the Grand Trunk Pacific or in any other way that the Government might arrange. Therefore I think it is advisable to try to get the road completed at the earliest possible moment; and, if there are a few sags, they can be remedied in another season. In that way the public would have the benefit of the operation of the road at an earlier date than if the sags were remedied now.
How many of these sags are there?

On contract No. 13, there are six; on No. 14, ten; and on No. 13, sixteen; making a total of thirty-two. The hon. member must hear in mind that, where there are any sags, the work has not been taken out of the hands of the contractors,
and they can all be remedied before the road is taken over. On the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk main lines, the railway companies are all the time using ballast trains for the purpose of improving the levels or filling the sags without any interference with the traffic as a whole. On this new road, I think this could well be done without interfering with the traffic, and it would be much better to get a regular train service at the earliest possible moment than to wait for the remedying of the sags before taking over the road.

As I understand from my hon. friend, all these so-called momentum grades cover a distance of 300 miles, namely, 100 miles west of Cochrane and 200 miles east of Cochrane; that is to say, there is a continuous portion of the road in which these grades are to be found. My hon. friend says, if it is found advisable these sags can be filled, as the work is still in the hands of the contractors.
Part of it. As regards the 100 miles west of Cochrane, the contractors have handed over the road completed.
That is ready to be operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific?
Yes.
Have the contractors any instructions to fill the sags or to leave them as they are?

The contractors who have
charge of the work for the 200 miles east of Cochrane are doing the work necessary for the completion of the road, and they will continue to work until the commission decides to take it off their hands. No instructions have been given to them to complete the work up to a certain standard. We can tell them to-day or to-morrow, even if they have the work up to a certain standard, to continue the work and make the grades up to a higher standard.

It is really refreshing,
after days of discussion, to find that my horn, friend, the acting Minister of Railways, has now thrown up his hands and is going to fix things. .

I have not thrown up my
hands.

Within 300 miles we can fix things before the contractors are re-

leased from their contracts; or, if the Grand Trunk Pacific do it, we shall pay them for doing it after the work is finished. I think we have accomplished something if we have accomplished that. I hope it is clear now that the country is to have a transcontinental line up to the standard agreed upon.
Quebec bridge construction-further amount required, $1,000,000.

Might I ask the minister when the ferry across the 'St. Lawrence at Quebec is to be ready? When he answers that, I think he might very briefly tell us in what condition of construction the Quebec bridge is. I remember, when another gentleman happened to be Minister of Railways he had to give this information about four times every session to the inquisitive Opposition. A very short statement will be sufficient.
The substructure is finished.
On both sides?

The contractors for the
bridge have stated to me that they will have it completed at the end of the season of 1917. The report that I have here says that during the season of 1913 the construction of the piers and abutments was completed, with the exception of such work as pointing, cleaning the stones, and clearing up the site, and that this work will be entirely completed during the season of 1914. The superstructure is under contract with the St. Lawrence Bridge Company. In 1913 the shop made good progress in the preparation of final plans; they have fabricated and shipped to the site some 9,000 tons of bridge material, have erected a large part of their plant at the bridge site, and have erected two approach spans on the north shore of the river, thus making a start on the erection of the bridge proper. The payments made to this company on account of raw material received at the shop and material fabricated and erected, are: Total to March 31, 1913, $310,491.26; total to March 31, 1914, estimated, $2,200,000.
The future programme for this work, as estimated by the contractors, is as follows:
Season of 1914:	to fabricate and erect
the major portion of the north anchor arm, weight of this portion estimated at 15,930 tons; cost of portion erected, $2,870,000.
Season of 1915: complete anchor arm, north shore, and erect four panels of cantilever arm; erect about half of anchor arm on south shore; weight of portion erected,

23,285 tons; cost of portion erected, $4,200,000.
Season of 1916: complete cantilever arm, north shore, and complete anchor arm and one-third of cantilever arm south shore. Weight of material erected, 16,385 tons; cost of material erected, $2,947,000.
Season of 1917:	Complete cantilever
arm, south shore, and erect suspended span and float same into place; weight of material erected, 8,955 tons; cost of material erected, $1,620,000. This will complete the erection of the bridge with the exception of the framing of the floor and riveting. According to this programme, trains should be able to run over the bridge by the end of 1917.
That is the report of Mr. Monsarrat, which is confirmed by the conversation I had with the contractors.

No changes
have been made in the plans as laid down?
None whatever. Mr. Monsarrat has had full charge, and there has been no change whatever.

Is this bridge company
giving satisfaction in every respect?
It is giving perfect satisfaction in every way, shape and form.

That is satisfactory to
me.
Welland ship canal construction-further amount required, $1,000,000.

As a matter of fact, there is no excuse for supplementaries like this. If they were needed the engineer in charge knew they were needed some months ago. The Department of Railways and Canals had come to be very little of a sinner as compared with other departments in this respect; they had practically got out of the supplementary estimate business to a large extent. If whoever is at the head of the department would sit tight and give his officials to understand that no supplementaries of this kind will ibe considered, this practice would be whittled down to the vanishing point. One of the difficulties is that at the last hour large supplementaries are presented to the House and we cannot discuss them. It is not the fault of the head of the department, nor of the deputy; it is the fault of the men in charge of the outside work, who figure at too small a price; but if they knew they could not get supplementaries they would figure on the safe side.

The Main Estimates were made up last fall. With the Welland canal, of course, we might let the Main Estimates go; but it is extremely important that the work should be all under way and completed as soon as possible. With the Welland canal as with the Transcontinental railway it is important to get the work completed. We could have let the Main Estimates go as they are, and not let any other contracts; but we decided to toy to get the work completed within a certain time, Mr. Weller, the engineer in charge, advised us that we might possibly exceed the Main Estimates and that we should have another million dollars in case the amount first asked for was not sufficient. I agree, however, that full provision for these works should be made in the Main Estimates; but with large works like these it is very difficult early in the fall to make an estimate covering all that may be required.

I do not want to lecture, and I know of some of the difficulties; but, if, when an estimate of this kind came-in, the fact were impressed upon the official that it could not be considered, the practice would not be kept up. On works like the Welland canal and the Transcontinental Railway Parliament does not stop at a million because they know that a certain amount has to be expended, and enough must be placed at the disposal of the Government, and that unless required the money will not be expended. Parliament is not niggardly in this respect, but on large works requiring millions, it is not fair to Parliament to have such large supplement-aries when the officer ought to know at the first that the money would be required'.

I agree with what the hon. gentleman has said.
Rideau canal-towards construction of bridge over Rideau canal at Pretoria avenue, Ottawa, $40,000.
There was a bridge over the Rideau canal in Ottawa for which the Department made a grant of $40,000. This is another, I presume!

This is the same one. There was an item of $40,000 towards the construction of a bridge over the Rideau canai, but the original proposed location has been changed. The bridge at Argyle avenue is being abolished, amid a change is ibeing made in the location.
Mr. GRAHAfM: Does the change meet with the approval of the department?

It meets with the approval of all parties concerned.
Trent canal-'further contribution to the county of Hastings towards the cost of construction of bridge over Trent river at Frank-ford, $2,540.
Are you sure there is nothing in this for provisions?

There was an arrangement made to pay a certain amount towards the construction of the Hastings bridge over the Trent river. The total was $22,540, and in the session of 1912, $20,000 was paid, leaving a balance of $2,540.

My point was: Is the minister sure there will be no charge for ginger ale, and that he will not find it necessary to appoint a commission?
Welland canal-Towards the construction of high level bridge over canal, $50,000.
Is this a bridge they have been building for some years?
Instead of a low-level swing, the city has applied for a high-level bridge.
What street is it on?

I do not know what street it is on. But the mayor and a deputation were down several times, interviewing the minister and myself, and the city are willing to pay a large proportion of the cost, and have asked us to make this grant.
Chambly canal-Macadamizing road, $15,000.
What road is that? Has that anything to do with the road with which the Department of Public Works was concerned?

This road is not under the Public Works Department. For a number of years the Government have been constructing a roadway along the Ghamhly canal, and this is to complete that portion that is not yet done.
Lachine canal-St. Gabriel shed No. 1, $25,000.

I have received many
letters from a gentleman in Quebec who claims to know something about engineering, and who states that the central arch of the Quebec bridge cannot be put up according to plans. The name of that gentleman is Mr. Richard. I do not know whether the Postmaster General has received communications from him, but he has written letter after letter to me and to one or two of my friends who are representatives



of the Quebec district. Has my hon. friend received any such letters?

Such letters have been received by the minister or by the department, and they have been referred to Mr. Monser-rat. The Department of Railways and Canals have the utmost confidence in Mr. Monserrat, and, of course, all such matters are referred to him. He must, therefore, assume the responsibility of whether or not the bridge is all right.
I can remember the time when there was trouble between the harbour commissioners and the Department of Railways and Canals with regard to harbour fees. Is there any difficulty now?
Yes, there is some difficulty now. I understand that it is the policy of the department to charge harbour dues in respect of the new leases that are granted.
Charge fees equal to the harbour dues?
Yes.
I am not sure that that is quite accurate.

Wharfage charges equal to
the harbour dues are charged by the commission; at least that is the information I have from the officials.
Under the new leases?

Under the new leases.
Rideau canal-Renewing swing bridge, Smith's Falls, revote, $12,000.

Application has been
before the department for a good many years for the construction of a new bridge over the Rideau at Smith's Falls. This vote is for the reconstruction of the old bridge, is it not?
This is for the reconstruction of the old bridge.
They are not building a new bridge?

Not yet.
Rideau canal-Improving banks, canal at Ottawa, $50,000.
Has my hon. friend a plan of the work to be done in the improvement of the banks of the canal at Ottawa?

The commission submitted
to me a statement of the work that should be done south of the Laurier Avenue bridge. They informed me that work amounting to

about $50,000 should be done this year and it is the intention to allow the Improvement Commission to do the work.

I know the
views of the commission upon the subject, and if this vote be for the purpose of carrying out those views, I am in favour of it. Since the driveway was built along the canal the use of pleasure boats upon the canal has greatly increased, with consequent damage to the roots of the trees, which may die in a few years unless they are protected. The plan is to have a concrete wall from the bridge at Laurier avenue southward. If that is the object of the vote, and the commission can do the work very well, then it is very much needed.
Railways and Canals-Investigations under the Inquiries Act, $2,000.

Is that for inquiries
which have taken place, or for inquiries which are expected?
That is to pay for investigations that have taken place.
That of Mr. Ferguson?

To pay Mr. Ferguson and his expenses, $1,600; E. H. Caron, $400; total, $2,000.
Railways and Canals-Branch lines-working expenses, revote, $500,000.

This vote is put in in
case you take over some branch lines, I suppose?
In case we purchase any or arrange to take them over.

My hon. friend contends that these branch lines cannot be taken over without special legislation; why does he want money to work roads that he says cannot be taken over? Our contention is that you can take them over with special legisation by making a contract and bringing it here for confirmation.
Hon. gentlemen opposite contend that they are prevented from doing that because the Senate has amended the Act. They can now take over these lines without any special Act except one confirming the contract. Is it under those conditions that the Government wants $500,000 in case it should exercise its right?

Of course we have now a Branch Lines Act, which was introduced by the hon. member for South Renfrew. Under that Act $500,000 was placed in the Estimates for the operation of any branch lines which might be taken over or leased

under the provisions of the Branch Lines Act. This is simply a revote for that purpose.
It does not say so.
It can be paid out of this.
It leaves the door open much wider. If the Government wants to take over other branch lines-
We may take over the line from Cape Tormentine. This is simply a revote.

Some days ago my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) asked the minister certain questions as to a survey party under the control of the Gov-erment working between St. Peters and the city of Sydney. Has the minister any further information with regard to that?

I told the hon. member the other day that I had received a telegram from the general manager of the Intercolonial saying that there was a survey party in that district with a view to finding out the best way of improving the grades of the Intercolonial railway. It may be done either by improving the existing line or by a diversion of the road.
Does the minister mean to say that the engineers are there with the idea of surveying the country for a line doing away with the present line between Grand Narrows and North Sydney?
They are there for the purpose of studying the whole situation and with the object of arriving at a conclusion as to what will be best for the whole district.
Have there been any negotiations between the Government and the owners of the St. Peter's road, with a view to taking over that line?
No negotiations of any kind.
Are the engineers Working on the St. Peter's end or the Sydney end of the road?
I have not that information, but will be glad to get it for my hon. friend. Of course, the chief engineer locates the survey parties.

On page 4629 of ' Hansard ' of last Friday the acting Minister of Railways is reported as follows:
Bridges are now being built across the river, or it is intended to build them.
322*
Is the minister providing for the construction of these two bridges? He says' they are now being built, but that .is an error. He also says that it is intended ti build them. Do I understand that the lederal Government will construct these bridges so that the residents on the south side of the river will be able to use the railway on the north side.

The matter is in the hands
of the general manager of the railway, and I do not know the exact position at the present time, as I have not discussed the situation with him recently. I understood from him last fall that bridges would very likely be constructed across the river that would be satisfactory to the people in that locality.

Will the Dominion Government undertake the construction of these bridges, or will they consider the matter? One of our local papers, commenting on the situation recently, said that it would be an unfair distribution of the public money if provision were not made for the construction of these bridges, that is, if the rails on the south side were to be taken up. Could not the minister provide a special vote for this special purpose of 'constructing bridges in order that the people on the south side of the river may have a connection with the north side? Without bridges it is impossible to get a vehicle across. There are no ferry facilities at all with the exception of an ordinary rowboat. If the Government are going to take up the rails on the south side of the river and take away from those people the privilege they have enjoyed for thirty or forty years, it seems to me that this Government should provide some money for the construction of bridges at that point. I know it will be contended that the local Government should do this work, but I do not think they are very flush of money at the present time, and they are already building a bridge opposite Newcastle. I think some funds should be provided for this purpose, even if it requires a special vote.

I cannot put another item in the Estimates this session. I am not sure just what arrangement the Minister of Railways made with regard to this matter, but I am under the impression that it is receiving his consideration, and I think his decision will be satisfactory to the people there.
Is it not possible to use a portion of this $500,000 for the building of these bridges?

The money could not very well be taken out of this item, which simply provides working expenses in connection with branch lines. There may be some other item in the Intercolonial Estimates that it might be taken out of, but I am not sure about that.

If the minister will simply assure me that the Dominion Government will build these bridges, I shall be satisfied to wait until another session if it is too late to put in a vote this session. I want to be able to tell the people in that section of the country that they will have a bridge connecting with the railway on the north side.

I cannot make any definite promise of that kind. The matter will have to be carefully considered by the Minister of Railways. He is going on a tour through the East .within the next month or so, and no doubt will have an opportunity of considering the whole situation.

I thought a definite
promise had been given to the people when the Minister of Railways was down there before. The people there were naturally aggrieved at having a railroad which had been in operation for some twenty-five or thirty years removed, and, as I understand it, the injustice was recognized and a statement made to the people that these bridges would be built in order to give connection with the railway on the other side of the river. It does seem, to me that unless the acting minister is prepared to tell Parliament that these bridges will be built the people down there ought not to be told that they will be built by a minister speaking in an irresponsible way outside of Parliament. They ought not to be deluded by being assured outside of this Parliament that this accommodation will be given when the acting minister is not prepared in Parliament to give the same assurance to the representatives of the people. It seems to me quite proper that this assurance should be given. It would be most unjust to take away the railway accommodation these people have enjoyed for so long, and not provide some relief

from the deplorable condition either by means of bridges or otherwise.

I do not know what the hon. Minister of Railways said to the people on his trip East, but whatever he said will be carried out. I am really not in a position to give information to the hon. member as to what he promised on that occasion. I understand that the portion of the road from which the rails were taken up had got into a very bad condition.
A great many bridges would have to be built, there was not a very great traffib on that portion of the road and the rails are being taken up. I understand .that the rails are still on the road where the mill is. The opinion I have from parties in that section of the country is that with a little bridge or two across the river they would really be better satisfied than with the road they had owing to its being impossible to operate heavy trains and heavy engines on account of the bridges. I have not seen much opposition to the present scheme.
He was more positive last week than he is now.
No, I am just as positive now that the bridges are to be built.
By whom ?
The hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) admits himself that the provincial Government is responsible for the bridges.
No.
The hon. gentleman just nods his head and says ' yes.'

What I say is that the local Government are responsible for roads and bridges ordinarily, but here is an extraordinary case. You have done away with a railway that the people have enjoyed for thirty or forty years, and it will cost a large sum of money to construct permanent bridges across the river. Under these circumstances it is the federal Government that we should look to far the construction of these bridges,

The hon. gentleman did not allow me to finish my remarks. The hon. gentleman admits that the provincial Government is responsible for roads and bridges

in New Brunswick, but he claims this is a special case.
Exactly.

Is it not reasonable that,
before final action is taken, the Minister of Railways and Canals should discuss the matter with the provincial Government and see what is advisable to be
12 noon, done, whether this Government or the provincial Government should build the bridges and where they should be located? That is the reason why it is very difficult for me to give definite information upon the matter or to arrive at a final decision.

The minister, as quoted by my hon. friend from Northumberland, stated a few days ago that bridges are now being built or would be built to accommodate the people. Had the hon. gentleman any authority from the provincial Government for the statement that they contemplated building these bridges?

I have no information from
the provincial Government.
That being so the minister must have intended to assure the House that this Government would build them. Is that not the natural inference ?

No, that is not the natural
inference.

When the hon. gentleman has no intimation from the provincial Government that they intend to build the bridges, and when he states to the House that they would be built, does it not follow that the Government intends to build them?
No, I do not see that it follows.

I remember the occasion when the Minister of Railways and Canals told the people of the locality that he proposed to take away that railway because it was, in his estimation, not a paying proposition, and that in compensation for the railway facilities he was taking away he would build a bridge, or two bridges-one for sure-across the river in order that the people might have connection between their homes and the station. When the Minister of Railways and Canals made that statement he made it positively and he conveyed the impression to the people that the Department of Railways and Canals in consideration of taking away that road would give the people their bridges
across the river. Therefore, it is the duty of the Department of Railways and Canals to assume that responsibility at once.

The department have had two years to consider this matter. It does seem to me that it is rather unfair to leave the matter over considering that the road has not been operated for nearly two years and make no provision for these bridges if the federal Government is to do the work.

Before the last general election, it being known that the late Government was committed to the policy of taking over branch lines of the Intercolonial railway, in which the people of Quebec and the Maritime provinces, and I think more especially New Brunswick, because there are a larger number there than in any other province, are interested, the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) endeavoured to strengthen his hand, not improperly, and he telegraphed to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), who was then in Prince Edward Island, and asked him for an assurance as to the policy of the Conservative party so that it might be published in order to satisfy the electorate of the province of New Brunswick. I do not know what the terms of the telegram were- probably they were of a somewhat appealing nature-we have not had them disclosed -but the answer was in effect that it was the policy of the Conservative party to take over the branch lines of the Intercolonial railway. In effect it was that it was in the interest of the country and of the Intercolonial railway that they should be taken over. That telegram was sent previous to the general election of 1911. Nothing so far has been done, and not a single branch line has been taken over by this Government, although three years have passed away. It is true that in the last session of Parliament a Bill was introduced. Hon. gentlemen will remember that it was of a most extraordinary character when it was presented to the House. It provided that the Minister of Railways and Canals might take over any railway between the Atlantic and the Pacific whether it was in any way connected with the Intercolonial or not. It was a Bill that no one on that side of the House or this could support. It was drawn up in the most slipshod way that it is possible to imagine. When the Bill was before the House the

consensus of opinion on both sides of the House was that it was desirable to provide additional legislation for the taking over of the branch 'lines. The Bill was amended so that it met the views of both sides of the House although even then it gave the Governor in Council pretty extraordinary powers. The Bill went to the Senate and the Senate amended it simply in this respect that any contract for the purchase or lease of a road should be submitted to Parliament for ratification. The opinion of the Senate, as expressed by the amendment and the reasons which were given, was that Parliament should be informed of the price at which a road was taken over and be an assenting party to it. That was not an unreasonable view for the Senate to take but those of us on this side of the House who were exceedingly anxious to see this policy carried out did not insist upon the view which the Senate entertained. I think there was a general feeling of. disappointment that the Senate had felt it to be its duty to make that amendment. But during this session there has been no effort made to promote further 'legislation, if further legislation is necessary, and the Government are simply lying back and saying they will do nothing. I do not think that is proper conduct for the Government if it is really desirous of seeing these branch lines taken over. Now then, my hon. friend comes down and asks this committee to vote $500,000 for the working expenses of branch lines. The minister ought to tell the committee whether or not it is really intended to use this vote. There is too much disposition on the part of hon. gentlemen on the Treasury benches to delude the people into believing they are going to do something when they intend to do nothing. They have a strange notion that if they can advertise in the newspapers in some way that they intend to do things, it will satisfy the people just as well as if they did them.
Like the Farmers Bank.

Yes, like their proposal with regard to the Farmers Bank, which their friends in another branch of the Legislature, who on every occasion will do whatever the leader of the Government desires they shall do, assisted most materially in defeating in the Senate.
The double-cross.

Yes, the depositors in the Farmers Bank got the double-cross. In this case the Government come down with this item of $500,000 to induce the people of New Brunswick to believe that they intend to do something or other to take over the branch lines, but the minister should tell us now whether it is intended to utilize this vote or not. Under the authority which the Government has they can take the branches, and they can use this vote for operating them, but do they intend to do so, or is the appropriation put here merely as a sort of soothing syrup to the people who are interested in these branch lines? If the minister intends to use this money to operate any of the branch lines, let him tell us so; if he does not, then let it be stricken out, for in such case it is merely a pretense. It was included in the Estimates last year, but it was included then in view of the Government intending to do something. This year it was left out of the Main Estimates and restored in the Supplementary Estimates, undoubtedly on the initiative of the minister, and such being the case he should tell us whether it is intended to begin the operation of any of these branch lines or whether it is not. I do not hesitate to say that the Government could properly utilize this amount by arranging to take over the operation of such branch lines as would be in the public interest to operate, but we should have no more humbugging .and no more deluding of the people by the insertion of this vote in the Estimates if it is not intended to expend it. Let the minister tell us now that it is intended to use this vote in a businesslike way, or, let the owners of these railways, and let the people who are interested in them, look elsewhere for their efficient operation. I for one am not disposed to allow this item to pass without objection, unless we are told whether it is bona fide intended by the minister to act upon the vote during the recess.

The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) states that during the last 'campaign the hon. member for K'ings-Albert (Mr. Fowler) had a telegram from the Prime Minister with reference to the branch lines, but he did not tell us what that telegram was.
I have given the effect of it.
The hon. gentleman said that the effect of it was tfhart; it was intended by the Government to take over some of the branch lines.
I did not say 'some'; I said the branch lines.

The hon. member knows that the Government, (through the Minister of Railways, did introduce a Bill to enable the Government to take over the 'branch lines, and he knows that under the Act of 1911 it was impossible to take over these branch lines and operate them in a satisfactory <way, without amending the law. It is true that when that Bill was introduced in this House it w.as not drafted in a satisfactory form.
The Government must be responsible for that. '
The hon. gentleman knows that when many Bills .are first introduced they are not drawn in satisfactory form, and that after discussion they are amended.
That Bill was the limit when it was introduced.

At all events the Bill was
made satisfactory to every member in this House including the hon. member for St. John, and it passed here unanimously and was sent to the Senate. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition came in the next day, and he was the only member on the other side who opposed the Bill. It went to the Senate and the Senate threw it out, thus placing the Government in the position that they were not able to take over the branch lines as they intended.
Is the minister correct in saying that the Bill was thrown out by the Senate?

It was amended in such a
way that it spoiled the Bill altogether, and the Government could no't operate under it.

Should a provision that
all contracts should be submitted for ratification to Parliament be considered as spoiling the Bill?
The hon. member knows that the amendment made by the Senate had the effect of changing-

The intentions of the
Government.
No. changing the construction of the Bill altogether.
The Government intended ignoring Parliament entirely.

Surely the hon. gentleman
will admit that when every member of the House, including the hon. gentleman himself, supported the Bill, the Government were not trying to do anything other than what was satisfactory and in the interest of the people of the Maritime provinces. Surely the Senate was not justified in so amending the Bill as to change its whole construction.

What are" you going to
do with this $500,000? Are you going to wipe out the Senate?

The hon. minister says that we have nothing on our statute-books now that will allow the Government to counteract the action of the Senate last year and to carry out their policy in regard to branch lines. If he is correct, this vote cannot be used; but he knows he is not correct, because there is provision in the laws of this country now for the taking over of branch lines. To say that the Liberal majority in the Senate was instrumental in killing the branch line policy of the Government is not giving this House a correct statement, and the minister should not make such a statement. He is on the horns of a dilemma. If he is right, it is absurd to ask for this vote. If he is wrong, he should make a correct statement to the House, and be honest enough to tell us that he is wrong. I believe that the whole alleged policy of this Government with reference to branch lines is for the purpose of bewildering, if not fooling, the people of this country.
In regard to the survey that is going on at the present time between St. Peters in the county of Richmond and Sydney in the county of Cape Breton, certain questions were asked of the minister on three or four different occasions by the,hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) and myself. When the question was first asked, the minister said that he knew absolutely nothing about such a survey. On the second occasion the right hon. leader of the Government was asked and he seemed to know nothing about the matter. Later on, when the hon. member for Richmond put the question direct to the acting minister as to what this survey party was doing in that part of the country, the acting minister said that it was with a view to improving or changing grades on the Intercolonial. The hon. min-

ister does not know anything about the situation there, or he would not make such a statement to the House. He made the statement again this morning. How can you change the grade on the Intercolonial at a point forty miles away from the Intercolonial where the survey party was working a few days ago? No negotiations have been going on for the acquisition of the St. Peter's and Point Tupper road, which is in that vicinity. I can tell the minister, from a telegram which I have just received, why the survey party is in that vicinity. There is a little council election taking place at G'oxheath to-day, and this survey party is in that district and is being worked for all it is worth in connection with that election. '
I do not think that is the case.

I have the telegram in my possession. From the answers given by the minister I am fully assured that there can be no other object in view, because to change Or improve the grades of the Intercolonial by making a survey forty miles away is absolutely absurd. If the minister knew the situation, he would realize the absurdity of his statement.
The question of branch lines has been dangled before the House and the country by this Government. The Government have apparently not been sincere in anything they have done. The acting Minister of Railways says that every member of the House agreed that the Bill in regard to branch lines was a good Bill. Does that mean that it was a good Bill? Bills have been sent to the Senate before, and amendments have been made to which this House afterwards has agreed as being good amendments. It is a childish argument to say that, because this Bill passed this House without opposition and was amended in the Senate, as I believe, to protect the public moneys of this country, the Bill was killed.
Spoiled.

It probably was spoiled. It spoiled the intention of the Government, without the approval of the representatives of the people of this country, to say: There is an election going on in the county of Restigouche, in the province of New Brunswick in a week or two, and we will take over another road in another county where there is an election in order to influence public opinion in that part of the 
country. That Bill was bad legislation, and the Senate were absolutely right in making this Parliament responsible for votes of money which might be granted towards taking over branch lines, and in not leaving the whole thing to the will of the Minister of Railways, who is after all but one member of this House. There is on the statute-books of this country to-day ample and sufficient legislation for taking over every branch line of the Intercolonial wherever it may exist.
Where is the legislation?
You do not need legis-[DOT] lation. There is written and unwritten legislation. I presume my hon. friend, who is a lawyer, is aware of that fact?
Where is the authority?

You do not need any
authority. Parliament can always take over branch lines. How did this Parliament take over the Canada Eastern? How did it take over any line that has been taken over by Parliament? '
By the Government coming to this Parliament and getting legislation.
After it was done?
That is just what I wish to see. I wish these matters to be in the hands of Parliament, and I say that the Senate were absolutely right in the manner in which they amended the Bill last year.

Of what advantage would the legislation of last year with respect to branch lines have been after the amendment made by the Senate, if it is always competent for Parliament to pass an Act to take over any single branch line? It would simply mean that Parliament could do what Parliament always can do, namely, pass an Act to do some special thing. In my opinion, the amendment of the Senate absolutely defeated the object of the Bill.

Parliament can take
over a branch line now. When I used the word ' legislation ', perhaps I did not use the proper word. This Government has the power to take over any branch line they want-
Subject to Parliament.

-Subject to ratification by Parliament. The acting Minister of Railways this morning said that we were not able to do that, because the Senate

had spoiled the Bill of last year. What was the necessity for this vote if the Government could not do it? They have done it in the past and they can do it now. I could point out to my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) various roads that the Government have taken over.

Would the Government have power to pay for a road, and could they afterwards have that power confirmed hy Parliament.
Mr. CARROLiL: Ilf they had a Governor General's warrant they could do it.

No, they could not.
Mr, CARROLL: I am not sure. They could do all the business that was necessary.
That ie exactly what the Bill of last year contemplated.

If it only contemplated that, I do not know what good it would be. It contemplated it in this way, that it handed over to the Minister of Railways power that should have been vested in this Parliament. It gave him the power to take over any indivdual road that he might decide to take over, without coming to Parliament for ratification and without being responsible to Parliament for the amount of money he might spend in connection with the matter. There ie .all the distinction in the world between the Minister of Railways going down to the province of Nova Scotia this year and negotiating with any company there for the taking over of iany lines that are feeders to the Intercolonial, making all the necessary arrangements and coming .to Parliament for ratification, in which case Parliament would know all the details of the arrangement, and this Parliament giving the Minister of Railways power to take over any railway without Parliament knowing afterwards whether the terms on which it was taken over were good or bad. My hon. friend from Cumberland and the hon. member from Prince Edward Island will see a very great distinction between these two lines of action.

Did you vote for the
Branch Lines Bill last year?
There was no vote taken.
Then you cannot criticise these terms now.

Did my hon. friend vote against every piece of legislation in this
House during the time he was in Opposition?

I cannot recollect. I
have been in the House for some years. But my point is: the -hon. gentleman cannot criticise this legislation now because he did not object in the previous session. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) supported the legislation and supported these terms.

My hon. friend is mistaken in saying that I cannot criticise because no legislation exists. What I am pointing out is that the Government had all this session to bring in legislation. The Bill brought down last session, in the estimation of the Senate, was faulty, and they amended it in such a way as to commend it to business men-not party politicians, but those who have the interest of railway enterprise- and of the public money at heart. I am going to conclude by saying that this is an absurd vote, if, as the acting Minister of Railways has told us, the Government have no power to take over roads, and that the unfortunate Senate-which helped out the Government so much last night in their difficulties with the Farmers Bank-made such a grievous mistake last year that nothing could be done to take over the branch lines of the Intercolonial railway. Why, the senator from Cumberland, an appointee of the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden), voted against it.

We are not talking about
the Farmers Bank.

I know it is not savory to the hon. member for Cumberland and to other hon. members opposite to know what happened in the Senate last night. I can only, in a humble way, voice the sentiments of the hon. member for St. John and say that the policy of this Government with reference to branch lines is not one which commends itself either to the House or the country. They have no policy. They are not endeavouring, and do not intend, to do anything in regard to branch lines. Their intention was to lead the people to think that the branch lines were to be acquired, and they have told the people that the Senate killed the Bill, when they have now full power to take over the branch lines.

It seems to me the issue is a very clear-cut one. If the hon. gentleman does not believe that the Government intends to acquire the branch lines, he

will be perfectly justified in voting against this measure.
Does the hon. gentleman know what Bill we are passing?
This item.

It seems to me unfortunate that in a Parliament, where apparently every member of this House is favourable to taking over the branch lines, some means could not be devised which would enable that thing to be done. Why *should Parliament declare itself to be absolutely helpless? This difficulty is that this House, led by this Government, does not seem to be willing to recognize that the Senate is an essential branch of the constitution and that the Senate has a perfect right to amend Bills in a way which commends itself to their judgment or to reject them. They do that frequently. They did it in regard to the Farmers Bank Bill; they did it in reference to the Bank Act and the Post Office Act; they do it constantly in reference to important matters.
They might do it too in reference to redistribution.

But the Government,
simply because the Senate made an amendment, seems to be in a state of sulks in regard to this Branch Lines Bill. They say, because the Senate may interfere with our legislation, we are not going to attempt tc legislate for what we believe to be in the public interest, but we will meet the matter' by putting in a vote for meeting expenses, and thereby we will induce the people to believe that we intended to do something, if it had not been for this wicked Senate. I would like to point out to the minister what was done at the last session so that we may see whether, after all, it wa? reasonable, and whether the action of the Senate does not open up a way by which this matter could be easily accomplished. As the Bill passed the House last year it gave authority to the Minister of Railways to construct any new lines to the extent of twenty-five miles. The Senate did not interfere with that, and allowed that power to remain in the Bill just as it was. The Bill provided for the leasing or purchase of any branch line not exceeding two hundred miles in length. The Bill did not provide an appropriation for the purpose, and I doubt very much if the Government would feel it to be within its power, even if the Bill had passed just as it went

through the House, to actually pay for the road until it had an amount put in the Estimates and voted by Parliament. What did the Senate do ? In the Bill as it passed the House it was provided that any agreement for lease or purchase should be laid on the table of the House within fifteen days after the opening of the session. The only amendment the Senate made was to put in the words ' for ratification.' Now, when the Government would come down with an item in the Estimates of so much money to pay for the branch lines which have been acquired, surely that would be a ratification. Therefore, the Government, by not actually providing that the money might be paid over in the Bill which passed through the House, recognized the propriety of the Senate doing exactly what it did. In the ordinary course the agreement would be laid upon the table, in accordance with the Senate amendment, and if there was an item in the Estimates to pay for the road which was acquired that would be a ratification by Parliament. Surely, if in the judgment of the Senate, that was the proper thing to do, in view of what is the ordinary practice, that was not taking such a course as to offend this high and mighty Government and make them say that they will withdraw into their shells and do absolutely nothing. If they would recognize that the Senate is an essential and important branch of the constitution and introduce a Bill at this session framed along reasonable and fair lines, I have no reason to doubt but that it would meet with the unanimous approval of this House, and that the Senate, in accordance with the view they expressed last session, would be entirely willing to pass it through. All the Senate asked for and intended to ask for, in my judgment, was that when the time came for paying the money, before it was actually paid over there should be an appropriation by Parliament. Suppose there was authority given to build a bridge, before the money would be paid the item would appear in the Supply Bill in the ordinary way, and that would be the case where there was the purchase of a railway. What I complain of is, that the acting Minister of Railways cannot tell us what it is intended to do with this item of $500,000 or whether it is intended to do anything. I say that is insulting Parliament, and the Minister of Railways must not think that he is above Parliament. Parliament controls the money of this country acting as trustees for the people, and before Parliament passes an appropriation of half a million dollars it

has a right to be informed by the acting minister as to whether it is intended to use that money and how it is intended to use it. I say that putting this item in is simply making a pretense to the people of the Maritime provinces and of Quebec that the minister intends to do something, while at the same time the acting minister tells us in effect that he has no intention of doing anything, because, forsooth, the Senate chose to amend the Bill of last session. I do put it to the minister in all seriousness and sincerity, as one who honestly believes that it would be in the public interest to have such branch lines taken over, that he ought to be able to tell us whether or not he intends to use this money to operate any branch lines. If he satisfies this committee that he does intend to do so, we will cheerfully pass the item. If he does not, he should not ask Parliament for a large appropriation which he does not intend to use, which he has no thought of using, and which he believes he cannot use. Surely in doing this he is not treating Parliament with the respect to which the representatives of the people are entitled.

I should not like the hon. member to think that in placing in the Estimates the item we are now discussing, I intended to treat him or any other member of the House with disrespect. The item was put in with the intention of spending the amount if the Government finds it necessary to do so. The hon. member knows that in 1910 the Branch Lines Act was passed, and that in 1911 the then Minister of Railways and Canals had to introduce an amendment to that Act for the reason that under the statute as it stood he could not take over branch lines. That is evidence that the Act was not workable in so far as the taking over of the branch lines in the lower provinces is concerned. The hon. member now admits that the first thing this Government did was to try to remedy that difficulty by introducing a new Act. It is true that the Act as first introduced was not satisfactory and was withdrawn, but a new Act was passed that was satisfactory to every member of the House. The hon. member says that the only change the Senate made was the insertion of the two words ' for ratification.' To anyone who did not have the Bill before him or who did not understand the situation, that would look like a fair amendment. But the hon. member knows that after the Bill had been discussed in
the House by the hon. member for the city of St. John, by the hon. member for South Renfrew, and toy every member on the other side of the House, who all agreed to the Bill as being perfectly satisfactory, the right hon. leader of the Opposition objected when it came to the third reading. The Bill, however, went through, and the Senate, in accordance with the wishes of the right hon. leader of the Opposition, put in two words which -changed the whole meaning of the Bill.
How did they change the meaning?

The Bill read this way:
Provided, however, that a copy of every such lease or contract of purchase shall he laid before Parliament within one month after the execution thereof, if Parliament is then sitting, or, if Parliament is not then sitting, within ten days after the opening of the next session thereafter.
They changed it to read this way:
Provided, however, that such lease or contract of purchase shall he laid before Parliament for ratification.
In this way they put the Bill back to the 3ame position in which the law was in 1910, making it of no effect. The whole question is: What are we going to do with the money iprovided in this -appropriation? As I understand the law of 1910, if a road is equal to the etandard of the Intercolonial railway, it may toe taken over and operated until Parliament meets. We may use a portion of that money for working expenses until such time. There is a portion of road between Sackville and [DOT] Cape Tormentine which we may have to take over, in connection with the car ferry, and we may require the amount for -that. This item of $500,000 has been in the Estimates for some time; we are just revoting that amount, -and if it becomes absolutely necessary to use it f-or some purpose of that kind, we shall have the money to pay working expenses.

At last the minister
says that he is of the opinion that under the legislation of 1910, in the case of a road which comes up to the standard and is certified by the chief engineer as being suitable for operation as part of the Intercolonial system, there is the power to lease and that this money may be used for operating pending the obtaining of further authority from Parliament. If the minister says seriously that it is intended to use

this appropriation for that purpose, I have no further objection to the item.

As the minister knows,
the new railway from New Carlisle to Gaspe is in first-class condition, equal to the Intercolonial railway. Unfortunately, a part of the road from New Carlisle to Mata-pedia is not in good condition. Last year the minister sent a commissioner down to the county of Bonaventure to hold meetings in the various parishes of the county for the purpose of taking up claims against those railways. The commissioner has reported to the Governor in Council that $82,000 should be paid in satisfaction of those claims. The acting Minister of Kail-ways and Canals referred that report to the Justice Department and the Justice Department has decided that the commissioner exceeded his powers; that he went far beyond the powers conferred upon him by his appointment and reported upon claims with which he had no business to deal. The people down there want to know whether they have been fooled again or whether any part of the money for the payment of their claims is to come out of this vote.

The matter has been submitted to the Justice Department, and, not having had a final report from the Justice Department as to what action should be taken, I am not able to give the hon. member any information.

The minister is aware that Mr. Newcombe has submitted his report, . and it has been brought down to the House in a return. Mr. Newcombe declares that there is no liability whatever on the part of the Government or of Parliament in the matter of these claims; that the sole liability rests with the Quebec Oriental railway, which acquired the Atlantic and Lake Superior railway under an Act of Parliament passed some eight, years ago. I managed to introduce into that Act an amendment providing that when the Quebec Oriental railway acquired this road it would become liable for claims for labour, board and material. Mr. Newcombe declares that the sole liability of Parliament towards the people of Bonaventure, who built this railway, is that of the Quebec Oriental Tailway. I should like to know whether the Government intends going beyond the report of the Deputy Minister of Justice and paying the other claims which have been reported upon by the commissioner.
 '

The matter is now before
the Justice Department for opinion upon the question as to whether we should take any further action in the matter or as to whether the parties themselves should proceed against the railway. We are awaiting advice from the department along that line.

At Matapedia a new gravitation water service has been introduced. A hydrant has been placed between the station and the Kestigouche club for the protection of the station and the freight shed. I would like to remind the minister that this small village which is huddled close to the station has been destroyed by fire twice within the last ten years. Should another fire break out and the wind be in a certain direction, the village would again be wiped out because the people could not cope with the fire with the appliances they now have. I would like to ask the minister if it would not be possible to have a long hose kept in the station so that in case of fire it could be used to protect the adjoining premises as well as the Intercolonial Tailway. I understand the minister intends to enlarge the freight shed, and this will bring it quite close to the village. The minister knows that the buildings are all in a bunch and lying in the bottom of a valley, and if fire were to break out under present conditions nothing could save the Kestigouche Club house and the other buildings.
There is another matter which I would like to draw to the minister's attention. As you emerge from the snow-shed you come to one of the most dangerous crossings on the Intercolonial railway. When trains are stalled people are often held up for an hour at a time. The proposal has been made by some people that a subway should be built underneath the crossing. Has any report been made in regard to that?

So far as better fire protection in Matapedia is concerned, I suppose the Intercolonial railway have just sufficient hose at present to protect their own property; but it is certainly a reasonable request that a few more hundred feet should be provided for the protection of the whole village. I have always thought it good policy to have a double quantity of hose in case of breakage. I will give instructions to the general manager to order a sufficient quantity of hose to protect the whole village. In regard to the other matter, there

is no item in the Estimates for a subway at Matapedia. This is the first time the matter has been brought to my attention, and I am unable to say whether a report has been made. I will make inquiries, and if we have a report in the department I shall be glad to mail it to the hon. member.

If no report has been
made, the minister might have the matter looked into, because Matapedia is one of the most important stations in that district. The traffic is very important and constantly growing.
If there is no report in the department I will write the general manager to have a report made so that it will be available at the next session of Parliament.

I would like to point out to the minister, although this is a matter under the control of the Minister of Public Works, that the approach to the interprovincial bridge at Matapedia has never been completed. Perhaps the minister will ask his officials to look into that.

I just wish to say a
word or two in reference to what my hon. friend has said about the future purchase of the Gaspe railway-the railway running from Matapedia to Gaspe basin-part of which is in good condition and part of which is not. I discussed this matter in the House some time ago, and I understood that my right hon. friend was going to consider the matter of the Government acquiring this branch line. I simply want to remind him that forty years ago it was contemplated to be a branch line of the Intercolonial and the first twenty miles were built, but the idea was abandoned and now the line is owned by a private concern. I think the Government under the present conditions could acquire the road on very fair terms, and I hope my hon. friend will give this matter his earnest consideration because the people of the whole peninsula are eagerly looking forward to the day when the Government will operate the read.

I have not forgotten the
request of the hon. member and will give it my consideration.

There is a very bad crossing at Sylvan valley, a short distance west of Antigonish station. I merely mention the name because the
facts are all in the office of the department. Several persons have been killed there, and certainly an overhead bridge should be built at that point. A new station should also be built at South river. It was virtually decided on by the late Government, but nothing has been done in that direction by the present Government. Repairs are also badly needed to the station at Tra-cadie. The health inspector some time ago reported against the insanitary condition of the station, which is in a very bad condition. This station should be put in proper shape and the grounds attended to. As I do not want to delay the Estimates, I merely mention the places referred to. The facts in each case are in the possession of the department already.
I will draw the attention of the general manager of the Intercolonial railway to the statements made by my hon. friend.

In. regard to the matter
to which I referred some time ago, I understood the minister to say that he was willing to have a bridge built from the south to the north side of the river. I believe the rule is for the Government to pay for approaches from the King's highway to a station, and I think this bridge would come under that policy. I would like to ask the minister if that is the case?

The Minister of Railways
will consider it when he is down there this summer.
Railways and Canals-To provide car ferry, construct terminals and necessary connections- Refund of security deposited by the Halifax Dredging Company, Limited, on tender for car ferry terminals at Carleton Point, P.E.I., $39,975.

This is a refund to the
Halifax Dredging Company, Limited. This company tendered for work on Prince Edward Island with the 'expectation o'f being able to use the stone on Prince Edward Island, but they afterwards found that it was not suitable for the purpose, and refused to go on with the contract.
Who was in the company?

I really do not know. The
junior member for Halifax and the Prime Minister have both urged that this claim be paid.
At one o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

Intercolonial railway, $1,887,100.

I desire to bring to the notice of the hon. acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) the dismissal of a man in my county who, I think, was not properly dismissed. A man of the name of Cameron, a railway conductor, was up for trial some time in the month of August, 1913, charged with drinking, and a brakeman named Brydon was called as a witness to prove that he had been drinking. In the course of his examination Brydon was asked: ' Do you drink yourself.' Brydon had admitted that he had taken a drink at his home at breakfast time, about six o'clock in the morning, and before he had gone on duty. With no other evidence against Brydon than that, he was dismissed. This investigation took place on the 18tli August, 1913, and on the first day of September, 1913, a new regulation came into force. This regulation started every man on the road with a clean sheet. I will not trouble the minister by reading it. It is ' Canadian Government Railways, Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island railway, regulation, circular No. 5,' dated the 1st September, 1913, and signed ' F. P. Gutelius, general manager.' This is the regulation that started the demerit marks. There were no demerit marks against anybody on the 1st September, 1913; everybody, as I say, was started with a clean sheet. Brydon, who now lives in Sydney, but who formerly lived in my county, started out with a clean sheet on the 1st September, and on the 27th October, without ever being apprised that there were any demerit marks against him, he received this notification from Mr. L. S. Brown, the superintendent of that division of the road:
' New Glasgow,
Monday, October 27, 1913.
Mr. D. J. Brydon,
Brakeman, Intercolonial railway,
Sydney, C.B.
Dear Sir,-This is to notify you that you are assessed for sixty demerit marks and your services dispensed with at once for using intoxicating liquor before going on duty at Sydney on the morning of the 18th of August last. You will please hand over to chief des-patcher Dunne any property you may have belonging to the railway.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) L. S. Brown.
I submit that this is pretty hard treatment. Here is a man who had stated, before this regulation came into force, that he had taken a drink of liquor before going on duty, and how, after this regulation is

introduced, he is told that the demerit marks were placed against him because he had taken a drink on the 18th August, although he had started out without the slightest stain on his character as a railway man on the 1st September. I am sure that the hon. acting minister is logician enough to see that it is absolutely absurd to go back into this month of August, collect these demerit marks and carry them into the operation of this new rule, which, on September 1, started this man off with a clean sheet. Mr. Brydon had a great many friends, and there was a petition sent to the department, signed by a great many leading Conservatives of the place, asking that a further investigation be held and that this man be given a fair show. I find that the petition is signed by Mr. W. G. Egan, president of the Liberal Conservative Association of Cape Breton, James Maddin, ex-Member of Parliament, who was a member of this House for a great many years, and a large number of the leading members of the party to which the hon. minister belongs. Brydon, having ibeen on the road for ten or fifteen years and having become accustomed to this kind of work, at his time of life is not very well fitted for hard work outside of the work to which he has been trained. I hope that the minister, particularly in view of this strong petition coming from leading men such as those I have named, will inquire further into the treatment meted out to this man and do for him whatever he thinks ought to be done in view of the circumstances.
If the minister will read the regulation of the 1st of September he will see that the crime in connection with liquor is to be under the influence of liquor while off duty or to take liquor while on duty. This subjects a man to dismissal, but the offence as presented by Mr. Brown in his notification was simply that this man had taken a drink of liquor before he had gone on duty on the 18th of August, 1913. I submit that does not come within the rule, because there is not a particle of evidence that he was intoxicated, and there is no evidence that he took a drink while he was on duty. The evidence is all the other way. That is all I have to say on that point.
I asked the minister some days ago for some information about a payment of something in the vicinity of $4,000 by the Intercolonial railway to my friend Mr. H. F. McDougall, a gentleman who was at

one time a member of this House, and a gentleman against whom I have nothing to say. I simply say that if Mr. McDougall thinks this Government is legitimate prey, and that he has as much right to get money from them as anybody else, and if they have money to give for which they have no justification, I suppose he might as well come and get some of- it as other people.
I want to know from the minister upon what ground this money was paid. I want it distinctly understood that I am making no particular charge against Mr. McDougall, because if he thought he could get easy money here he had a right to come and look for it. Mr. McDougall sells sand and gravel, particularly to the steel works in Sydney. He built a siding somewhere in the vicinity of Grand Narrows to a sand beach and it was built so badly that the ordinary engines of the Intercolonial could not go on the siding without breaking through. Mr. McDougall was told that if he was to receive the services of the road it would toe on a special agreement that had to get a light engine and pay a special rate which was agreed upon -as $35 for each trip of the engine and crew. The engine came a distance of seventy-five miles from Sydney to Grand Narrows, that is, the round trip, whenever occasion was required to take Mr. McDougall's cars from the siding to Sydney. That went on for many years; tout as soon as this Government came into power Mr. McDougall -made a claim against the Intercolonial railway for over $6,000 for this extra charge for. the use of this engine. Every officer of the road was against the payment of this claim. Mr. Brady, t)he general superintendent, was dead against it, Mr. Pottinger was against it, and Mr. Campbell the chairman of the board and the deputy minister was receiving letters from these parties and trying to reconcile the advice he was receiving from his officers with evidently what the minister wanted to do. At last they appointed a commission to inquire into the matter, and they agreed they would abide by the finding of Mr. J. B. T. Caron, who was the legal adviser of the Intercolonial Bailway Board. Mr. Caron went to Sydney and took sworn evidence from every man who 'had anything to do with the hiring of the train and the hauling of the sand, and Mr. McDougall was given every opportunity of putting his evidence before him. The report of Mr. Caron consists of five typewritten pages, and is dated the 5th of June, 1912, and (he reports to the department that Mr. McDougall has
not the first shadow of a claim to compensation.
Mr. Caron says that Mr. McDougall was treated precisely like every other man who was doing business with the road, and that he had a well-defined agreement for the use of the engine and crew and that he deserved nothing. In face of that report the Minister of Bailways got an Order in Council through directing that about half this money should be paid. I submit that there was no justification for this. What was the good o'f appointing a commissioner if it .was not the intention of the Government to stand by his finding, which was [DOT] clear-cut and explicit. Mr. Caron reported that there was no money due to Mr. McDougall, and yet in the teeth of that we find the Government paying this money without getting it voted by the House, on the pretext that it is for legal expense. I protest against the paying-out of the money of the people in this way. If the Government has presents to give to old friends I am fully content that Mr. McDougall should get his share, but if moneys are to be paid out on any kind of just principle, I would like to know on what principle this money was paid out.
There is another matter to which I wish to call the attention of the minister. The Intercolonial is now operating the new section of the road1, between George's Biver, Sydney Mines, and North Sydney, and I understand that there are no station agents at Florence and Little Bras d'Or which are important points, and at which a good deal of business is done. I would ask the minister to see that the road is manned in such a way that those who do business with it shall be given every convenience and facility.
1 am also informed that, where this extension of the line is going through the town of North Sydney, it is taking a very zigzag, irregular course, and that the width of the right of way is not by any means uniform, the narrowing and widening being done for the purpose of avoiding the trouble of taking property that might be regarded as expensive. In going through a town, a road can do a good deal of damage at best; but it is certainly desirable that the width of the right of way should be uniform, and I think that the damage would be lessened by making the whole road of the same width. In going through this town, the road crosses at least three streets; and so far as I know, it is intended that the road shall cross- them at dead level. In the busiest parts of the town it is very

dangerous to cross streets on the level, and I trust the minister will see that overhead crossings are put particularly at the busiest streets. I am sure it was decided under the former Administration to put an overhead crossing in the town of Florence where the railroad crosses the busiest part of the town, and it was also decided to put an overhead crossing where the railroad crosses the highway right at the end of the bridge at Little Bras D'Or. It was thought by Mr. Brady that the proper and only safe way was to make an overhead crossing .there, and that it was not a difficult thing to do. These are the principal matters that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister.
So far as the discussion that has taken place this morning in regard to branch lines is concerned, I am not going to discuss that question now. The Government know where I stand upon that question, and I trust that before long something will be done to accommodate the people of Victoria in particular, who have no railway accommodation at all. If the minister is able to give satisfactory replies in regard to these matters, I do not think I shall bother him again on his Estimates.

In regard to the Ibrakeman
on the Intercolonial who has been dismissed, I must admit that I am not fully aware of the whole facts, not having had them before me up to the present time; but it is quite evident from the statements made by the hon. member that this man has been dismissed for having taken liquor. Every one will agree that, if any official of a railway, and especially a conductor or brakeman or engine driver, is found guilty of an offence of that kind, he should be relieved at once of his position, because life is in danger. In this case, it appears, however, that the offence was prior to an order that had gone into effect in regard to drinking. In cases of this kind on the railway, I understand that an investigation is held by the officials of the railway; and, if the results of the investigation are not satisfactory to the employee, the latter may appeal to the Trainmen's Association to which he belongs to look into the case, and they would take the matter up if they found that the employee had been unjustly dealt with. I will, however, look into this man's case again; and, if there is anything that can be done for him, I am sure the Minister of Railways will have no hesita-

tion in reconsidering the matter of the facts justify such action. It appears to me, however, that his case must be weak, because the Trainmen's Association usually take up a case when any official has been found guilty of some act and has been dismissed.
With reference to the case of Mr. H. F. McDougall, the facts are practically as stated by the hon. member. A refund was made to Mr. McDougall. It is true, it was charged up at the time to legal expenses. The item was paid through that vote, and was immediately afterwards transferred to the proper vote of the Intercolonial at Moncton. It does not follow from the fact that this refund was placed in the item of legal expenses that Mr. McDougall was paid for legal expenses. The hon. member stated that a commissioner was appointed, namely, Mr. J. B. T. Caron, and that he reported against this case. As I understand it, Mr. Caron was one of the commission appointed for the management of the Intercolonial; and he looked after the claims made against that railway. An appeal was taken from the decision of Mr. Caron to Mr. Cochrane, Minister of Railways and Canals.
