Mr. Cochrane and the officials of his department went into the case again, with the result that they found Mr. McDougall had been charged $35 a day for a special engine to draw the freight on this line of railway; and that he had also been charged the full freight charges, so that he was paying for the engine and the freight charges as well. After going into the matter thoroughly, it was reported to Mr. Cochrane by the officials of the department that, in their opinion, Mr. McDougall had been overcharged. Accordingly Mr. Cochrane and his officials decided that- a portion of the amount for the freight should be refunded to Mr. McDougall. They retained the amount for the use of the engine and a portion of the amount for the freight; and in that way the matter was settled, and the Order in Council as recommended by Mr. Cochrane passed.
Who made the contract with Mr. McDougall for the use of the engine?

Mr. Brady, the Superintendent of the Intercolonial railway. It is a very usual thing for any person who has a claim against any department, if he feels that his claim is justifiable, to appeal to the deputy minister and the head of the department for their further consideration and decision.

That has been the custom in every department for very many years. This is a case in which an appeal of that kind1 was made to the minister with the result that he confirmed Mr. Caron's decision to a certain extent; in other words, he gave about half of what was claimed to Mr. McDougall. So far as I can understand the matter from the Order in Council, I do not think that the decision of the minister was unreasonable. If Mr. McDougall was paying $35 a day for an engine to draw his oars, and paid the full freight in addition, it really seems to me rather exorbitant, and that the minister was justified in refunding to him a portion of the freight so Maimed.
With reference to the line in Victoria, as I understand the situation-of course, the hon. member understands it much better than I do, for I have never been in that section-the original line runs from George's River to Sydney, but the grade was very heavy and a diversion was made from George's River to North Sydney; and now the line is being built from North Sydney to Leitoh's creek in order to make that connection. That work is under contract and is toeing proceeded with as fast as possible. The hon. member complains that the railway company is making the right of way in some.places a little narrower than usual in order to save expense, whereas he thinks the railway should take all the property and keep the right of way a proper width. I have not heard of that complaint before. I agree with the hon. member that the railway should be kept a uniform width, and I think that has been the custom not only on the Intercolonial railway but on all railways. But there are cases where it may be advisable, on account of valuable property, to take not the whole property, but just the width that would be necessary to run the trains. Perhaps at this section, there may be something of that kind. I can only make inquiries of the general manager and see what the situation is, and learn why he is deviating from the policy of having the right of way a uniform width.
Then there is the other complaint, that the railway has been completed for several months and that there are no agents at the stations to accommodate the public and to receive freight, etc. As I understand it, that road is really not in full operation yet; we have not put on a regular service.

I understand that all
the freights go around that way.

That may possibly be; but
I understand that they are really not giving passenger and freight services yet. But the placing of a few agents along the road for a short distance is not a serious matter.

They are needed in
only two places.

I cannot see. any objection
to that. The cost would be small, and unless the train service is very limited I see no reason why it should not be done. I will take the matter up immediately with the general manager, and find out why agents are not there, with a view to having them placed there at once.

It is a serious matter for me to have brought up this matter of the payment of the money to Mr. McDougall, but I want very briefly to justify the position I have taken by reading the following letter from the general superintendent, Mr. Brady:
Moncton, N.B., February 13, 1912.
A. W. Campbell, Esq., C.E.,
Chairman, Government Railway managing Board,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-Replying to your communication of the 5th instant, referring to mine of the 2nd relative to H. F. McDougall's application for refund, am returning you herewith the documents you sent me.
Replying to the portion of Mr. McDougall's letter which is underlined: No application was received from him for any siding except for one at Christmas island, in 1910, when he was informed we would put it in at his expense under the usual agreement.
We would consider requests at any time on the above basis.
Replying to the questions on the statement attached as follows:
Answer to question 1:	The rate of $35 per
day, in addition to the freight charges, was quoted because it is fair rate.
It was distinctly understood at that time that the $35 was to be separate and apart from the freight charges.
Trainmen have to be paid, for 10 hours for any length of time less than that, and engine-men have to be paid for 10 hours if out over 5 hours. The distance return trip is 79 miles.
The engine rate was imposed because, had the siding been in such condition that we could have put our standard road engines on to it, we could have handled the product at no expense over and above the cost of haulage.
See Minute No. 1352 reading as follows: H. F. McDougall of Sydney, writes re charge of $35 per day for the use of which we make of a locomotive on his siding outside of Sydney, and further asks that we furnish him with a number of rails to extend this siding. Question No. 2 :	No such thing has ever occurred to my knowledge. Rule No. 28 ' general instructions to agents and contractors ' governs such cases and is not departed from.
This case is not exactly similar to the case in the rule but amounts to the same thing so far as expense to the railway is concerned.
Then, he has questions here that I have not got:

No similar service is given to any with no extra charge for the engine to my knowledge.
Question No. 4 :	The rate of $3 per hour is

General Superintendent.
The whole case has been gone into by the general superintendent, and he returned it June 4. If there aTe officers in the minister's department who can be frightened into changing their rulings, and giving a different verdict altogether within a few hours, it is inexplicable to me, but that is what was done.
Mr. BOU'LAY: I want to .say a few words about the question of branch lines on the Intercolonial railway before the subject is concluded. I heard several members on the other side express the opinion that it will be detrimental to the interest, not only of the Intercolonial railway, but of the whole country, if these branches that are paying expenses are not bought as soon as possible. I will mention the Baie des Chaleurs railway, the Caraquet railway and the International railway, I am particularly familiar with the conditions respecting the International railway. This is a short road, but a great deal of traffic is carried upon it, and if it were a branch of the Intercolonial, I think it would pay three or four times the expenses of its management. Many people of my county do business along that railway and they are greatly inconvenienced by the fact that it i3 a private road and that there is no connection at all with the Intercolonial. If we want to make a trip of 125 miles on that road, it takes us forty or forty-eight hours to do so. If it were the property of the Intercolonial railway, surely the same trip could be made in twelve hours. Until the road is made a branch of the Intercolo-

nial, I hope that the management of the Government railways will make an arrangement with the owners of the road with a view to connecting with the Intercolonial at one point at least, so as to enable us to avoid staying overnight in Campbellton every time we go down the line. If the Government makes up its mind to lease any railway, I think this should be the first one to be leased, because it is one of the most important lines in that district. It is used by many passengers and a lot of lumber and general freight is carried over the road.
I presume the minister did not clearly understand what I said in French the other day, and I may be permitted to repeat my remarks in English. I complained that we did not have our fair share of patronage on the Intercolonial railway, particularly in connection with the sleeping and dining car service. There are twenty-six conductors on the sleeping cars, and only four are taken from the province of Quebec. If the minister would drop a line to the manager of this branch, Mr. Archibald, I think he would be willing to give to the province of Quebec in this respect the justice which it deserves. Now is the time to put new men on; I think he should take eight or nine from the province of Quebec in order to give us fair play. With respect to the dining car service, it would be a very easy matter to satisfy the people of the province of Quebec. The dining cars are left off at Ste. Flavie on every triip. When an express train goes down from Montreal in the morning, the dining cars are taken off at Ste. Flavie and left there until the next morning. It would be just as well to run the dining cars from Montreal to St. Flavie. It would mean the same amount of shunting and movement of trains, would mean no additional expense and would give the province of Quebec a chance to furnish conductors, cooks and others who are employed on these cars.

I am thankful to the
hon. member for having come to my assistance in the matter of the Caraquet railway. It has been my duty every session for a number of years to call the attention of the Government to the conditions affecting that line. It is certainly one of the most important branches of the Intercolonial in the province of New Brunswick, and I hope that the voice of the hon. member for

Rimouski will have some influence upon the Government and particularly upon the Department of Railways and Canals, and that his desire will be fulfilled within a short time.
What rolling stock does the minister intend to buy?

That $1,000,000 is really a
book-keeping item. I think that for some little time for the purchase of rolling stock there has been an amount paid over and above the vote, and the amount has reached such a sum that it is necessary to put in a special item to cover it. I think the Finance Department advances money for the purchase of rolling stock.
Has the minister any plans for new rolling stock this year?

Last year we purchased 600 freight cars and about 25 engines; we are not purchasing very much rolling stock this year. We are providing twelve steel sleeping cars, six suburban cars, one 120-ton wrecking crane and one scale test car. I remember that the hon. member for the city of St. John was complaining very much about suburban cars, and I found the same condition at Halifax. I put in the Estimates, therefore, an amount to provide for the purchase of three suburban cars for St. John and three for Halifax. With the amount provided .in the Main Estimates, this is all we will require for rolling stock this year.

The present financial conditions are felt so much by the railways that most of them have stopped giving orders to the places where railway stock is manufactured. If the Government really require cars at the present time, I would suppose that they could make very favourable contracts with the parties who are engaged in that business.
Some orders have been given which will be paid out of this vote. We are giving orders for all that we require; in fact, for more than we require.
How many freight cars does the department require this year ?

We do not require any this year. As I have said, the Government last fall ordered 600 freight cars, and no additional cars are required during the present year. These 600 will be coming in for this year's use.

Towards the construction of a railway to connect Montreal with the National Transcontinental railway, $1,000,000.
What is this $1,000,000 for ? Is the Government going to build a road ? If so, where, and how much is it going to cost ?

I am afraid that I cannot answer the hon. gentleman's three questions very fully; but I can say that when the Transcontinental railway was being constructed from Winnipeg to Moncton, no connection was provided between the Transcontinental and the city of Montreal other than that of coming down by Cochrane. It has been felt by the people of Montreal, and indeed by the Government, that a connection should be made between Montreal and the Transcontinental, and the Government have decided to build this connection themselves as part of the Transcontinental system.
Has any contract been made with the Grand Trunk Pacific to operate that section?
Nothing has been done yet in that direction.
How much will it cost?

We cannot have an estimate until after the surveys and plans have been made by our engineers. We are asking for $1,000,000 for the purpose of making the surveys and plans, and if the cost is not unreasonable, we shall have something left with which to start the work.

The Government of the province of Quebec has taken a very deep interest in that branch line. As my hon. friend is aware, the Government of the province of Quebec has subsidized a railway to be built from Bell River to some point	on James bay.	That	company	hashad	surveys made,	and	I think	hasselected its terminus on James bay. During the last five or six years the Government	of the province of4 p.m. Quebec,	and	especially	the
Department of Colonization, has received some very interesting reports concerning that section of the country. The soil is fertile and well adapted to cultivation. In fact, something like twenty townships have already been surveyed, and not more than a month or so ago a number of settlers from the old parishes went up to that part of the country, on the first train to run from Harvey Junction to some point on the National Transcontinental

railway, for the purpose of selecting homesteads.
There was a special train load of them.

Besides the question of colonization and settlement, for which, as my hon. friend knows, the French Canadians are peculiarly fitted, the Government of the province of Quebec is under the impression that in the years to come when the Hudson Bay railway is built, tapping as it will the rich and fertile wheat belt of the Northwest, and when the Hudson Bay strait is closed as it is for about seven months in the year, the grain can be carried from Port Nelson or Fort Churchill across Hudson bay, which is open practically all the year round, to the James bay terminus of the Quebec railway, in the northern portion of Quebec, thence to Bell river, and from there over the Government road to Montreal, Quebec, St. John or Halifax as the case may 'be. So I think the plan of the Government is a very laudable one, and will be very much appreciated by the people of the province of Quebec, and especially by the people of Montreal. I do not suppose that either Government ever contemplated that a great Transcontinental would be built without going to a big city like Montreal, which is the commercial metropolis of Canada. This connection will not only develop Montreal but all the ports of Canada. I understand that the company which has signed a contract with the Quebec Railway Department for the construction of a road between Bell river and James bay has already completed its surveys from the Transcontinental to Montreal, that they have gone to very great expense and are practically on the eve of starting the work, but I do not know just what has been done. I understand that the Government subsidized that line. At all events, the company has gone to great expense in surveying that section of the country, and perhaps the Government could utilize those surveys which were made by very eminent and practical engineers, and without rushing the work begin construction at the earliest opportunity. I believe that this section between Montreal and the National Transcontinental will be of the greatest benefit not only to Montreal and the province of Quebec but to the East generally, and to the West also. I therefore hope that the minister will consider the possibility of utilizing the surveys that were made by this company, as that would obviate the delay of two or three years in the construction of 
this road which would elapse if the Government undertook to survey this section themselves.

That your petitioners would most respectfully present the claim of the city of Woodstock for free mail delivery both from the amount of business transacted and the earnings of the office. This city is the home of a: number of large manufacturing establishments, as well as the centre of one of the best farming districts in Canada. The population of the city, including the contiguous territory, served by the Woodstock post office, is about 12,000.
We would direct attention to the subjoined list of fourteen places in Canada which have free mail delivery, but the revenue from which in 1912 was lower than that of the Woodstock office.
Your petitioners therefore pray that the department may be pleased to direct that the city of Woodstock may be granted the benefit of free mail delivery. And your petitioners as in duty bound will ever pray.
There is also a letter from the board of trade along the same line. On March 13 I put to the Postmaster General the following questions:

Niagara Falls: On the 30th May, 1911, under the late Government, when the population was less than 12,000, and the revenue a little less than $20,000. It is presumed that this was done for political reasons.

Fredericton:	Service established 7 th May,

St. Hyacinthe:	Service established 29th
August, 1907, under the late Government, presumably for political purposes.
The population of St. Hyacinthe was 9,500, and the villages of St. Joseph de Hyacinthe and La Providence, both of which were in the area to which the letter carrier service was given, had a population of 1,500 and 1,000 respectively, making the total 12,000.
The revenue of St. Hyacinthe was $10,799.91 and that of St. Joseph de Hyacinthe $246.80, making a total of $11,146.71. (There was no post office in the village of La Providence the residents used the St. Hyacinthe post office.
Owen Sound. Service established 1st June, 1910; population, municipal census 1909, 12,091; revenue, $23,633.72 ; population, last census, 12,558.
There is nothing wrong with that, except that the revenue was $23,633, as against $30,000 in Woodstock. I would draw your attention to the fact that the requirement of the Post Office Act is that there shall be a population of 12,000 and a revenue of $30,000.

Sault Ste. Marie did not have the necessary population; but had a revenue of $22,751. According to the census of 1911 the population was 10,984, but according to this answer the Postmaster General received very reliable information that the population was over 12,000, and he acted on that information. I could easily have got that information for him myself in regard to Woodstock. All you have to do is to swell the municipal assessment a little. My hon. friend objects to giving us mail delivery because we have not the necessary population. I have read this letter to show that my hon. friend was very ingenious in his answers. He tried to answer in such a way that I would not be able to publish them at home, but he was fooled there entirely. He did not know the fellow he was dealing with, for I did publish them at home showing that the late Government had given letter delivery in places not entitled to it ' for political reasons,' as my hon. friend says, and also for other reasons. My people were not so ignorant as not to see that my hon. friend could easily find reliable information when he wanted to give a particular place letter .carrier delivery. I do not know that I have anything further to say about the matter except that it would have been very easy for the Postmaster General to have overlooked the population of Woodstock .seeing that our post office has a revenue of ^30,600, and that with the suburban residents who come to Woodstock for their mail our population is easily 12,000.
My hon. friend thinks the answers were prepared in such a way that their publication might be hurtful to him.
To my party.

And he says that the people could see through the letters. I am very happy that the information given in the answers was such that my hon. friend could publish it, and get the benefit he thought he would get.
Why did my hon. friend think it necessary to add ' for political reasons ' when I did not ask for that at all?

It will tell my hon.
friend why. If I had not said that, my hon. friend would have had a strong case against me and my party.
No stronger than I have now.

That is a matter of
opinion. I will return my hon. friend's compliment, and say that his questions were very clever too, and of such a nature as to put me in a hole if I had not been on my guard. I do not think that the most shrewd cross-examiner 5 p.m. could have framed the questions in a more clever way. My hon. friend has been trying to get letter delivery in Woodstock for a long time. We told him that the rule in the department was to give letter carriers only to places that had a population of 12,000 and a revenue of $20,000. My hon. friend asked: Have you not established rural mail here, there, and the other place where the population was not 12,000 and the revenue not $20,000? If I had simply given him a yes or no answer the hon. member would have published it and said: Look how unfairly Woodstock is being treated. Instead of that, I gave him the facts. It is true that letter carrier delivery has been esablished in certain places which had not a population of 12,000 or a revenue of $20,000. Take the city of St. Hyacinthe, for example. The people in the province of Quebec know that there were strong political reasons for giving that place letter carrier delivery, although it did not come within the rules. My hon. friend did not ask about Hull, which is the worst case of all; so much so

that I have considered whether we should not take their carriers away. Once a letter carrier delivery is established, however, it is not easy to take it away.
What is the population of Hull?

I am informed that it is between 7,000 and 8,000 I am giving my hon. friend from Oxford that information although he did not ask for it. Let me tell my hon. friend why we have to keep within the rules as much as we can. The service is developing, particularly in the West, to such an extent that every other day I receive requests to extend the mail service. Some are wanting a more frequent service, and others who are brought in touch by a branch railway being completed want an improved mail delivery. If all these requests were granted, our expenditure would be increased by $3,000 or $4,000 every day. My hon. friend will understand that if the Post Office Department is to be administered in such a way that it will not be a financial wreck, it is impossible to grant all these requests. We have to keep within certain rules, and the rule laid down is that the place must have 12,000 population and a revenue of $20,000 before it gets letter carrier delivery. Woodstock has a very large revenue of which my hon. friend has reason to be proud, but the question of population is of more importance than revenue.
I should think it would be the opposite.

No. Places with a
large population must have letter carrier delivery in order to receive a proper service. Delivery prevents the post office from being crowded by all these people coming in for their mail.
They will come anyway.

Our experience is to the contrary. Wherever we establish letter carrier delivery the post office is relieved of a good deal of work, and from the congested condition it would otherwise be in. My hon. friend has made several requests for letter carrier delivery in Woodstock, and so have several other gentlemen to whom I gave the same answer as I gave my hon. friend. My hon. friend seems to doubt that we have reliable information in regard to Sault Ste. Marie. As a matter of fact,

I could not have had better information. The municipal census had been taken, and the facts were placed before me by the hon. member for the county (Mr. Boyce). I am speaking from memory, but I am pretty sure that is the case.
I asked the gentlemen from Woodstock who were here if they had a municipal census as a result of which they could show that they had the required population, and I said: ' The moment that you show you have the population you will get the letter delivery because I do not want you to run away with the idea that I am refusing Woodstock on account of political reasons. The moment you can show to me that the last census is wrong, or that since then the population has increased to a sufficient extent to entitle you to a letter carrier service in the city of Woodstock, I will give it to you.' I told them just what I told my hon. friend from North Oxford today. We do not go absolutely by the rule that the last census shall govern, because, if we did, we would be ten years without a change of conditions and without establishing a letter carried delivery system in important towns. The last census showed that the city of Woodstock had a population of less than 12,000. My hon. friend says that he can show that the population is really 12,000 or over. If he does show me that he will have the letter carriers.

My letter from the minister lays it down as a condition that the revenue should 'be $20,000. I do not agree with the minister that the population should govern rather than the revenue because the whole system depends on the revenue. If we were not getting a revenue from it we would not be able to continue the service.
Of course, revenue is a factor.

Revenue is the whole
factor in the Post Office Department, and I do not agree with the minister that revenue should not govern more than population. Our town has a third, or a half, more revenue than is required. I do not say that I can give reliable information as to a population of 12,000, but I do say that I can give just as reliable information probably as the towns that got this delivery service because we are accustomed to these boosting towns, their claims as to population and that sort of thing, and I have not much faith in a municipal census. However, I will say for the minister that he did

give the same answer to his political friends that he gave to me; so that they did not get any more satisfaction than I did from him.
Mr. WM. CHISHOLM: Did time permit, it would be an interesting subject, if only from the psychological point of view, to analyze and discuss the attitude and position of the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) when on his feet in this House making explanations and discussing his department, as compared with his position while operating and performing in his department. When he is in the House asking for appropriations, he surrounds himself with a halo of virtue, and appears to 'be the personification of all that is fair and just, the acme of political righteousness and fair play. Politics will not influence him in the slightest. He is only concerned in performing his duty as Postmaster General in the interests of the country as a whole. He recognizes that he is the trustee and servant of the people, and that he must give a wise, honest and just administration. When he is operating fn his department, however, he is not the innocent Mr. Hyde that we have here, but he is the cynical Dr. Jeykell. The minister pretends to be fair and just in these matters. I want to call attention to several cases of injustice, to show how absolutely unfair, unjust and tyrannical is his conduct in the administration of his department, and particularly in connection with the cancellation of mail contracts. Not only is his conduct illegal, inexcusable and unjustifiable in every particular, but it is conduct that a big man, such as a minister of the Crown, the Postmaster General, should not be guilty of. When it comes to taking advantage of poor contractors in the country, who have not the wealth of the country behind him to enable them to go into court and get justice, I think it is time that the House should know the attitude of the Postmaster General. I was reading just at noon a commentary on Shakespeare, and I came across the following description of I ago, in Othello, the Moor of Venice:
Iago is cruel and fraudulent because he finds a pleasure in fraud and cruelty; he has no belief in honesty-does not think there is any such thing in the world. .	. He has a natural
turn for dishonesty and trickery, and would rather gain his ends by deception than by straightforward conduct. He is proud of his cunning, and is witty also-full of that ill-natured sarcasm which delights in giving pain to others.
This description could not apply to the Postmaster General, but there are acts performed in the department of the hon. gentleman that could be attributed only to a. character of the description of Iago. If Iago were supervising the work of the Post Office Department, I do not think he would resort to anything more cruel than some of the acts which have been performed by officials in his department, particularly in regard to the dismissal of postmasters and the cancellation of contracts, and, reading the evidence that has been given us of the deception, dishonesty and meanness which have characterized these cancellations, we must conclude that some Iago must have access to the department and must be running things there.
Let me refer to the case of a contract that was entered into for the carrying of the mail between North Lochaber and West Lochaber. When the minister enters into a contract with a contractor for the carrying of the mails between certain dates, the minister has no right to cancel the contract until the termination of the period of service for which the contract was entered into unless he can show that in the public interest it is necessary to do so. He must show that there are grounds in law and justice for such cancellation. They must be reasonable grounds. He can cancel a contract, it is true, but it must be for reasonable cause and for some reason which is in the public interest. He should not break faith capriciously. Now, let me come to the case of this contract for the carrying of the mails between North Lochaber and West' Lochaber. This is the case of the renewal of a contract; it is only a small thing, but it is the small things that show how the business is conducted in the department of the hon. gentleman. In this case the contract was for carrying the mails a distance of five miles, and the amount involved was $81.50 per annum. That contract expired on the 30th June, 1913. On the 21st May, the superintendent, Mr. Anderson, wrote to the post office inspector authorizing a renewal of the contract, and on May 26 the post office inspector wrote to the contractor offering to renew his contract on the same terms and conditions as the service was previously performed. I am going to read the post office inspector's letter, so that you will see for yourself what it contains:
Halifax, N.S., May 26, 1913.
Dear Sir,-I beg to inform you that the Postmaster General has been pleased to authorize the renewal of your contract for the mail service between North Lochaber and West Locha-

ber for a further term of four years, dating from 1st July next (1913).
Please inform me as soon as possible whether you will be willing to accept this offer of the department. You, of course, understand that a contract can only be renewed on the existing terms and conditions. If, however, you do not care to continue at the present rate, the service will have to be put to tender.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) W. E. Maclennan,
Post Office Inspector.
There was an offer, not solicited by the contractor nor suggested by any of his friends, but an offer made by the department of its own motion. Mr. Stewart answers:
North Lochaber, June 5, 1913. Post Office Inspector,
Halifax.
I have decided to take a renewal of mail contract for the term of four years.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) George A. Stewart,
North Lochaber.
You will observe then that this was an offer to renew the contract for four years, and that he unqualifiedly accepted the offer. Mr. Stewart decided to carry on the work as usual. On the 5th of August, 1913, after Mr. Stewart had been running his contract for nearly two months, this letter was written:
Antigonish, August 5, 1913. Hon. L. P. Pelletier,
Postmaster General,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Pelletier,

A mail contract at West Lochaber now held by one George Stewart has expired. I should like to have this contract transferred to Mr. Hugh D. Cameron.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) E. Lavin Girroir.
I ask any hon. gentleman on this side of the House, if after this contract had expired and a new contract had been entered into, he would write to the late Postmaster General when the Liberal party was in power, asking him to perpetrate such a high-handed act. What must have been the mental condition of Senator Girroir when he wrote this letter to the Postmaster General, asking him to violate the King's word given in a solemn contract with this subject of His Majesty. Did the Postmaster General reply to this letter that the department had entered into a contract with this . man, and that he would have to keep his word, and that it would be a despicable thing to perpetrate such an injustice; did he inform Senator Girroir that hp had been notified the previous March that the contract was about to expire and that he did not make a representation then when he was asked to? Did the Postmaster -Jr. W. Chisholm.]
General tell Senator Girroir that a contract had been entered into with Mr. Stewart, and that it could not be broken unless for some good reason in the public interest? Not at all. Let the Postmaster General look at that file and he will not see on it any reason in the public interest to break this contract with Stewart. The Postmaster General did not write to Senator Girroir in the strain you would have expected him to, deception, dishonesty, and what is virtually fraud, in order to break the contract, and they alleged that Mr. Stewart had entered into a different form of contract altogether. On August 5 Senator Girroir wrote to the Postmaster General asking that Stewart's contract be transferred, and on August 29 there is this letter of the post oflace inspector written to Mr. Stewart:
Post Office Inspector's Office,
Halifax, August 29, 1913.
Dear Sir,-I am in receipt of authority, from the department at Ottawa to arrange for a transfer of your contract for the mail service between North Lochaber and West Lochaber to Mr. Hugh D. Cameron. I am, however, instructed that you must first duly execute and return the forms of renewal for a further term of four years from the first of July, 1913, which forms were sent you on the 24th July last. When this has been done, the necessary form to effect the transfer to Mr. Cameron will be forwarded foi execution. If the same sureties who signed the renewal do not intend to act for Mr. Cameron, the names, occupation and addresses of his proper sureties should be submitted at the same time.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) W. E. Maclennan,
Post Office Inspector.
Mr. George A. Stewart,
Mail Contractor,
North Lochaber.
The Post Office Department makes the suggestion to the post office inspector that Mr. Stewart wanted to have his contract transferred, but the fact is that Mr. Stewart knew nothing at all about the proposition until he received the letter which I have read on the 29th of August, and to that he replied:
North Lochaber, September 1, 1913. Post Office Inspector,
Halifax.
Received yours on the 29th, you were mistaken about handing me forms. If you did I never got them, you wrote me asking if I would accept a renewal of mail contract. I wrote you that I would but I am not going to take it and transfer it over, if the Tories thought they would get me to do that they are mistaken, let them get Hugh Cameron to fix up his own papers. I am not going to hunt bondsmen for him, that is just what I expected from the dirty Tories there is nothing too low for them to stoop to.
(Sgd) George A. Stewart.

That letter is commented upon by some of the officers of the department who, although servants of the people, seem to think that men working for the country in humbler positions as mail couriers are of commoner clay, and they intimate that this fellow is very saucy and impudent, and deserving of ill-treatment because he dared to write that letter.
Was the contract to Stewart renewed for a further term of four years ?
Yes.
Was it actually renewed ?
I am not aware of any formal contract being entered into.
It seems to me that it was not renewed.

The post office inspector wrote to Stewart saying that he was authorized to renew the contract on the same terms and conditions. There is the offer to Stewart. Then Stewart wrote an unqualified acceptance of that offer, stating that he accepted the contract on the same terms and conditions, and he continued on with the work, and as a matter of law and justice it was a binding contract.
My hon. friend says that the Post Office Department broke the contract, but there is nothing in what he has stated to show that Stewart's contract was renewed for a further term.

Every law student
knows that when you make an offer, as was done in this case, and that offer is unqualifiedly accepted, that is a binding contract whether it is under seal or not. When a man proceeds to carry on the work under the same terms and conditions as was ths offer here, the contract is just the same as if a new contract had been entered into. Senator Girroir still keeps busy and anxious, and on the 10th of September he writes:
Antigonish, September 10, 1913.
G. C. Anderson, Esq.,
Superintendent Mail Contracts,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Would you please let me know how mail contracts of George Stewart west side Lochaber stand. I have written about this before, but apparently the matter has been overlooked.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) E. Davin Girroir.
Senator Girroir does not suggest there was not any renewal of the contract; he does not suggest there was not any binding agreement between His Majesty and George
Stewart, but he knows his man and he says: You must break this contract with Stewart and transfer it to Hugh D. Cameron.
Why would he require to enter into another contract if he had already entered into one ?

The Postmaster General had to enter into a new contract with Hugh D. Cameron, the friend of the Tory party. I am surprised at my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) trying to bolster up a bad case of this kind, when I remember the high and lofty-minded position he assumed when he was in opposition. I know he feels in his heart that this thing is so reprehensible that it cannot be defended, and he is ashamed of it. On October 13 the Postmaster General is written to. Mr. Stewart naturally thought that the Postmaster General would be a man of honour and that he would not allow such an imposition on him by the Halifax office, and so he thought he would appeal to the fountain of justice and fair play, and he wrote:
North Lochaber, N.S.,
October 13, 1913.
Hon. L. P. Pelletier,
Postmaster General,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir-On the 26th of May last I was advised by the post office inspector that the Postmaster General had been pleased to authorize the renewal of my contract for the mail service between North Lochaber and West Lochaber for a term of four years, dating from the 1st of July next ensuing. I agreed to the renewal of the contract and made my arrangements accordingly. On the 29th of August I received a letter from the post office inspector at Halifax stating that your department had arranged for a transfer of my contract to one Hugh D. Cameron. This I thought pretty high-handed dealing. If your department considered it necessary to make a change in the contractor, why did you not make the transfer on the 26th of May-
The day that the department authorized the renewal.
-or on the 1st of July?
The date that the contract would expire.
Instead of that His Majesty the King, through the Postmaster General of Canada, solemnly contracted for the carrying of the mails for a term of four years. I am aware of the fact that the Postmaster General or the King reserves the right to cancel a contract, but I have also understood he exercises that right only where the cause should be assigned. Had the mail been given to Hugh D. Cameron, or anybody else, last July, I would not complain, but having made different arrangements than I otherwise would have made by reason of the fact that the Postmaster General renewed the contract on his own motion and not at my request,
514C

I consider that you are guilty of a downright injustice for which there should clearly be redress between man and man. On the 24 th ultimo I have another letter from the post office inspector stating that the temporary arrangements under which I was performing the service would terminate on the 3rd of September. There was no temporary arrangement. It was a definite contract for four years from last July, and the letter of the 24th of September shows to what depths your department will go to find excuses where no justification for such high-handed conduct exists. Why resort to such misrepresentations? Is it any wonder that all decent, self-respecting people are disgusted with the manner in which your department has degraded itself? I expect that in common decency you will at least give me three months wages inasmuch as you cancelled the contract virtually without notice.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) Geo. A. Stewart.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Stewart intended to leave the country. He had other arrangements in view; but as he got a renewal oi this contract and for certain other reasons, he decided to remain at home. He made arrangements for the carrying of the mail; for instance, he invested in a new carriage for the purpose. Therefore he had a right to complain, and he said to the Postmaster General that the least the department ought to do for him would be to give him a three months' allowance or to compensate him for the expenditure to which he had been put. The postmaster General did not reply to Mr. Stewart's letter; but Mr. Anderson, superintendent, was made to reply as follows:
Ottawa, 16th October, 1913.
Dear Sir,-I am directed to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 13th inst. with reference to the contract for the mail service between North Lochaber and West Lochaber.
Your contract expired on the 30th June last, and the department will authorize a renewal. Renewal forms were sent for execution by the inspector, but were never returned. As the service was being performed after the 1st of July without any signed contract, and you had been given an opportunity to renew it and had not done so, the department decided to give the contract to Hugh D. Cameron at the same price.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd) G. C. Anderson,
Superintendent.
I know Mr. Anderson, and I know that he would not of his own initiative write a letter of that kind unless he was required to do so by some higher authority, because there is a suggestion of falsehood contained in that letteT, as was pointed out quite clearly by Mr. Stewart when he wrote again to Mr. Anderson as follows:

North Lochaber, N.S.,
December 8, 1913.
Mr. George C. Anderson,
Superintendent Mail Service,
Ottawa, Can.
Dear Sir,-In reply to your favour of the 16th of October re service between North Lochaber and West Lochaber in which you allege as a reason for cancellation of the contract made between the King, represented by your minister and myself, and the giving of the contract to Hugh D. Cameron, that I had failed to execute renewal forms at the expiration of my contract on the 30th of June last. I have only to say that this is a miserable excuse, a subterfuge unworthy of any honourable business man, to say nothing of a representative of the Crown. I hold a letter from the post office inspector who, I would take it, is authorized to act for the department in . this matter, which letter is dated May 25, 1913, and in which it is stated as follows:
' I beg to inform you that the Postmaster General has been pleased to authorize the renewal of your contract for the mail service between North Lochaber and West Lochaber for a further term of four years, dating from the 1st of July next. Please inform me as soon as possible whether you will be willing to accept this offer of the department. You, of course understand that a contract can only be renewed on the existing terms and conditions. If, however, you do not care to continufe at the present rate, the service will have to be put up to tender.'
To this I replied that I was willing to continue on the terms of that letter. The renewal was, therefore, completed on the then existing terms and conditions. I was not asked to sign any new contract or give any new bonds for the reason as you will see that such was not necessary, my acceptance of the contract being on the terms stated in that letter. If a new contract were necessary, why is it that my attention was not called to it in the meantime? I have, therefore, only to repeat what I have stated in my letter of October 13, and to insist that under the circumstances at least three months' w'ages should be paid me.
I went to expenses that I would not have incurred believing entirely on the good faith of the King's representative and his agreement to a renewal of the contract for a further term of four years from the 1st of July last under the same conditions which I carried the mails during the four years previously.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) Geo. A. Stewart.
It is common knowledge, that when the time comes for the renewal of these contracts, although a renewal form is provided, this form is not sent immediately. Weeks, months very often elapse-in fact I have known of cases where over a year has elapsed before the formal new contract had been entered into. The binding agreement was there the moment there was an acceptance of the offer made. The formal contract was only the evidence of that, and it would be necessary for the purpose of binding the sureties; but in these small

contracts everyone knows that the department, where the contractors are reliable persons, is not in a hurry about having the formal ccmtracts entered into. That is the position so far as Mr. Stewart's case is concerned.
I have several other cases of a similar knd where the department has broken its contract without assigning any reason whatever for doing so. In this case it is only a matter of $87.50, hut it is an outrage that any citizen of this county should be treated in that manner. That is not the worst feature of it. It iss debasing to the department. What will the officials of the department be expected to do when they know that the high and mighty minister himself not only countenances these things, but actually authorizes them? If it were for no other reason than that, namely, the degradation, the lowering of the tone of the department and of the country generally, this House should censure such conduct. What can we expect from the smaller men when the biggeT men break their word of honour, violate their agreement with impunity, as has happened in this case?
I am not going to refer to a few other eases of a similar kind that have arisen in my own county. But I must call attention to another case of juggling with tenders. The Postmaster General calls for tenders; the tenders are received, instead of awarding the contract to the lowest tenderer, he communicates with the holder of the patronage in the particular district and says: To whom do you want to give the contract? and they manipulate the thing, and invariably a Conservative gets the contract at the lowest tender if he wants it. If they can find a pretext for passing the lowest tender over if it happens to be from a Grit, it is done, and the contract goes to the higher tenderer when he is recommended by the patronage committee. I protest against that sort of thing, because it is doing away with the system of tender and contract and fair competition. It is making a farce of calling for tenders. Often a man has asked me to fill out a form of application for tender, and I have said to him: What is the use of your putting in a tender? You are a Liberal and you will not get the contract. Unless you want to hurt your Conservative friend and neighbours who may also be tendering by making them come down to your figure, you had better 324
not put in a tender at all, because you have no chance of getting the contract even if you happen to be . the lowest tenderer. If there is a Tory who will accept the contract at your figure it will go to him.
Let us isee how that worked out in the cage of the Livingstone iCove-Antigonish service, which is a pretty large contract, namely, about a thousand dollars. Tenders were called early in tire winter and there was ample time for the receipt of tenders in 1912, because the service was to begin on the first of July, 1912. I find on April 13, 1912 a letter written, from Mr. J. J. Cameron, who was the late Conservative candidate in Antigonish, and who was defeated.
I may say that there is not a more high-minded, upright and honourable man in the county of Antigonish than Dr. Cameron. As a politician he has been a hard hitter, and has worked and struggled for his party in the days of adversity in Antigonish, sacrificing both time and money; and if there is any man who deserves recognition at the hands of the Conservative party in Antigonish, or who should receive decent treatment and common courtesy, it is he. I am sorry to say that the Conservative party there has not treated him with that decency and courtesy which he deserves, not only as a man, but as the candidate of the Conservative party who ran several elections for them. I repeat the treatment accorded him by selfish politicians who ousted him was shameful in the extreme. Although Dr. Cameron, being the candidate, was supposed to look after the patronage, the Tories there turned him down. It is the only case I know of in the history of Canada where a defeated Conservative, who desired the control of the patronage not for the patronage itself but as a matter of selfrespect, had that privilege taken from him. If he was good enough to be the Conservative candidate and put up such valiant fights for the party as he had done, he surely was good enough to handle the patronage. But they got him out of the patronage. On April 17, thinking he still had the patronage, so he thought, for he wrote the Postmaster General:
Dear Sir,-Would you be good enough to let me know the names and prices of those who tendered for mail contract from Livingston's Cove to Antigonish which will expire July 1st next. As a candidate at the last election for this county I would like to get this information and in return will give some direction or



recommendation as to what is best to do and believe me.
Yours respectfully,
(Sgd) J. J. Cameron, M.D.
You would suppose that that information would he sent him, hut what does the Postmaster General, through his assistant deputy minister do? This is the answer he makes:
April 20, 1912.
Dear Sir,-I am directed by the Postmaster General to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 17th instant, asking for the names and prices of those who tendered for the mail service between Antigonishi and; Livings ton's; Cove.
In reply, I am to say that the matter will receive the consideration of the department.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) H. B. Verret.
Very polite indeed. It ' will receive the consideration of the department.' But they did not give the Conservative candidate- who was supposed to get it, the information. They added insult to injury. To insult him still further, the assistant deputy Postmaster General writes to Senator Girroir, who had secured control of the patronage, as follows:
April 20, 1912.
Dear Sir,-Dr. Cameron of Antigonish, under date of 17th instant, has asked the department to furnish him with a list of the tenders for the mall service between Antigonish and Livingston's Cove.
I am directed to furnish you with a list of the tenders for such action as you may deem desirable. The following tenders were received,
viz:
J. R. McAdam, Malignant Cove	$ 944
Angus McPherson, Georgeville	 990
Chas. McNeil, Morar	 1,000
There are altogether eight tenders; I need not read them all.
The tender of J. R. McAdam of Malignant Cove at $944 per annum being the lowest was accepted on the 4th instant.
H. B. Verret.
On April 20, the assistant deputy writes to Senator Girroir that the tender of J. R. McAdam, being the lowest, was accepted. You would suppose that steps would be taken at once to put that contract into force, but what do we find? On June 29, 1912, Senator Girroir writes to the Postmaster General as follows:
Dear Sir,-I enclose herewith copy of a letter which I have received from Mr. Verret, Assistant Deputy Postmaster General, and reply thereto with respect to above matter.
I am very anxious indeed for many reasons to have this contract awarded to Mr. Angus McPherson and can only repeat what I said my letter to Mr. Verret.
Would you kindly give this matter immediate attention and let me know what can be done for Mr. McPherson.

McPherson, as I stated, was not the lowest tenderer, but the second lowest, and you will observe that Senator Girroir has the effrontery to write to the Postmaster General suggesting that Mr. McAdam should be passed over without giving any reason to justify it. What opinion must he have of the Postmaster General? Did he know his man when he made such an indecent suggestion? What an undignified position for the Postmaster General to be in, when the senator suggests that he should depart from the spirit and letter of the law, and not award the contract to the lowest tenderer? But that is what happens when Dr. Jekyll is working in the department now in the Langevin block. The senator writes that he is anxious * for many reasons ' to have this contract awarded to Mr. McPherson. I find a note from Mr. Anderson, the superintendent, on May 21, 1912, to the inspector. (Is the date correct?)
Re Antigonish and Livingston's Cove.
The tender of Mr. J. R. McAdam at $944 was accepted on the 4th ultimo.
Will the inspector be so good as to say what action has been taken on this tender and how the matter stands.
There is no question there as to his not being entitled to have the contract awarded to McAdam; it states distinctly that it is his. The next thing that happened is a letter of June 29, 1912, from Senator Girroir, in which he refers to another mail contract-St. Andrews and Beauley service -suggesting that the lowest tender in that case be passed over and the contract given to the next man, Mr. Punch. Then he says in this same letter:
I have not heard from you with respect to the Livingston's Cove mail route. You will remember that I wrote to you some time ago expressing a desire that this contract be awarded to Mr. Angus McPherson and alleged that McAdam, the lowest tenderer, was not a man of means and that he would not be in the position to give a good service.
I am writing the minister to-day about the matter, also in order -that he may give it consideration at the same time with you.
I trust that there will be some way of arranging this contract for McPherson, as the public generally are desirous that he obtain it.
It seems to me that in the meantime Senator Girroir became wise-whether through correspondence or an interview with the department, I do not know-to the fact that it was necessary to allege some reason for passing over the lowest tenderer; and they framed up a charge that this man was not a responsible person. I am going to show in a minute or two a telegram in which the senator says: Give

it to Mr. McAdam if not to Mr. McPherson. He was apparently quite reliable enough then; the public service would have been served then, and everything would have been perfectly satisfactory. Now he says: ' I trust there will be some way of arranging this contract for McPherson, as the public generally are desirous that he obtain it.' I want to direct attention for a minute or two to who this McPherson is. He was virtually a myth. When later on he had an opportunity of getting the contract he said in effect: ' I did not put in a tender for myself at all. I will have nothing to do with it.' What I am getting is the suggestion by Senator Girroir that the responsible minister should pass over the lowest tenderer in violation of the spirit and letter of the law. Here is a telegram from Senator Girroir, addressed to the Postmaster General:
Want to know at once what decision arrived at in respect to Livingston's Cove and Anti-gonish mail route. If contract cannot be given Angus McPherson would prefer it to go to lowest tenderer and be awarded at once.
I do not know the date of this telegram. The copy brought down is not dated; likely it was early in September, but the senator states that he would prefer that the contract should be given to McAdam, the man whom he stated on the 29th of June had no property and was not a responsible person, because he was ' not a man of means.' Of course that statement was false, as I will show later on. We go on a little further. Mr. Anderson writes to the post office inspector, inquiring whether the contract had been entered into, and whether McAdam's sureties have signed a bond. Then there is a telegram from Inspector McLellan, dated September 30, 1912:
Ee Antigonish and Livingston's Cove, inquiry not yet completed. One surety good, the other said to be without property. McAdam prepared to furnish satisfactory security in the same way as tenderers in other cases.
In order to get some pretext for passing over McAdam, the Conservative friends of Senator Girroir searched the records and discovered that there was no real estate in the name of J. E. McAdam. He is a married man, forty-two years of age, with a family, and was living with his father and mother at home; and the father's property is worth something in the vicinity of $3,000, I should say. He is a taxpayer and an elector of the county.

Is he a Grit?
324i

Yes. They discovered he had no property in his own name. But' Mr. McAdam got on to this, and wrote a-letter saying: I will give you any surety you require, if my present sureties are not satisfactory. This letter does not appear on the file, but there is just as good as it on the file. A telegram to Superintendent Anderson, from Inspector McLellan, advising McAdam, who was prepared to give any security required. In his letter, to which I referred, he offered other security-two sureties in the sum of $25,000 each, who would justify under oath, or, if that was not satisfactory a bond from a guarantee company.
What are sureties for, I should like to know? Is it the policy of the department to refuse to accept a contract from a man because he does not happen to have $1,000 in his own name? Is a man less able to take charge of a mail service simply because he does not happen to be registered as worth $1,000 or $2,000 in real estate or personal property? If a man is of good character and provides proper sureties, the department should not refuse to accept his services. Although McAdam was prepared to arrange satisfactory surety, the department passed over his tender, which was the lowest, refused to recognize him, and [DOT] awarded the contract to Mr. McPherson. In the meantime the service was being performed at a loss to the country. The man who performed the service from July 1, 1912, to May 1, 1913, was being paid $125 a month. Ten months at $125 is $1,250; and if McAdam's tender had been accepted, the cost of the service during that period would have been only $786. The department, therefore, simply threw away about $500 in an effort to dishonestly favour a friend. These, I presume, are the businesslike methods to which my hon. friend the Postmaster General was pleased to refer to a little while ago when he was talking about free delivery. On October 26, 1912, the following letter was written by Angus McPherson in reply to a notification that the contract had been awarded to him;
I received your letter of the 23rd instant notifying me that my tender for the Antigonish, Livingstone's cove mail service was accepted with instructions to commence on 1st November next.
Now, in view of the fact that I tendered for this mail service to begin on the 1st of July last, as was stated in my tender, and the department failing to notify me until nearly four months afterwards that my tender was accepted, I concluded that my tender was rejected and therefore made arrangements mak-

I do not intend to make a speech of the same length as my hon. friend. If he thinks the matter to which he referred is of sufficient importance to keep the House in session for an hour, it is his plain duty to do so; and I am not going to quarrel with him about it.
If there is any fault, it lies on your side; you should have brought down your Estimates earlier.
I am sorry I have not the file, so that I could answer the remarks of my hon. friend.
I will hand it you.

I have frequently asked gentlemen on the other side to notify me as to when they intended to bring up any special matter like this, in order that I might have the files here and coul-d not be accused of any lack of courtesy.
Here is the file.

Just one moment. My hon. friend has had his -say for an hour, and now it is my turn, although I will not speak for that length of time. During this session and last I have put on the table of the House about 425 returns, some of them very voluminous. I do not suppose that it is expected that I shcul-d carry all these matters in my head, or be able to deal with them as any hon. gentleman can who has a particular file before him. My hon. friend has used some violent language, and seems to have a great dislike to myself and to Senator Girroir, hut I am not going to take -any notice of that at all. I am going to he as courteous as any man could be, and will take no notice of the big words he thought he ought to use. People who use language of that kind without justification generally regret it themselves, afterwards. My hon. friend seems to have a special kind of hatred against Senator Girroir, 'but I have no douibt that if he were here he would 'be able to answer my hon. friend.

I rise to a question of privilege. The Postmaster General has intimated that. I made an attack on Senator Girroir. I said nothing unkind about Him; all I did was to read his letters. So far as the Postmaster General is concerned, if Ins conscience troubles him he is welcome to think I have not the respect for him his

position should command. I did not condemn or attack men but their acts and deeds.
* Mr. PELLETIER:	My hon. friend has
risen to a question of privilege in order to force me to my seat, but it turns out that it is not a question of privilege at all. I say that my hon. friend was not justified in using the language he did. Dr. Jekyll and Hyde-that is all right, but it does not amount to a rupee so far as I am concerned. If my hon. friend has all these bad ideas, what can I do ?
Do not do it again.
I am going to do in the future what I have done in the past, because I have always done what I thought was right.
Lord have pity on him then.

In regard to these
automobiles about which my fion. friend from Rouville has inquired. The first automobile bought in Montreal was a Packard. It was purchased by the former Postmaster General for $6,500. The second car was also a Packard, the original price of which was $6,500 but as it had been damaged by fire we got it for $4,500.
By whom was it bought?
By Mr. Gaboury.

During the time my
hon. friend was Postmaster General?

Yes. This car was
sent to Ottawa and is now in use at Sherbrooke for the installation of the rural mail delivery.

I am very glad my hon. friend has given the information. I thought the deputy minister had made a mistake when he said that I bought that second car. Are the Post Office Estimates to be taken up again this evening?
No, I think the Marine Estimates will be up. The Poet Office Estimates will likely be up again tomorrow.

I would like information on two points before the Estimates come up again. First of all I would like in round figures the number of rural mail boxes per province; and secondly, some sort of statement as to how the parcel post system is working out. As parcel .post is a new de-

partment I would like my hon. friend to make a little statement on that matter. I also intend to say a few words about parcel post.

I have a statement
about parcel post here.
At six o'clock the 'committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Department of the Naval Service-to provide for the maintenance and upkeep of ships, naval college and dockyards of Halifax and Esquimalt, $1,000,000.

My hon.
friend has no statement to make?
