speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have no particular statement to make. This item is the same as that which was included in the Estimates last year. It provides for the upkeep of ships, the naval college, dock-yards, and everything of that sort. The items are made up as follows:
Pay of officers and men, stores, repairs to ships and vessels, repairs to dockyard machinery, miscellaneous dockyard services, repairs and maintenance of buildings, new machinery on dockyards at Halifax and Esquimalt, construction of lighters and other service boats, harbour defences, and naval volunteer reserve.

The information of my hon. friend is certainly short and-I will not say, sweet nor sharp-but it does not give anything more than we have in the printed book. We shall be interested to know where the naval college is, how many professors are there, and how many pupils.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At present on the roll of the naval college there are eighteen cadets who joined in January, 1911, eight who joined in January, 1912, six who joined in January, 1913, and six who joined in August, 1913. The reason for the division in 1913 is that the date of the opening of the college was changed. That makes thirty-eight students. Of that number eight are on H.M.S. Berwick.

What is the
course of study and what is its duration?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The course of study is now three years. The course of study originally was two years, but it was changed to three.

What does
the course include-mathematics, literature, languages and technical studies?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The course includes technical and other studies. It embraces English literature, mathematics, and studies of the sort which will fit a man for service in the navy or in any technical profession.
French also ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Are there any diplomas issued at the end of the studies ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
What becomes of the students when they have their diplomas ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Of those who entered
originally a number are given commissions in the Royal navy and arrangements have been made by which eight graduates will be given commissions in the British navy each year. Other cadets will no doubt enter upon careers in connection with the hydrographic survey and work of that sort. The course is one which, like the course of the Royal Military College at Kingston, fits a man not only for naval work, but for work in any other profession that he chooses to go in for. Only a small proportion of the graduates from the Royal Military College at Kingston enter upon a military career. Many of them engage in civil engineering, engineering of other sorts, and other scientific pursuits. It is believed that the course of the naval college will equip men equally well for naval and other careers.

There is a difference between the naval college and the military college. The military college prepares young officers to take service in the Canadian forces; but, if I followed closely what was said by my non. friend as to what became of the young men who were instructed at the naval college, there are many careers open to them which my hon. friend mentioned, but he never mentioned the Canadian navy. They can enter any service other than the Canadian navy. I suppose it is not intended that they should become officers in the Canadian navy ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When we have a navy, of course they will be.
Is it anticipated that we shall have a navy, or that we shall not have one at all ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is a question of policy which I think my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) will have to inform the House about at a later date.

I thought in my innocence that the Minister of the Naval Service would have something to say about that; but I am surprised-no, I am not surprised-that he is the minister in name only, and that as to the policy of the department over which he presides he cannot say anything at all. Well, we will take it at that. My hon. friend has told us that there is also a ship, the Berwick, engaged in this service. I never heard the name of that ship before. Where did we get her ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is not our ship. This is a ship that belongs to the British navy, upon which the young cadets who joined in 1912 have been granted by the British navy the opportunity of cruising and of receiving practical naval instruction.

Has it been
lent to the Canadian navy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. By arrangement with the Admiralty they are taken for training on board a ship which belongs to the British navy.
What becomes of the famous Niobe?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The famous Niobe is in
good condition and is being taken care of, but she is at present lying in the harbour at Halifax not doing any cruising.
Is it intended to use the Niobe in any way?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is a matter that may develop in the future.
My hon. friend is rather chary of information on this subject; but the ministerial papers say it is intended that the Niobe and the Rainbow shall become training ships.
Training ships for what?
I do not know; I am not very inquisitive.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They may be used in connection with the naval volunteers that will be organized very shortly.

Perhaps I
shall be more fortunate in getting information if I ask about the dockyards at Esqui-malt and Halifax.

Perhaps it would be
better for the Minister of Marine to ask his two colleagues, the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) to retire for a few

moments while he is giving this information. He perhaps might feel more easy and comfortable.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think we are getting
along very we'll. The dockyards at Halifax and Esquimailt were taken over by Canada from the British Admiralty on the understanding that they would be maintained by us in a proper state of efficiency. They are being so maintained and they do a large amount of work in making repairs, not only for naval vessels, but for vessels of the fisheries protection fleet and other Canadian ships. These dockyards also do work in connection with the buoy service.
How much of this one million dollars is intended to cover the expenses of the naval college?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will give you the details of the vote. Niobe, $270,730; Rainbow, $125,635; naval college, $81,710; dockyard at Halifax, $188,000; dockyard at Esquimau, $88,600; naval volunteer reserve, $200,000; salaries at headquarters, pension contribution to imperial navy, miscellaneous, $45,325.
Will the hon. gentleman give us some information about the naval volunteers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I shall be gi

 to give the right hon. gentleman full information. The force will consist of officers and seamen raised by voluntary engagement from among seafaring men and others who may be deemed suitable for the service in which such volunteers are to be employed. The term of engagement will be three years, and re-engagement for successive periods of three years will be provided for up to the age of 45 years. The purpose of this volunteer force is to provide men to take active part in the naval defence of the Dominion. They would be required for the following purposes amongst others:
1: To serve on board His Majesty's ships.
2.	As personnel for the Examination Service at the defended ports.
3.	As personnel for the mine-sweeping service at the defended ports.
4.	To supplement the existing staff at the wireless telegraph stations.
5.	To man the visual signal stations on the coast.
6.	To act as censors of wireless telegraph messages.
7.	To collect naval intelligence and act as intelligence officers.
8.	As personnel for steamers which may

require to be hired by the Naval Service Department in time of emergency.
The details of the organization of the naval volunteer force have not yet been finally worked out, hut the main lines will be approximately as follows:
The force will consist of one main division, with headquarters at Ottawa. This division will be subdivided into three subdivision's :
Atlantic-from the Atlantic coast to longitude 72 W.
Lake-from 72 W. to 102 W.
Pacific-from 102 W. to the Pacific coast.
The city of Quebec is thus included in the Atlantic subdivision, and the city of Winnipeg in the Lake subdivision.
The force will be organized in companies of 100 men, and it is proposed at the beginning to organize such companies in some of the larger centres. LateT on it will he possible to have companies formed in smaller places, or even to organize parts of companies in places which could not raise a full company.
The volunteers will be divided into three classes as respects the training which they will receive:
Class 1

will drill partly on shore at their headquarters and partly on shipboard. This class will embrace volunteers living reasonably close to the naval stations or who can easily be reached by a training ship.
Class 2-will drill ashore at their headquarters-will receive instruction in boat work, signalling, gunnery, etc. This class will embrace the volunteers who would find it difficult to leave their headquarters to train on shipboard.
Class 3-will not drill on shore but will receive training on board ship. This class will embrace, fishermen, seamen and men who follow the sea as a profession. It is proposed that they should be given training on the Niobe or the Rainbow or ships of the fisheries protection fleet, so as to acquaint them with the rules and discipline of the navy and to train them in gunnery, signal work, etc.
This classification would probably be varied to suit local conditions, and could hardly be rigidly adhered to.
It is proposed that the training shall consist of twenty-one days annually or its equivalent in drills counting five drills as equivalent to one day.
Instructional officers would have to be provided and it is hoped to obtain these from the British Admiralty.
The sum estimated for the expenditure on this service amounts to $200,000 and would be distributed as follows:
Instructional force-pay	$ 12,000
Naval volunteers	 18,000
Recruiting expenses-advertising, medical inspection, etc	 4,000

Guns	$ 40,000
Erecting guns	 6,000
Clothing	 35,000
Victualling	 3,000
Boats	 6,500
Naval stores-permanent	 4,000
Naval stores consumable	 3,000
Gunnery stores-permanent	 30,000
Gunnery stores consumable	 6,000
Hire of drill halls	 7,000
Hire of boathouses	 1,500
Caretakers	  3,000
Travelling expenses	 7,000
Stationery and printing	 3,000
Furniture, fuel, light, etc	 3,000
Freight	  3,000
Contingencies	 5,000
Total	$200,000
The pay provided for the officers will he the same as the pay adopted for the Canadian navy. The men's pay will be a trifle higher than that provided by the naval regulations so as to bring it about at a par with the pay of the militia.
Requests have been received from several places for information with regard to this movement, and certain places have expressed a desire to organize companies immediately, and it is anticipated that there will be no difficulty in obtaining the required number of recruits as soon as the organization has been definitely provided for, and the department is prepared to provide instructional officers.
During the last year there has been a purely volunteer organization of this sort carried on at Victoria, B.C., and there has been a great deal of enthusiasm about it. The only assistance it has received in any way from the country has been that we have placed at the disposition of that organization certain properties in connection with the dockyard at Esquimalt, where the men carry on their drill. This organization is especially anxious that it shall receive recognition as a volunteer force in the same way as naval volunteers are recognized in other parts of the British Empire.
That in general is an outline of what is proposed to be done in connection with the naval volunteer movement. It will be a purely volunteer force like the Militia of Canada; and, as I have pointed out, instruction will take place in various places so as to fit these men for serving on board ship, acting as signalling officers, taking charge of guns, etc., for purposes of defence.

Under what
statute is my hon. friend proceeding?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Naval Service Act.
Is it still in existence?

I do not
know if I caught aright the information given by my hon. friend. I understood him to say there were to be three or four stations,-one on the Pacific ocean, one on the Atlantic ocean, and one on the Great Lakes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
This matter
invites some discussion. But, before I proceed with the main discussion of the item, let me call the attention of my hon. friend to the station which he intends to place on the Great Lakes. I am not sure as to the wisdom of the policy elsewhere-as to which we shall probably have a little more to say later on-but *as to the wisdom of my hon. friend having a training station on the Great Lakes, I am fully awaTe that there are training stations on the south shore of the lakes-volunteer organizations. My hon. friend, however, is aware that these are state organizations, not federal organizations. I am pretty sure of what I say, namely, that up to the present time the federal authorities have resisted all pressure put upon them to have a training station upon the Great Lakes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are partly federal
stations.

Since when
have they been so?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Recently, some time this
spring.

I shall be
obliged if my hon. friend will bring down the correspondence and other information in regard to that point. If there has been any such development as my hon. friend has stated, it must !be of very recent date. The federal authorities have tolerated the action of the state of Michigan and the state of New York in having training stations at different points on the lakes; but,

in view of the treaty of 1817, which limits the armaments on the lakes, they have always refused up to this spring to have any such training stations. That being the case, it would have been far better for my hon. friend to remonstrate with the federal authorities against this innovation and to endeavour to get them to continue the condition that has existed for nearly a hundred years, namely, that neither the American Government nor the Canadian Government should have any force on the Great Lakes. If we are now opening the door and commencing to have training ships on one side and on the other, there is no telling what development will take place; and, if we engage in a contest with the Americans, the certainty is that they will be the iron pot and we shall be the earthen pot; that is, they will have a very strong force and we shall have a limited one. Apart from the merits of the question, to which I shall allude presently, I must express to my hon. friend my sincere regret that, instead of doing what he has done, namely, following the action of the Americans, he has not remonstrated with them and endeavoured to have them undertake to continue the treaty, which has been kept in force scrupulously by both parties for nearly a hundred years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Canada has always protested against the establishment of training ships or foreign war vessels on the Great Lakes; but we do not propose to have war vessels or training .ships upon the lakes. The naval volunteer force will be at places like Toronto and other places on the lakes. The men will come under one or other of these two classes:	Class 1 will
drill partly on shore at their headquarters and partly on shipboard; class 2 will drill ashore at their headquarters, receiving instruction in boat work, signalling, gunnery, etc. This class will embrace the volunteers who will find it difficult to leave their headquarters to train on shipboard. There is no intention of establishing any ships whatever on the Great Lakes. Petitions have been received from several places for the establishment of this volunteer naval reserve force. Nothing will be done that might conflict with the understanding that has existed for so many years with regard to armed forces on the lakes. These men will be simply naval volunteers. If it is necessary to give them training on board ship, they may be sent to Halifax to Ibe instructed on the Niobe for a few days, just

in the same way as troops are being brought to Petawawa for the purpose of being trained and drilled.
I can assure my right hon. friend that there is no intention whatever of taking any steps that will do violence to the understanding to which he refers, and which has existed for so many years. With regard to whether or not those volunteers on the American side are recognized by federal authority, my information is that at the present session of Congress an Act has been passed which recognizes them from the federal standpoint.
I understand there are to be no training ships on the lakes. Am I right?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is quite right.

We have two training ships-the Niobe on the Atlantic, and the Rainbow on the Pacific. We have certainly moved within the last three years, and the present Government have taken a step which was not anticipated at all at the last election. Perhaps it is just as well, since my hon. friend has not done it, that I should read an Order in Council passed by the Government, which was laid upon the table at my request, and which is in these terms:
The Committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report dated 14th May, 1914, from the Minister of the Naval Service, stating that several recommendations and representations had been received from persons and parties in the Dominion urging the organization of a naval volunteer force.
The minister observes that an independent organization of this nature has already been established in British Columbia and has been carrying on drill and training under the directions of various officers of the Department of the Naval Service, so that the time seems opportune for the organization of such a force on the following basis, namely:
1.	The officers, petty officers and men of the naval volunteers shall be persons who volunteer to enroll to carry out the prescribed annual drill or training and to serve in the Naval Service when called out.
2.	The naval volunteers, if called out in the event of an emergency, will be required:
(a) To serve in the vessels of the Naval Service of Canada or in those of the Royal navy;
(b)	As personnel for the examination, minesweeping and other subsidiary services at the different ports;
(c)	As signalmen, wireless telegraphists and in such ranks and ratings as are required for establishments on shore.
3.	The force to be raised shall consist at present of 1,200 men, together with the necessary officers and permanent staff.
4.	The training of the naval volunteers shall comprise seamanship, including handling of

boats under oars and sail, knotting, splicing, rigging sheers and derricks; drill with guns and rifles, including firing practice; company and field gun drill; torpedo and electrical instruction ; engineering and stokehold work; signalling, wireless telegraphy, first aid and kindred subjects.
This training shall be conducted in such manner as shall be prescribed by the Minister of the Naval Service from time to time.
The committee, on the recommendation of the Minister of the Naval Service, advise that a naval volunteer force be organized forthwith in accordance with the provisions above set forth.
As I said a moment ago, the Government has advanced a long step since the election of 1911. In that year it was well understood that if the Conservative party came Into office the Naval Service Act, which had been passed the year before, was to be wiped off the statutes; it was not satisfactory to a certain portion of the Conservative party, chiefly located in the province of Quebec, because that branch of the Conservative party did not believe in any naval expenditure whatever. It was not satisfactory to some portions of the Conservative party in other provinces, because it created a Canadian service, and the motto of the party then in opposition, now in office, was: ' One Throne, one Empire, one Navy.' Sir, one thing is settled now- that the Naval Service Act is to remain in force; as to that there can be no dispute. My hon. friend is organizing a force under this Act, and he tells us-I put the question to him, and he told me in so many words and syllables-that the present force is organized under the Naval Service Act of 1910. Therefore, it is settled once and for all that the Naval Service Act is to remain on the statute-book.
My hon. friend is commencing now to organize a volunteer force of 1,200 men. These men are enlisted for three years, like the volunteers in the militia force; they take an oath; they become responsible to the call of the Government; they are liable when called for service-at the present time let us hope that there shall be no occasion to call them except for drill-but in an emergency, in case of war, they can be called out. But they are called out for what? To serve in the vessels of the Naval Service of Canada and in those of the Royal navy; that is to say, we are training men at the present time for the service of the Canadian navy. One Throne, one Empire, one Navy! This is the natural corollary, and it is the policy of the Government-to train naval men for the service of the Imperial navy. It cannot be for a Canadian navy, because my hon. friend the minister in charge of the department (Mr. Hazen) has just told us that he is not sure that we shall have a Canadian navy. This is still in the air. But in the meantime we have understood that at some date or other we should have a permanent policy upon this question. It is slow in coming; it has not come; it is coming by degrees; and this is one of the first steps to be taken.
Now, Sir, to crown the cup of humiliation of the gentlemen who are behind the Government, there are two things. The despised Niobe, the contumelious Niobe, which has bad so much ignominy heaped upon it, is to be made use of; she is not to be sold for old iron, as we have been told, but is to be kept in the waters of a Canadian port to serve as a training ship. This is to be on the Atlantic. On the Pacific we shall have a repetition of the offence. The despised Rainbow, which was taken from service some few years ago for the patrol of the waters of the Pacific ocean, is also to become a training ship. Another humiliation : we have been told on the floor of this House more than once that the Canadian people were so engaged in other things that it was impossible to recruit soldiers; that if we wanted to have sailors we would have to go elsewhere; that we could not find men; that the men on board the Rainbow and Niobe had deserted; and that the task of trying to recruit in Canada had been given up in despair. My hon. friend expects to have 1,200 men in the service; he thinks there will be no trouble at all about securing them. He tells us there is great enthusiasm already. I am aware that there has always been great enthusiasm in the province of British Columbia for a service of that kind, and that there has been a volunteer association there. I am not aware that there has been any such association in Quebec or in the Maritime provinces so far. But, perhaps under the fostering care of my hon. friend, he will be lucky enough to develop enthusiasm in the hitherto recalcitrant provinces.
I again call the attention of the House to these words: that these volunteers will be called upon to serve on the ships of the Royal navy. So that, in case of emergency, the men who are to-day going to volunteer in British Columbia, on the lakes, on the St. Lawrence river and on the gulf, can at any time be called upon to serve, not upon Canadian ships, but upon the ships of the

Royal navy, and to be scattered all over the world,	and disembowelled upon
the seas	of Japan and	China.
Here we are .just where we were three yeaTS ago. Who could have imagined that my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), my hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Coderre), my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nan-tel), and, shall I say also, the right hon. gentleman who presides over the deliberations of the House at this moment, should have lived to see the day when under the aegis of a Conservative Government men should be taken from Canada to be disembowelled upon the seas of China and Japan? Sir, revenge has come to many of us upon this side of the House who endeavoured at much cost and sacrifice to do what we believed to be our duty. We wanted to have a navy on our shores for our own defence, and we acted in accordance with the views of our friends on the other side of the House. They, however, have changed their minds, and now we have what was never contemplated: Canada becomes a training station for the imperial navy.

Is there no explanation from the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Borden)? No explanation from the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier)? No explanation from the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel)? Well, if they are not willing to explain, I shall have to say a few words in order to put plainly before the public the facts of the case. We all remember the policy adopted unanimously by this House in 1909, when the right hon. gentleman, then leader of the House, and my right hon. friend the then leader of the Opposition, both agreed upon a Canadian naval policy. We know further that in the following year an Act was passed entitled the Naval Service Act of Canada. We know that this Act was assailed from the moment it was placed upon the statute-book. In the province of Ontario it was attacked by the frothy jingoes, who 'contended that it was a separatist policy. In fact, the whole stock in trade of the jingo Tory party 'in Ontario was: First of all, Laurier was responsible for the Ne Temere; then, in sixteen or seventeen constituencies, Fielding had ruined the depositors of the Farmers Bank; in some other constituencies, Laurier was aiming at the annexation of Canada to the United States; and in many back concessions it was whispered that Laurier was the agent of the Pope of Rome. The cry in the province of Quebec, engineered

by the Postmaster General, the Minister of Inland Revenue, the chairman of this committee, and many others, was that Laurier had sold Canada and the French-Canadians to John Bull by placing upon the statute book that most nefarious legislation, the Naval Service Act of Canada. My hon. friend the Postmaster General and the Minister of Inland Revenue stated everywhere they spoke on the hustings that the poor children of French Canadians would be compelled to serve on board the battleships of John Bull and expose their lives for the defence of a flag for which they did not care. In fact, one of them said that in order to secure our political liberty our ancestors had been obliged to bore holes with bullets in that flag. The enlistment of our young men was not to be a voluntary enrolment; it was to he a conscription such as they had in Germany, in France, and generally on the European continent. In the election of Drummond and Arthabaska our friends on the other ' side of the House, the tri-coloured fiag-wavers, even sent emissaries into the back concessions with brass buttons-it was at the time of the census-and these pseudo officers were asking the good wives and good mothers how many children they had, because forsooth that .infernal Laurier wanted to take their children and, under the Naval Service Act, enlist them in the Imperial navy. We know what success such misrepresentatione had in the province of Quebec. Sir, in 1911 the Liberal speakers in that province could barely be heard on the platform when they attempted to explain the provisions of the Naval Service Act of 1910. After the election, the right hon. the present Prime Minister, our opponents said, was going to repeal that diabolical Act-yes, Sir, repeal it on the first day of the first session of this Parliament. When Parliament convened, the following question was put by the hon. member for Yamaska (Mr. Mondou):
1.	Does the Government intend to propose to repeal the Naval Service Act?
2.	If so, does the Government intend, in case of such repeal, to propose another act containing the policy of the Government in the matter?
3.	If such other act is proposed, is it the intention of the Government to submit the same for the approval of the people before being put into force?
The following reply was made:
Mr. Hazen:	The answer to each of these
three questions is-'Yes.'	After such consideration and inquiry as may he necessary, the Government will present its naval policy

to Parliament and to the people. That policy will undoubtedly require legislation which will involve the repeal of the present Naval Service Act. In the meantime that Act will remain on the statute book for purposes in connection with fisheries protection service and otherwise. Before any permanent naval policy is put into force, the people will he given an opportunity to pronounce upon it.
Sir, are we now to be told that our young men who are going to serve as volunteers not only in the Canadian navy but in the Imperial navy as well, will serve fqr the protection of the fisheries ? Mr. Chairman, you know as well as I do, so does .the Postmaster General, and so does the Minister of Inland Revenue, that according to this Order in Council, surreptitiously passed in the dying days of this session, our young men will be called upon to serve in the Imperial navy, nothing more and nothing less; And the Niobe and the Rainbow-the tinpot navy-will be used as training ships for our Canadian boys, thus fulfilling every condition embodied in this abominable Naval Service Act of 1910 with this exception, however, that according to that Act, our young men could not serve in case of emergency on the other side of the water without the sanction of the Canadian Parliament. That was a manly policy, it was a Canadian and truly patriotic policy. Sir, by this Order in Council our young sailors can pass automatically to the Imperial navy without the Canadian Parliament having ever been consulted. It is only right that this should be made known to the people of Canada, and it will be made public between the few months that will elapse between prorogation and the convocation of Parliament next session.
Sir, we were told that Canada could not afford to man ships, that the seamen serving on 'board the Rainbow and the Niobe were not Canadians but mostly all English. When the Postmaster General delivered that great Imperialistic speech of his on the floor of this House in December, 1912, he declared that wo could not enlist Canadians in the British navy. Of course the Prime Minister had previously said that we could not expect to have a Canadian built navy within fifty years. My hon. friend the Postmaster General went one better, and said that besides we could not get the men. I have his exact words here. Referring to the Liberals, he said ('Hansard,' page 1099):
Do they know that practically they could not get men in this country even for the Niobe and the Rainbow? Do they know that we must go to England to get men to man those ships? Do our friends know what wages-
Of course, he was sizing up the question to his own measurement:
-what wages are paid on hoard those ships, and what wages are paid on hoard British warships? It is an interesting matter to know this, when these great men are launching this great policy. Let me tell them. In Canada ordinary seamen are paid 50 cents a day in Great Britain they are paid 28 cents a day.
I would like to know what wages our young men of the Niobe and the Rainbow will be paid when they will be called upon to serve on ships in the Imperial navy. Later on, when my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) interrupted him, the Postmaster General asked:
Mr. Pelletier: Where, then, are you going to find your men?
Mr. Beland: We are going to find them in Canada.
Mr. Pelletier: Let me tell my hon. friend from Beauce, who was Minister of Marine and Fisheries-*
He made a mistake there.
-for a few days, that, without either increase of pay or conscription, he would not get enough men in Canada for a sltarboard watch. Now, our hon. friends have told us they are not in favour of conscription. But their theory does not hold together, their policy does not stand on its own feet. I have here something that may help them. I have been handed a little Bill, which never saw the light of day very much hut on which I find the following words:
And then he quoted an Act which wajs supposed to have been introduced by the late Mr. Prefontaine when he was Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Aikins) also spoke on the naval question on that occasion. He was speaking of conscription, and I asked the following question:
Mr. Lemieux: Why should we have one in Canada?
Mr. Aikins: I will tell you. The people of Canada are occupied in the development of Canada. We have a young population. They are occupied in the development of Canada; they are receiving very high wages, and, assuming that the three dreadnoughts, which are to be for a time part of the Imperial navy, were to he manned by Canadians, the rate of pay would have to he twice as much or more in order to induce Canadians to go on board, than that paid to the seamen that are on board the dreadnoughts In the old country.
Mr. Lemieux: Can Canada afford to pay?
Mr. Aikins: Canada can afford to pay; hut can the people of the United Kingdom afford to double the wages of their ordinary seamen in order to man their own vessels? I would consider myself wanting in duty if I did not say a few words in this discussion from an angle a little different from that occupied by my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux). My right hon. friend leading the Opposition and my hon. friend from Rouville, would be perhaps a little less human than they are, if they did not take what party advantage there is to be got from the policy that *stands behind the vote .under the consideration of this committee. Personally, having learned my politics in the old land, I endeavour to view matters of foreign policy-and I think the committee will, do me the justice that in the many debates we have had upon this .subject I have given, evidence of that fact-I have endeavoured to view questions of foreign policy from a non-partisan standpoint, as often as it is possible to do so in the common interests of this country and of the British Empire.
I rise to congratulate my right hon. friend at the head of the Government, and the Government, upon the policy, as far as it has been outlined and developed by the Minister of Marine this afternoon, and as far as I understand it. My right hon.

leader said that the Government had advanced; but there is a very important sense in which they have receded. We aTe voting to-night one million dollars of expenditure, while last year there was a proposition from that side of the House to spend a concrete sum of $35,000,000, and to go from $35,000,000 to $1,000,000 is receding, not advancing. In receding, I am bound to say that the Prime Minister is not unaccompanied, because while he made a proposition to spend $35,000,000 in a certain way which I very strenuously, and I hope always respectfully and in all seriousness, opposed, there was another proposition which involved an expenditure I should say somewhat larger, so that there has been receding all around upon this question. I want to congratulate my right hon friend and his Government, from my peculiar angle, and with my somewhat ardent views, perhaps, upon that very outstanding feature of the situation. As far as this vote develops a policy, I want to congratulate the Prime Minister further; I want to congratulate him upon the moral courage of having his Minister of Marine stand up here and lay down a policy which I believe, in common with my friends near me, is the nucleus of a proper policy for Canada. I do not think that to recede from a false position-and I do not want to assume any more than my right hon. friend would be prepared to admit himself-is a matter for humiliation. On the contrary, it is a matter for congratulation; it requires moral courage to recede from a false position. Perhaps I should offer my congratulations to both sides of the House, because I do not see that there is any great enthusiasm at the present moment for what are known', I think, as fleet units.
I want to congratulate my right hon. friend the Prime Minister still further on being a party, with his Government, to the development of Canada along sane lines of national progress. On the whole, I think that the policy as it has been expounded by the minister in charge will meet with very lllarge approval from the people of this country. The Minister of Marine has given us the nucleus of a policy which is creditable in every way to a self-reliant people. I stand absolutely where I have always stood in principle upon this matter, and I rise from a sense of absolute duty to protest against any too-partisan view of this question, and to make it easy for the Government to take what I believe to be a sound
position, and a position in which they will lead the whole Canadian people along the lines of a sane national development, inside, if you like, a sane imperialism. I think the committee will do me the justice of feeling that I have the right to congratulate not only the Government, but the members of the Opposition, and the country, and the empire-for I also am human- upon the fact that those of us who from the beginning of these debates over five years ago pleaded that we should not be carried away by what is commonly called, jingoism, to the exaggeration of emergencies or to the imagination of emergencies, are justified by the events ot to-day.
It is a long time since this navy question emerged; It was in my first session of Parliament, I think, on the 29th of March, 1909, that these debates began, and while it is true that upon the occasion of the very first debate my hon. friend who now holds the portfolio of Trade and Commerce had considerable war-paint about his person, I am not at all sure that my right hon. leader was not attired in hues almost as glaring. There was a good deal of emergency in the air at that time. I think I owe it to myself to recall that even in that debate I protested against our being carried away too far by this idea of emergencies. Last year there was an emergency on to some limited degree, more limited on the other side of the House than on this side, to the extent that $35,000,000 would be less money than would be necessary to buy two fleet units. I think the country should be congratulated that the emergency is over. I rose to offer very sincere words of congratulation to the Government upon the sane point at which we have arrived in our national history, and I trust my hon. friend the Prime Minister will not be too much put out by what has fallen from the lips of my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). If I were to criticise my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) I would say he has no excess of that generosity which would characterize a brave man in the moment of what he even conceives to be a victory.

Do not be too hard on
me.

I should not like to be one-tenth as hard on my hon. friend as he was trying to he on my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. I beg to offer these congratulations in the very best spirit; congratulations to the Government, and

congratulations to the country, and congratulations to the empire, that for the moment the German menace and a lot of menaces are not as near as they were, and that the nation has a fair chance of being embarked upon a non-partisan, rational development of its naval defence policy.

I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Michael Clark) that I was not very much affected by the remarks of my hon. friend from Eouville (Mr. Lemieux), because he seemed throughout his speech to be engaged in firing only blank cartridges. He resorted a good deal to the scrap book; but he did not give us any reminiscences of the young man who, a good many years ago, wrote a certain noted letter with regard to the absolute duty of Canadians not to take any part whatever in naval defence, and who uttered a stirring rebuke to the Chamber of Commerce in the city of Montreal for their venturing to pass a resolution with regard to that subject.	[DOT]

My hon. friend is not
too accurate. I shall have to make another speech.

If the next speech of my hon. friend is not more accurate than the one which he has just uttered, I think he might spare the House. Also he did not give us any reminiscences of a young man who engaged very actively in a campaign in 1896 in the province of Quebec, which campaign was largely directed towards making the people of that province acquainted with the enormity of the Conservative Government, which under very peculiar conditions had brought down a certain grant for arms and ammunition. My hon. friend the member for Eouville has no recollection of that campaign, no recollection of participating in it, no recollection whatever of the literature which was distributed by the party of which he was a member in that province at the time. If he had any recollection of these incidents he would perhaps consider himself very much humiliated by the speech which he made to-night; but, as he has no recollection of them, as these matters pass very gently and easily from his mind, my hon. friend is inclined to be somewhat exuberant in his criticism of the Government. I have not yet learned whether or not he is opposed to the proposal made by the Government.
I am against the Government.

I think that is the explanation of the whole matter. My hon. friend is against the Government, whatever it may do; and in that respect he offers a striking contrast to the broad-minded example of the hon. member for Eed Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) who sits behind him. It would be better for my hon. friend the member for Eouville to fashion himself in that regard a little more upon the hon. member for Eed Deer, who when important matters are under consideration, is able to free himself for the time being from the feeling that he must always oppose the Government on every conceivable subject, and who is ready to give the Government credit if he thinks it is taking a commendable course according to his judgment and his point of view. My hon. friend from Eouville, however, can hardly be expected to change his mode of thought and his general temperament at this stage of his career, and I have no great hopes that he will follow the example of the hon. member who has spoken from the seat just behind him.
I am not going to rehearse the naval debate at all. We had enough of it last year. All I have to say with regard to it-
We had a lot of it.

I think my hon. friend
from South Eenfrew agrees with me. All I can say is that I never used the word ' emergency ' in the speech with which I introduced our proposals, but I presented to the House a statement from the Admiralty which as I believed gave a true appreciation of the conditions with which the empire was confronted with relation to the necessities of common defence, and I based upon that statement certain proposals which passed this branch, but not the other branch of the legislature. As to the truth, accuracy and sincerity of the statements which were furnished to us from official sources, and upon which we based our proposals, I have only this to say, that, since our proposals tailed in this Parliament,
for reasons upon which I shall not dwell, it has been found necessary in the mother country to make a certain provision by reason of our failure to bring that assistance which we had proposed to bring. According to my apprehension, that perhaps is as good justification of the action which we proposed to take at that time as any one in

this House or in this country ought to desire.	.
My hon. friend the member for Rou-ville could not get through his speech without referring to the word ' autonomy.'
It is in the dictionary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is in the dictionary,
but it is not so much in the dictionary as it is in the mind and brain of my hon. friend. It haunts him; it gives him bad dreams all the time. Whenever he wakes up in the morning, he thinks his autonomy is to be destroyed; and when he goes to bed at night, he dreads lest it shall be gone when he awakens in the morning. My hon. friend really has not any fear about it; but he thinks that it is a good catchword, and that it will be useful later on when he raises the bugbear of the disappearance of our autonomy. Who has threatened the autonomy of Canada? Has the British Government or the British Admiralty done so? Has any one on this side of the House or on the other side done so?_ I have yet to learn that anything of the "kind is contemplated; the reference of my hon. friend in that regard is absolutely gratuitous, and it has absolutely nothing behind it in the mind of himself or of any other gentleman on the other side of the House.
So far as this proposal is concerned, it is based upon requests which have come from different parts of Canada, that men might be permitted to engage in certain naval training just as men in Canada are permitted and indeed encouraged to engage in military training. It was thought desirable that the opportunity should be given to them. Is my hon. friend for or against our action in that regard? He has not told us. If he really is against it, I suppose he will make a motion condemning the Government for having embarked upon a proposal of this kind. If on the other hand he is in favour of it, then it seems to me he is taking up a great deal more of the time of the House than is necessary under the circumstances.
Some reference was made by my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and also by the hon. member for Rouville to what was said last year as to the difficulty of getting men to engage in a permanent naval service in Canada. Every one in this House knows that the permanent force of Canada at the present time is composed, if I remember rightly, of 75 or 80 per cent of men born outside of Canada-in the United Kingdom. The Royal Northwest Mounted Police is composed, to the extent of 75 or

80 per cent, of men born in the United Kingdom! What is the reason for that? The reason, which I explained last year, is, that there are so many opportunities in Canada for men to engage in active pursuits which are more remunerative that they do not feel inclined to enter either a permanent naval force or * permanent military force, or even the Northwest Mounted Police, which presents many attractions to men who are fond of military life. That, however, is entirely consistent with the fact that a great many thousand people enroll themselves in the volunteer militia force of Canada. What is the reason why Canadians engage in the one and not in the other? It is that men can enter the militia force of Canada without foregoing the opportunities which this country affords to them of making a livelihood, of saving money, of doing well in the world; whereas if they become members of a permanent military or permanent naval force, those opportunities would be absolutely lost. Therefore, while it might be a very difficult thing to get men in Canada, either on the Atlantic' or on the Pacific coast, to become members of a permanent naval force, many men are eager to enter a volunter naval force just as they enter the volunteer military force of this country.
In either case, as I said last year, all material considerations to which I have alluded would disappear absolutely if the country had need of their services; and therefore, there is nothing incongruous in the proposals of the Government, which are perfectly sane and reasonable and along the lines laid down on this side of the House last year. It would be very difficult in this country at this time to raise a permanent naval force, just as it would be difficult to raise a large permanent military force. But it is quite possible that we may make a considerable advance in the organization of the force which my hon. friend the Minister of the Naval Service proposes. I hope that the proposals which he has placed before the House will result in the training of a large number of men; and I do not doubt that, if occasion offered, and an emergency arose, these men would be quite prepared to serve their country either in the Canadian navy or in the Royal navy.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to have the
commendation of my hon. friends. I am glad that on this question at least we are united in our views. This view is not new, so far as I am concerned, because I said the very same thing last year. I said that while men in Canada would not be disposed, by reason of the considerations to which I have alluded, to engage in a permanent military force, I did not doubt that Canada from one end of the country to the other would be ready to come forward. in any emergency if the country were in danger-That is all that this means. I did not doubt that then; I do not doubt it now.
My hon. friend from Bouville seems to be disturbed by the provision in the Order in Council that these men may be called upon to serve in the Canadian navy or in the Boyal navy. That is a term of the Order in Council. Every man engaging in naval service will know precisely what it means and what his dnties will be in case war should come; and no Canadian, I think, will be disposed to shrink from entering the service on that account. I do not doubt that a considerable force will be raised under these proposals, nor that it will be useful and effective, when occasion requires.
Something was said by my hon. friend from Bouville about this Order in Council having been passed in a surreptitious manner. May I ask to what he alludes?

At the end of the
session.
I see. Are all orders passed at the end of the session surreptitious measures?
Some.

Seme, but not all. My hon. friend argues that Orders in Council passed at the end of a session are surreptitious only in some cases; that is the only qualification which he gives. This Order in Council was passed in the same way as other Orders in Council. Intimation of it was given to tho press, and when my right hon. friend noticed it in the press he made inquiries across the floor of the House, and asked that it be laid on the table, and it was laid on the table at once. If there had been any desire for secrecy it might have been left until the 325J
session was over. It was not left ; it was passed during the currency of the session, and intimation was given to the press, because we had nothing to feaT by reason of the passing of this Order in Council; we were not afraid of any criticism that might "be directed against it; and my hon. friend the member for Bouville did no justice to himself when he endeavoured to insinuate, rather than state, that, there was some attempted secrecy; there was none, and no one in the House knows it better than he does.

One of the ministers in the debate yesterday quoted these words:
While the lamp holds out to burn
The vilest sinner may return.
We are taking the sinners over in a bunch to-night, and there never were bigger sinners on this naval question than the gentlemen I see looking at me. But do you not think, Mr. Chairman, that the Government is out of order? They are discussing a matter which is on another part of the Order Paper in the form of. a Bill to abolish the Naval Service Act. If the Speaker were in the Chair I would ask him for a ruling. The Government has actually introduced ;an item and brought on a discussion upon a question which has been side-tracked in another part of the Order Paper. But I am afraid I would not like to appeal to the Chairman upon it, because I might get him tangled up on details. How are we going to be extricated and see where the Government is? The hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. L'Esperance), who has just left the Chamber, early in the session gave notice that he was going to wipe the Naval Service Act off the statutes; he was going to do it because some twenty men around him in the House had given their pledge that it should be done. Whatever else the others might do who are in the Government, or wanted to get in, he, at least, was going to clear the air and wipe out this Naval Service Act. Of course, he did not show the courage necessary to wipe off a slate with a sponge. His Bill has been put in the governmental scrap heap, and the Government have brought in an item which, my hon. friend the minister of the Naval Service says is to be expended under the Naval Service Act, which was to be wiped out a few weeks age. A good many bon. gentlemen bad promised to vote for that Bill. I am told, that if it came to a vote, at least fifteen or twenty would be forced to vote for it. Now it has gone the way of all the earth.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They said that some on the other side were going to vote for it too.

They were not well informed. The Government made sure it did not come to a vote either. I am not sure but that they invited the hon. member for Montmagny to go away for a trip, which he did; and, after going away and enjoying himself, after serving notice on the Government, he returned to find his baby, buried, or as the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) says, embalmed and cremated-dead beyond hope of resurrection; and the Government he has followed so faithfully actually introduces an item under the Naval Service Act. We may take this for granted, that the Naval Service Act is not going to be repealed; the Government dare not repeal it, and we told them that months ago. I can imagine I see some hon. gentlemen hanging back a little. They may need some helping along, but they are coming, and, after taking this first taste of the Liberal policy of a naval service developed under the Naval Service Act, they will get accustomed to it. After all, it is the only policy for the Dominion of Canada which is worthy of its citizens. And I am not chiding the Government. I am just sympathizing with them in the difficulties they are in, and I hope the hon. member for Montmagny will not be too severe upon them for taking advantage of him.
Just one other point. I am glad that hon. gentlemen opposite now repudiate all their criticisms of the Niobe and the Rainbow. The afflictions of office are bringing them to a saner frame of mind. You know, Mr. Chairman, that all over the country the Niobe and the Rainbow were jeered at as being of no use. It was claimed that the money spent on them was wasted, and whenever an accident occurred to one of these steamers, it brought joy to the hearts of the Government members. Whenever there was an accident; whenever the Rainbow or the Niobe ran on a rock, there was great rejoicing among hon. gentlemen opposite; the Government almost seemed sorry that the boat had not gone to the bottom, and the Conservative press featured it with big headlines. I am glad that the Government has seen the error of its ways and that it has rebuked its followers in that respect. To-night the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who, under the Naval Service Act, is the head of the Naval Service of Canada, which will never 
be repealed, says that the Niobe and the Rainbow are going to be used for the identical purpose for which the Liberal Government purchased them. These two ships were never purchased as fighting ships; they were purchased from the British Government at the suggestion of the British Admiralty for the purpose of training men for a Canadian navy. I welcome the Government in their adoption of the only sane policy which can be imagined for the Dominion of Canada. I shall not gloat over the Government's accepting the policy of the Liberal party; I merely refer to it as a fact. I earnestly entertain the hope that in the future the Government will follow the procedure which they have now started, and that they will not be stampeded by any body into an emergency that is only in the clouds. I hope and trust that they will not see thunderbolts when there is no thunder ; that	they will not see any
flashes of lightning where there is no cloud. I congratulate the Government upon their gradually getting back to the policy unanimously adopted by this House in the year 1909. So long as they proceed along the lines of developing in Canada, slowly it may be, something that will be our own; something that will be Canadian; so long as they proceed along the line of defending our own commerce as it grows in time of peace and of coming to the assistance of the mother land willingly and gladly in time of trouble, they can count on my support as a member of this House.

I am not, I confess, so charitable as the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark). I cannot congratulate the Government upon the course which they have adopted, because they have gone only part of the way; they have shown some repentance, but they have not shown any desire to correct their error. It is quite true that at last we have adopted the Naval Service Act; we are thankful thlat this matter is settled. We shall no longer have public opinion diverted from its true purposes, because it is a settled fact that the Naval Service Act will be maintained. But my hon. friend has met the Naval Service Act only half way; he is giving us a Naval Act emasculated of its best features. My hon. friend told us a moment ago that he wanted to have naval volunteers as we now have volunteers on

land. But wbat is the use of having naval volunteers if we have no ships? The policy of my hon. friend last year was ships without men; this year his policy is men without ships. What is the use of going to this expense? The hon. member for Bed Deer a moment ago congratulated the Government for having taken a fall from $35,000,000 to $1,000,000. I may point put that they could have fallen still lower, for what is the use of training men at an expense of $200,000 if we have no ships to put them	in?	If we	are to	haveno navy,	we	do not want	anysailors; it	is	absurd	to talk otherwise. My	hon.	friend	tells us	that
the men may be taken into the imperial navy. For my part, I object to that policy, and have always objected to it. I have [DOT]always taken the view that if we are to take any part in our own defence-and I believe that we should do so-we should do it ourselves, like men, having our own ships and our own men also. But that is not the policy of my hon. friend. He does not realize to what dangers he exposes himself on the part of his national allies. Last session when another branch of the legislature rejected the offeT made the Government of $35,000,000 to buy ships, we were told in the province of Quebec that that policy was much better than the policy of the late 'Government, because the proposal was to offer ships and ships alone, whilst our policy was a tribute of blood. For my part, I cannot congratulate hon. gentlemen opposite; nor can I be .as charitable as is my hon. friend behind me, foT although the Government have gone so far, they have not gone far enough.
This is >a very interesting and amusing spectacle indeed.

I wish , Armand
Lavergne were here.

other side. Let my hon. friends opposite get out of that what comfort they can.
That is funny.

The hon. member for Rouville has succeeded in making a mountain out of a mole hill. Our good friends on the other side say that we are without a policy, without any issue on which to go to the people, and they think that they themselves have at last

'To pervert it,' I added.

Those were not the words used. My hon. friend sees now that he has gone too far, and would like to recall that sentence. We have not gone back to the Laurier naval policy, and I hope to God we never shall.

The hon. member for South Renfrew has told us that the Laurier policy was simply to use the Nioibe and the Rainbow as training ships. What are the twelve hundred men forerunners of?

Let us stick to my question. We .have bean told to-night that the policy of the late Government was simply to have two ships for training purposes. Let us look at the statute-book; look at the declarations which have been made on the flooT of this House; look at the Order in Council; look at the tenders which were prepared by the late Government, and you will find that it was proposed to have a navy which could not fight -a ridiculous and impossible navy, composed of ships which would have been a disgrace to Canada. That is what the Laurier naval policy amounts to. There it is, and there it is to stay, and history will speak of it as an ahsnbitely-if I may

be pardoned the word-absurd and impossible proposition. Is that our policy today? Nobody will say that it resembles it in the least. The	right hon.
leader of the Opposition himself says that we axe going to have	men
without ships. The Laurier naval policy was to have ships which would be unable to fight, and to put men into those ships. The distinction is easily understood by gentlemen who will understand it. I have described the Laurier naval policy of 1910. What was the policy of my right hon. friend last year? It was to have two fleet units, one on the Atlantic and one on the Pacific. Is that a fact or is it not? That is the latest policy of the right hon. leader of the Opposition. To-day we are asked by a certain number of young men who have been training of their own volition to allow them to enter upon a naval career. We have said: Yes, that is all right.

You fooled them once.

Next summer perhaps.

My hon. friends are
very desirous of having an election next summer. They have been asking for an

election ever since we have been in power. These hon. gentlemen, instead of devoting their energies to the promotion of measures for the welfare of the country, have been clamouring for an election. We saw the results in the Liberal stronghold of Chateauguay. We were told that we dare not go before the people of Quebec with our naval policy. We had a by-election in Chateauguay, our policy on the naval question was put side by side with the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, the electors were invited to decide as between them, and in that Liberal stronghold where never since Confederation had a Conservative been elected, and where, as we were told, we dare not show ourselves before the people, our candidate received the approval of the electors. I asked the hon. Postmaster General a question and he said he was coming to it. He told us that the Niobe and the Rainbow were the forerunners of a great fleet. I asked him what the 1,200 men were the forerunners of but my hon. friend has failed to give me an answer.

I just answered the
hon. gentleman. I said that we had been asked by a number of young men, principally in British Columbia, who had volunteered to organize themselves, to give them opportunities for a naval training. They told us that they were willing to adopt this as their career and that it was a career that- they, as young Canadians, would like to enter upon. We have simply met their wishes by giving them the opportunity which they desire. We are told by hon. gentlemen opposite that this is an organization under the Liberal Naval Act. Well, everybody who is in good faith, and I know that everybody opposite is in good faith, will admit that this movement could have been organized under the old Cartier law. But that law was repealed by the Liberal Administration in 1910.

You should
have said that in 1911.

What features?

into that. I have said that many times on the floor of this House and I am not going to repeat myself to-night even if it were to please my hon. friend from Rouville, and everybody knows that it is such a great pleasure to me to please him as often as I can. To-night he will have to excuse me if I do not gratify him and discuss all these matters.

Not for my sake, but
for the sake of Armand.

Armand can take
care of himself. My hon. friend has too many people to take care of. My hon. friend has not forgotten the meeting which he had with Armand at St. Hyacinthe and be has kept Armand in remembrance ever since. My hon. friend .always has a keen remembrance of anybody who has .done him what he considers a bad turn, and therefore he brings Mr. Lavergne into the discussion to-night. My hon. friend remembers the very sad day of the great St. Hyacinthe meeting. But, at all events', I think, as I said at the outset, that my hon. friend has really found a mare's nest. He is trying to build up a mountain out of a most natural and most reasonable thing and a thing which, to my .mind, is very far from the Liberal policy and the Laurier Naval Act. I may be right or I may be wrong, but hon. gentlemen will admit that after all my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) sounded the right note to-night. But that does not suit some hon. gentlemen opposite for the reason that they would like to make a little political capital out of this matter.
We do not know anything about that.

I know that my hon. friend from Three Rivers does not; he is a saint in politics and never makes any political capital, but perhaps other hon. gentlemen do. Let me commend to my hon. friends opposite the patriotic words which my hon. friend from Red Deer has uttered here to-night and which I think might have been accepted by hon. gentlemen if the strong desire to make political capital had not been burning in their hearts. I think we will understand one another better after this and that my hon. friends will realize that -they are trying to do an impossible thing when they undertake to make the people believe the foolish things which they have said here to-night or to accept the

appeals which they have addressed ifco them and which they were apparently -able to get them to accept -during the last fifteen years. But, the day for that is gone.

My hon. friend has discussed every other subject which he could think of but he has not answered my question. He has told me that a number of young men in British Columbia had asked the Government to allow them to train as seamen but I want to know what the 1,200 men are the forerunners of and, furthermore, upon what ships they are going to train.

I have answered the
question.

I want an answer as to
the ships. Is it the intention of the Department of the Naval Service to purchase new ships, or to have new ships built, or to use those that they have?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think that my h-on. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) was not in the House when I explained what had occurred and what it is proposed to do. These men will train a -certain number of days each year, just as the militia train now, and then they will supplement the training which they receive on shore by training on 'board ship and for this purpose the ships -that belong to the country, ships like the Rainbow and Niobe, and ships belonging to the fishery protective service, will be used.
Is it intended that these men will ever fight?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am quite sure that if
the occasion -comes when any fighting has to be done, being Canadian, they will not run away.
I notice that mine sweeping is one of the subjects that the cadets are to be trained in. Will the minister be good enough to tell us what that branch is?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is a well known branch of the training in the navy. In cases where harbours have been mined, and where there is danger of the mines being exploded by ships passing into the harbour, means are taken to what they call sweep the harbour so as to protect vessels from the danger of the explosion of these mines.
Does it involve submarine vessels ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

The Postmaster General has taken considerable satisfaction out of the

congratulations of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark); but it strikes me that the congratulations of the hon. member would have been somewhat more justified had the Prime Minister shown the same courage in 1911 as he has to-night. Had the right hon. gentleman in 1911 insisted on giving his naval policy to the electors of the province of Quebec, he would not have been placed in the humiliating position of being unrecognized by his supporters and allies in that province. It is well within the memory of most men in this House that in 1911 the allies of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec, many of them its most influential members, refused to go on the same platform with the Right Hon. Mr. Borden because they did not share his views on the naval question.
They will go now.

It is a question whether they will or not. The Postmaster General has just told us that the naval policy of the Government was endorsed in the late election in Chateauguay. Had the Postmaster General when he was in Chateauguay during that election, proposed the policy that has been propounded to-night, and had the Conservative candidate been then returned, he would have had some justification for his statement. But during the campaign in Chateauguay last fall, not only did the representatives of the Government, from the minister down to the humblest speaker of the back concessions, not present any permanent naval policy, but the people were told distinctly by the Postmaster General that the Government would not present any permanent naval policy before it was submitted to the people. Le Devoir of the 7th of October, stated in a leading article, commenting on the Chateauguay election, that the Government could take no credit for the people having approved their naval policy, because as a matter of fact the Conservative candidate was a man of peace and had run away from the naval policy of the Government. This editorial in Le Devoir states emphatically that the Postmaster General told the people of Chateauguay that no naval policy would be entered on until it had been submitted for the approval of the people. Apparently the Government have now developed a little more courage and, as has been pointed out, they are taking another step in advance. But when the Postmaster General claims that the people of Chateauguay pronounced upon the policy of the Government

oi65
in the Chateauguay election, he is contradicted directly by his own leading organ in the province of Quebec.

Translation.) Mr. Chairman, the sight witnessed in this House to-night is of exceptional interest. How far we are from the principles proclaimed at the Lorette meeting! What a wonderful change has been wrought in the men and their views! However; as regards the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) my surprise is not so great. The hon. minister has accustomed us to sudden metamorphoses. Like some butterflies he readily adapts his colouring to that of the meadows over which he flits.
I am somewhat more surprised at the stand of some other members hailing from the province of Quebec and especially from my district. While the hon. member for Rouville had the floor I noticed the hon. member for Montmagny suddenly effecting his exit. Is it not that same hon, gentleman who, in the early part of the session, introduced a Bill for the repeal of the Laurier Naval Act? He had made that promise to his constituents and the contents of his Bill were published in every newspaper of the province of Quebec. Unfortunately, the state of his health did not permit him to carry out his pledge, and shortly after he departed to travel over the high .seas and breathe the invigorating air of European climes. To-day he is back, we have seen him in this House a few moments ago, and now he has this rare opportunity to call on the Government to do away with every vestige of that law which he denounced in such strong terms.
All the other representatives from the district of Quebec who support the Government had also promised, and even sworn, to have that Act repealed, if their party were returned to- power. Yourself, Mr. Chairman (Mr . Blond-in), you remember that all the church steeples in your county were called to witness that this accursed Act, ae you called it, would be struck from the statute hook at the very first session following on the elections. Indeed, I remember well that you prayed at the church door of every parish in the fine county of Champlain, the patron saints of both sexes,-since the hon. ' .member for Three Rivers heard you make that same appeal to St. Genevifeve,-to esn-(lighten the electors under their protection, so that they might vote against that nefarious Act the effect of which would be to have our children butchered, for the sake of the British, in every quarter of the [DOT]world.
My hon. friend from L'Islet, whom I do not see at his seat just now, is also losing a fine opportunity of fulfilling his pledges to his electors. Great heavens, what .abundant tears did he not shed! We have now reached the third .session, and as yet nothing has been done. And what do these hon. gentlemen say in the province of Quebec to excuse the apathy of their Government? They say the Laurier Act is not repealed, but it is practically a dead letter in the statutes and we have not carried it out.
Hear, hear.

Let the hon. gentleman who has just said 'Hear, hear', get up, .if he dare, and assert that the Order in Council creating a naval reserve is not *based on the Laurier Act and even does not exceed its provisions.
The hon. Postmaster General, though he .was far from favouring the Naval Bill of *1910, seemed to rejoice over the statement *made by the hon. member for Rouville that .the Government, in passing that Order in .Council, had given effect to that Naval Bill which he had so mercilessly condemned. The hon. Postmaster General is making a grievous mistake. That Order in Council goes a good deal farther than the Naval Bill of 1910. There is nothing in that Act to justify this paragraph of the Order in Council, dated May 18, 1914:
2. The naval volunteers, if called out in the event of an emergency, will be required:
(a) To serve in the vessels of the Naval Service of Canada or in those of the Royal navy;	[DOT]
I challenge the world to find a paragraph, a section, a single word, in that Act of
