1910 that warrants the provision in the Order in Council which I have just read.
The hon. Prime Minister has made fun of those who speak of autonomy. Has he forgotten that, of his supporters in this House hailing from the province of Quebec, not one was elected in 1911 as a Conservative, hut all of them as autonomists. Not one of them acknowledged the right hon. Prime Minister as his leader. All are aware of it. They repudiated him on every husting and refused to appear by his side during the electoral campaign.
The hon. Postmaster General contends that the leader of the Opposition in this House voted last year for the establishment of two naval units, one on the Atlantic and the other on the Pacific. The hon. gentleman well knows that it was not the right hon. leader of the Opposition who then had in hand the destinies of the country. A Bill was introduced. toy the Government providing for the expenditure of $35,000,000 to build three dreadnoughts which were to be handed over to the British admiralty.
The stand we took -was that if we were bound to disburse that money we preferred applying it to the creation of a Canadian mavy destined exclusively to the defence of Canada and the protection of Canadian interests. In other words, we contended, and we still contend, that it was preferable to spend our money in the country rather than send it over to Great Britain. We do not regret that stand, and we are Toady to compare it before the people with that of the Government, so soon as an occasion offers.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if the sarcastic references of hon. gentlemen on the other side, when speaking of the Niobe and the Rainbow, wiill he reiterated by them after the establishment of that naval reserve. These two velesels will be used for the training and drilling of the men whom the Government is going ,to enlist under that Order iim Council.
I say, in conclusion, that the Government has by its action justified and vindicated the stand taken by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, in respect to that naval question. It is also the condemnation of the campaign carried on in the province of Quebec by his opponents, and the supreme humiliation of those who were returned as a result of that campaign. Their course in this House has been in open

contradiction to the views they advocated with .such violence.
I do not hesitate to say that the statements made and the stand taken by the Postmaster General to-night are marked by a show of political cynicism which has no parallel in the history of Canada,
(Translation.) I throw back with contempt that insult at the face of its author.
(Translation.) The hon. gentleman has so much contempt heaped on his head, that he can spare some for the use of others.

I want to call attention to a sentence made use of in 1910, which seems to be in line with this discussion. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) stated that the Niobe and the Rainbow were not intended to be used as fighting ships, merely as training ships. The questions that suggest themselves to my mind are these: Why were they training ships? What was the object in training men? The reason I ask these questions is because of the words made use of by the right hon. leader of the Opposition when he was introducing the Naval Service Bill in 1910. At page 1733 olf ' Hansard ' of January, 1910, you will find him using these words:
No man in this country, under the Naval Service Act or any other, will he liable to military service on the sea.
Why the training ships? For what purpose are the men being trained? The right hon. the leader of the Opposition says to-night that the former policy on this side of the House was ' ships without men,' and now it is ' men without ships.' I might refer my hon. friends opposite again to the words used by the right hon. leader of the Opposition himself in introducing the Naval Service Bill:
No man in this country, under the Naval Service Act or any other, will be liable to military service on the sea.
What is his explanation of that?

I am surprised at the question of my hon. friend. The explanation is the same as if he were in England. He knows that there are men there who are trained for the service; he knows there is no compulsion, and that' every man who goes on board a ship does so voluntarily. It will be the same thing in Canada as in England.

I understand that a man who goes on board a ship for naval training signs up for a certain length of time. In the event of war, during the time for which he had signed up, would he be free to step off the ship, or would he have to serve?

I am again
surprised at my hon. friend's question. Every one knows that every volunteer, whether on land or on sea, binds himself for a certain number of years to obey the command, whether it comes from the naval or from the military authorities.

That is exactly as I
understand the situation; but it seems to me that it is not in line with my right hon. friend's words in introducing the Naval Service Bill, namely, that no man under that Act or an.y other will be liable to military service on the sea. It seems to me that, if a man signed up for three years and during that period war took place, he would have to serve.
He would be a volunteer in the first instance.
I am assuming that he had volunteered.
That is a different matter.

Take a number of men signed up to train on the Niobe or the Rainbow for three years. I assume, if hostilities occurred during those three years, they would be obliged to serve. Yet we are distinctly told by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition that they would not be liable to serve.

He said they were not
forced to sign.
I am giving the words of the right hon. gentleman.
You have misunderstood him.

I do not think the hon.
member is serious, because the whole fight in the province of Quebec was on the question of allies, of masters or servants; and whether the Act was an Act to force every man over eighteen years and under sixty years in the province of Quebec to go into the navy, to sign an agreement whether or not he wanted to serve. The words of my right hon. friend mean that, if a man does not want to serve, he need not enroll. It must have been an effort of imagination on
the part of my hon. friend to endeavour to give it any other meaning the same as it was at the time of the debate last year when he tried to believe that I was not a Canadian.
The Postmaster General said that it was very funny to-night to hear this debate. For once in my life I agree with him. It is not only funny, 'but ridiculous. When you look back to 1911 and think of the fight that was waged, Mr. Chairman, you do not have to scratch your head very hard to remember how you said: We do not want any of our children to be disembowelled outside of the limits of Canada; it is enough to have a volunteer land force; we do not want our men to be compelled to go on the high seas of China or Japan and to be disembowelled.
I confirm what my hon. friend the member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) has said. This is the greatest piece of cynicism ever worked by any man inside or outside of Parliament. You remember yourself, Mr. Chairman, when you came to Three Rivers on the 6th of August, 1911, what was said. You said that Laurier was the destroyer of the French-Canadian race, in fact of the whole Canadian race. Mr. Bourassa, Mr. Monk, yourself and others said that is was a shame to enact such a law as the Laurier law. The .man you put up against me denounced the drill hall that bad been built at Three Rivers under Liberal rule, because, as you said, it was bringing into the hearts of the children the idea of warfare, o.f destruction of their fellow citizens; that we were holding before them a red rag, and that all we would create in Canada would be a thirst for blood. To-night the Postmaster General, after having fooled the electors of the province of Quebec, after having stolen the elections by carrying them on under false pretenses, with the assent and approval of the Tory party of Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and other provinces -we all know that they were fighting the election on the disloyalty cry, and you were fighting it on the disembowelling and the bloodshedding of our grandchildren-the Postmaster General, in answer to the question, which I put to him when he said that the Niobe and the Rainbow were only the forerunners of a greater fleet which was to be built for carrying our children, born and unborn, to foreign seas to be disembowelled-as to what this was the forerunner of, said: This is to allow a few boys in British Columbia who want to go on the ships and train, and for that purpose we

want a million dollars. The Order in Council reads:
Several petitions and representations have been received from persons and parties in the Dominion urging the organization of a naval volunteer force.
That shows that British Columbia is not the only province from which representations have come. But be that as it may, I want to impress upon the House and upon the country that, in 1911, the Nationalist party, allied with the Tory party, with you yourself, Mr. Chairman, attheir head,claimed that we were not to allow our children to serve in the Royal navy under any circumstances, although to serve in the Canadian navy would not be so bad; and they hunted up all the dictionaries and encyclopedias to make the word 'may' mean 'shall.' It was said that the power to dispose of their children was in the hands of this toad man Laurier, who did not care about sacrificing his children, because he did not have any. I do not want to make any allusions to the Prime Minister or the Postmaster General; they are young yet. They said that Act was such an awful thing that a man who had children would never dare to put on the statute book such a law as the LaurieT Naval Act.
A great outcry was made because Mr. Fielding had s-aid in the House: 'When England is at war, Canada is at war'; therefore, they said: 'Gentlemen, and you mothers and sweethearts, supposing England has to fight Japan or any other country, your children will be carried away under this nefarious law of Laurier, who has no children and does not know what the love of .children is, to be disembowelled on a foreign sea. - It is rather a ridiculous spectacle to-night to see the Postmaster General get up and say he is just doing his djuity, and to see him roll the British flag around his head and shoulders and lift his hands to heaven-as some hon. gentlemen lifted their hands to the steeples and saints of some of the churches-and say: 'I am the only patriot, the only Britisher; I never had any policy, I never preached anything else to my fellow-citizens but patriotism, but giving their blood to England, not only in the Royal navy but in the Canadian navy.' You may well say it is funny. Well, Mr. Chairman, the Postmaster General said we could not fool the people. There was a very clever American, revered in the United States, who said that you could fool some of the

people some of the time, tout that you could not fool all of the people all the time. The people were fooled in 1911, but I can tell my hon. friend the Postmaster General, who has just come in, and will give me his ear for a second, that he succeeded in fooling them in 1911; but let me te'l him that he cannot fool them again. They are awaking to his promises, and to his acknowledgment of leadership. My hon. friend just now said that the hon. member for Rouville must have had some axe to grind in referring to Armand Lavergne. Not at all. I understood the hon. member for Rouville to mention him as the leader of my hon. friend the Postmaster General. And if I remember aright, and if his paper L'Evenement reports him aright, he made that acknowledgment and bowed and offered his services as one of the most humble followers of Armand Lavergne at the meeting held at nomination time at Lorrette. Under the circumstances, I think I will not go as far as my hon. friend from Red Deer did in congratulating the Government-a Government which has taken three years to find out it has been in the wrong and to open its eyes to the light, and another party called the Nationalist party, who took so long to find it out. They do not deserve congratulations. I think the people at the head of affairs in thie country ought to find out in less than thirty-six months what is required for the good of the country. You cannot deny the fact that the policy of training these men. on the Niobe and Rainbow is exactly what we wanted to do.
Not for the Royal navy.

My hon. friend is right: it was for the Canadian navy but what they want it to be is for the Royal navy. How are my hon. friends opposite going to redeem their pledges? One of them said: In twenty-four hours-and another, a little wiser said in two weeks-after we come into power that nefarious law will be repealed.	Yet it is still on the statutebooks. My hon. friend from Montmagny (Mr. L'Esperanee), who is just coming in, has still on the Order Paper .a Bill to repeal the Naval Service Act. Is he going to force it through or not? Under what law is this volunteer force established if not under the Laurier law? And under that Act it is expected to raise 1,200 men as volunteers, and in the future

12,000 and more. As my right hon. leader said:	If you cannot give ships without
men to England, you will give England men without ships. Where will they stop, and what is the meaning of all this? I say, Sir, as has been said by somebody just now, I do not know who, it is because there is need of cementing the two parties, which were at the antipodes at the time of the election, and which had to come together to form the majority of my right ' hon. friend the Prime Minister, and they are giving on one side and on the other.
I understand the thing is going to be worked because the emergency has gone, and the $35,000,000 with. it. What surprises me is the great scandal that was aroused by the provision in the Naval Act that Parliament should be summoned in fifteen days, and could place the battleships at the disposal of His Majesty to be sent to the battleline and put into action. And to-day, without any summoning of Parliament, without any Order in Council even, just under the direction of the minister, any of these seamen in British Columbia or in the eastern provinces will be sent as sailors to the Royal Navy. I say, Sir, if there is any cynicism in this world, it is in the denunciation of Laurier as being unpatriotic and so selfish that because he had no children he did not care about sacrificing the children of others under his Navy Act. And these men, who brought terror into the female population in the province of Quebec, come to-night and say: We must do it; of course we formed an alliance with the Tories and we must stand our share; therefore we have to swallow it, and swallow it we will; and your boys will train, and if we see fit to send them across the sea you need not be afraid, thfcy will not be disembowelled, they will get fat lighting and by getting lead in their bodies. That is the only explanation I can give.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I cannot feel indifferent to this navy question; it did cost me so much work, so much worry, so much hardship and so many sacrifices, that I would fail to get my share of justice were I not permitted to make a few observations. Here is what I have to say: A talented man, a man of note, a smart orator, an extraordinary demagogue, took part in the contest of 1911. He caused us very much
trouble, he did our friends and our party a great deal of harm. I have mentioned Mr. Bourassa, the chief editor of Le Devoir.
Mr. Bourassa scoured the province and cried out.everywhere:	No navy! Cursed
be the navy! Laurier is a miscreant, he has no feeling, he would, by all means, send our children over to Japan and to China, and have them killed in behalf of England; children will be taken away from their mothers' womb and be sent out to get killed. And the people believed him.
Mr. Bourassa had with him the Postmaster General, a talented man^ a distinguished man, but an artful blade. He cheered heartily at what was said by Mr. Bourassa. I do not blame Mr. Bourassa, he was paid for his treason. He succeeded in getting $100,000 from the Conservatives to start a newspaper in which he owns most of the stock, and, moreover, he was paid $5,000 a year as chief editor.
I do not blame the Postmaster General either. He became a minister. But he changed a good deal.
I do not blame the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Nantel). He wanted to be a minister and he is a minister. But I remember the time when he cried out with indignation: ' No navy! I would have one of my wrists cut off rather than to see a navy under construction.' Well you may believe me, Mr. Chairman, he did not put his arm, he did not even cut his little finger.
The Hon. Mr. Coderre succeeded in unhooking a portfolio for himself. He is a distinguished man, a talented man; I know him very- well. But he had never been in this Chamber before, hq had no political training. This gentleman cried out everywhere : No navy! Down with Laurier! He is a miscreant, he has no feeling.
The hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. Lesperance) made similar utterances. This one is a brave man, although he has somewhat brought me into danger. I told him I would vote for the repeal of this naval law if he "pressed the adoption of his Bill. But he made off to Europe, and to-night he will vote in favour of the navy. He said: I want this law to be repealed; it must be torn off the statute-book, or I shall resign my seat.
Well, Sir, what are you doing with your promises? What surprises me in all this is the fact that men of note, honourable men, representatives of public opinion, and even ministers of the Crown, do not keep their word.

Mr. Bourassa said, when I met him in the parish of Sainte Julienne, in my county: The members who voted in favour of Laurier's law will be cursed by their children and by their grandchildren. He advised our children to curse us because we used our judgment, because we acted according to the dictates of our conscience and to the opinion of a leader in whom we had confidence.
That navy question caused me very much trouble and came pretty near causing my death. To-day, those gentlemen on the other side of the House testify to the fact that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was right.
The hon. member for Montmagny has given me no opportunity to vote for the abolition of the navy, so far, because he remembers that I told him, at the beginning of the session, that I would vote with him. Why did he not press his Bill? Yet, those gentlemen claimed that the naval law was awful, that it was robbery, tremendous squandering. Was not that Mr. Laurier a terrible man, though! Such was the language they used, and all the speakers on the Nationalist or Conservative side were cheered to the utmost. They condemned Laurier, but they added that Borden's policy was still worse. They said: He is not our chief, he does not know what he wants and we shall drive him out when we get to power. When the Prime Minister came to the Monument National, all those good Nationalists secreted themselves. He was accompanied but by Mr. Marechal, an eminent lawyer, I admit. Mr. Monk refused to go there because, to his mind, Borden's policy was still more dangerous than Laurier's policy.
When those gentlemen came to power, they asked Parliament to vote $35,000,000 to England as a contribution. The Prime Minister went over to London and promised to have those $35,000,000 voted for ilie Imperial navy. But he forgot that there were Liberal senators at Ottawa. Mr. McKay, Mr. Dandurand, Mr. Beique and others refused to vote those millions. The thirty-five million contribution was voted down by the Senate and so quick, too, that it did not even begin to savour of firkin. The Liberal members of the Senate know what Canada wants. They refused to send thirty-five millions over to London and secure work for the workmen in England while our own workmen are dying with hunger. No, they would not, by any means send thirty-five millions over to England. Honour to them ! If we have

kept our millions we owe it not to the Conservative but to the Liberal members of the Senate; they are serious, disinterested men, men who have the interest of the country at heart, and they have just given another proof of it by refusing to vote in favour of the Bill concerning the Farmers Bank. They want justice to be done.
The Postmaster General told us, a moment ago, to wait and that we would see later on. Let me tell him, in my turn, to wait and that he will see later on. When we find that a man has deceived us once, we are done with that man; we do not want to have anything more to do with him. Henri Bourassa, who is a man of refinement, an able writer, was deceived and he will not be caught again. He went everywhere to address the electors and he was left at liberty to tell lies wherever he went, because nobody came forward to contradict him. But when he visited my county I went to meet him, and I said to him: 1 You do not tell the truth,' and it did not take me long to satisfy my electors, and my opponents did not succeed in defeating me as they did in the case of so many other Liberal candidates. They said: If Borden or those who will be called upon to lead the country fail to repeal that law, we will resign under no delay.
There was just one of them who did keep his word, and I am glad to testify to that fact. That man was the late lamented member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). He had declared that not a cent would be spent previous to this legislation being submitted to the people. The poor gentleman has disappeared; let us respect his ashes. He had entered the Cabinet because he was confident that they would be true to the word which had been given. He stepped out of it, he resigned when he discovered that they were about to deceive him. Yet, the Postmaster General said to-night: ' We are united.' Yes, you are united, just about like Mr. Monk was riveted and padlocked to his portfolio, as he said, although he went out of the Cabinet a few days later. Maybe the ministers are just as united as they were at that time.
The hon. Prime Minister has alluded tonight to the speeches delivered by the Liberals during the contest of 1896 against the purchase of rifles by the then Minister of Militia (Mr. Desjardins). So we did denounce that purchase because those rifles were worthless, they went off by the breech, they were plateless rifles which killed the men who used them. We were

against the idea of buying such weapons as those.
The Order in Council now before the House shows that children may be asked, may be ordered even, to serve outside of the Canadian soil. I deny the Prime Minister and the Government the right to call Canadian children out to serve outside of our soil. I say that you have no such right under the constitution, and that such an order would be illegal and unconstitutional.
To the hon. gentlemen who are now sitting on the Treasury benches, to those who cried out:	' Cursed be the navy!'	' Down with
the navy!' I say:	'You have no right to
pass that Order in Council before taking a referendum, before making sure of the trend of public opinion on this question.
' I have no fear,' said the right hon. Prime Minister to-night. I know that those gentlemen have no fear. But we will see, when the people have been consulted, what has become of them. Speaking for myself, I say that it will be so much the better for those who change their opinion so suddenly if they can get re-elected. The people will remember that they swore everywhere that not a cent would be spent previous to a referendum being taken. And when the people take offence he kicks pretty hard and it is a serious thing, you know.
The Postmaster General said that he had no fear either. He does not fear to contradict himself and to reverse his own opinion. It is his business. I am not here to abuse anybody. I make my remarks in good faith and because I think I have a right to make them. But I wonder if there is anything more precious in a public man than being true to his word. A poor man, a poor devil who would fail in this respect would be told that he has no honour, because he did not keep his word. And those who preside over the destinies of the nation should be permitted to come and reverse their own opinion? I do not believe so, and the electors, who are their judges, will call them to account. The hon. Postmaster General knows that the opinion of the people does not always agree witn his own. He has had to put up with many defeats, as I had to put up with some myself.
I took part in the by-election in Chateau-guay and so did the Postmaster General. He heard the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny) declare and assert that $35,000,000 would absolutely be all we would vote for the British Admiralty, and that the Government had given no other pledge. There again fraud was indulged in. They
made all kinds of promises, they promised even railroads and bridges. In order to carry the election, they promised a railroad, a bridge which they would build on the St. Lawrence to connect Chateauguay with the shore opposite, they bought sheep at high prices-
(Translation.) A wager of $100 was laid.
(Translation.) Who talks of a wager? The hon. member for Vercheres! Here is another Liberal who became a Nationalist and then a ministerialist, and forgot all his promises.

(Translation.) Was not
the hon. member to resign his seat if the Liberal candidate in Chateauguay were not elected?

(Translation.) No.
The member for Dorchester was to resign his seat; but he dared not do so, because I was not afraid to meet him. He was to resign his seat, also, if the naval law were not repealed. He had promised his electors, in 1911, to do so, but he did not keep his word. They made all kinds of promises in order to deceive the electors, and to-day they are forgetting them all. It is easier. In a by-election a government is always stronger. All the Conservatives gathered together in Chateauguay, all the ministers went there and resorted to all the means of influence they had at their disposal. The election was protested. What will be the result of this? I do not know, for nobody can tell what the end of a lawsuit will be. But I say that, were the campaign to begin over again to-morrow, the Liberals would get their candidate elected and secure the defeat of the present member whom I respect.
The hon. Postmaster General claims that he has not changed his opinion; but those who have some experience and who have been acquainted with him, who have lived with him, know that he has not always been of the same opinion in politics. In 1886 he was our most prominent Liberal orator, he has made us some very fine speeches; but he has changed to a great extent since that time. I do not blame him for it, it is his business; but when he says that he never changed, we must take his word cum grano salis.
The Postmaster General was not serious when he said that what the leader of the Opposition did was a disgrace to Canada. Did not Mr. Laurier lead the country for

sixteen years and with honour in every respect? How then can the Postmaster General come to the conclusion that he was a disgrace to Canada? The hon. minister has forgotten himself, evidently, because he does talk and discuss better than this, as a general rule. He was wrong in saying that our leader was a disgrace to Canada, and he brings no evidence to show that he may be right. A man who has led the country for sixteen years and who has been in public life for about fifty years cannot be a disgrace to his country. Later on, when the Postmaster General comes to know where he is, he will admit that this expression of his was altogether uncalled for. He is not unconscious of the fact that he failed to do justice to our leader and to himself by using a word of that kind.
The Postmaster General said that the Liberal party intended to build two fleets, and to have the one on the Atlantic and the other on the Pacific. But he forgot to mention that they were to be built for the protection of Canada and not for England. Those ships were to protect us and to protect our trade. What harm would there have been in this? You are approving tonight what we did when we voted the naval law and you are doing us justice at last. If Henri Bourassa were present, he would no more advise my children to curse me. He did not know whereof he spoke; but he wanted to win the price of treason. He was obliged to fight us, as he had severed his connections with the Liberal party. The Conservatives had enlisted him, they had him in their ranks, and, of course, they had to pay him. But he became comical to the utmost when he taxed us with corruption, with slavishness, with being at the manger. Well, the ministers who are sitting on the Treasury benches to-day are at the manger, in their turn. There is no harm in that, but what makes them guilty and condemn-able is the fact that they accused us of invading the manger, of being corrupted and slavish. Do we not love our families as much as they love their own? Do I not love my wife and children as much as they love their own? Is not the piece of land on which I live as dear to me as the piece of land on which they live is dear to themselves? Have I not as much patriotism as they have? They accused us of being slavish and corrupted because we thought otherwise than they did. Well, gentlemen, you are doing us justice to-night by accepting what we have done, and you are using this as a stepping-stone to make yourselves

greater. You had succeeded in satisfying the people that Laurier's policy was not good. That was your right and your business, as it will be our right to come back to power. Shall we succeed in coming back to power? We do not know. The life of governments is very uncertain. I remember that, when Alexander Mackenzie went again before the people in 1878, he had a majority of seventy-five in this House, and that, when the election was over, he had a minority of seventy-five. In 1911 Mr. Laurier had a majority of forty or fifty, and after the election he had a minority of about the same number. Yes, the ministerial life of parties is most uncertain; but what I know is this, that the people will do us justice. Shall we be able to plead our case well enough and to bring forth enough arguments to get a verdict in our favour? History will tell. At all events, we find such serious contradictions in what the hon. ministers have done since 1911 that, as for me, I do not dread my electors. If I had but the contradictions of my opponents to show them, I would have enough already.

(Translation.) They are
going to leave you.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to reply to the hon. member for Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune). He is a very good fellow, but I think there is a great defect with him; he seems to suffer frbm a lack of memory. Having spoken about twenty minutes on this navy question last year, he could have dispensed with repeating to-night the same thing as he said then. The hon. member alluded to an Order in Council, and the hon. member for Kamouraska has quoted it also. 1 would like to hear that Order in Council read, so as to know the contents of it.
(Translation.) Here it is. Would you, please, Mr. Chairman, have this Order in Council handed over to the hon. member for Rimouski?

(Translation.) It is a
pretty long document to read; there are two pages to it, I think.

(Translation.) Just one page, and if my hon. friend allows me, I will read him paragraph 2, that is, the one we are dealing with:
2. The naval volunteers, if called out in the event of an emergency, will be required:
(a) To serve in the vessels of the Naval Service of Canada or in those of the Royal navy;
This is the paragraph you were alluding to. The hon. member for Kamouraska said that there was no clause in the law of 1910 having reference to this question, and that the Order in Council went beyond all that which is contained in this law. I think the member for Kamouraska and the member for Montcalm are lawyers-
Have you any doubt about it?

-and that, as suet, they must have understood the law of J010. They were present in Parliament and they must have understood each clause of the law. Section 26 of this law, in favour of which those gentlemen have voted, says that:
26.	The Governor in Council may organize and maintain a force to be called the Naval Volunteer Force.
This is most explicit. And section 27 adds:
27.	The Naval Volunteer Force shall consist of officers and seamen raised by voluntary engagement from among seafaring men and others who may be deemed suitable for the service in which such volunteers are to be employed.
Therefore, the Order in Council referred to does not go beyond the intention of the law of 1910 at all, and, if it does, I fail to see how, because section 26 provides for the creation of a volunteer force of the navy.
My hon. friends on the other side of the House would like to see us get rid of those two ships, the care of which they have imposed upon us. It is not our fault if we have to support the burden of maintaining those two ships. We are not going to run them ashore or to leave them unemployed. According to our friends on the other side, the reason why those ships were bought is that they should be used only as school-ships. If we utilize them to that purpose



I do not see how our friends can find anything amiss in that.

(Translation.) But
you were to sell them as scrap-iron.

(Translation.) We cannot sell them; they are not good enough. The Niobe, after being staved in against the wharf at Yarmouth, was refitted with wood. It cannot be used any more as a warship.
We are pretty well pleased with the answer of the hon. Minister of Marine to a question which was asked, last year, by the hon. member for Yaraasku (.Mr. Mondou), and I think that the forecasts of our opponents will not be realized. The hon. minister declared that nothing would be done with respect to a permanent naval policy before the electors had been consulted. True it is that we have asked and shall ask again that the law of 1910 be repealed, but we are fully satisfied with the statement we got from the Government, and I am sure that the electors in my county are fully satisfied with it also. The previsions of the hon. member for Kamouraska do not always come to pass, and the proof of this is that when he addressed a meeting in my county, on the 14th of September, 1911, he predicted that I would be defeated by a great majority, whereas, on the 21st of September, seven days later, I was elected by a majority of 432. I hope he is making another mistake as to the result of the coming election.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to take part in this debate, but I wish to criticise some of the assertions made by the hon. member for Rimouski. He told us that the Niobe and the Rainbow were good for nothing. We have heard a good deal said about those ships during the election of 1911. My opponent told the electors that those ships were only good to be sold as scrap-iron at half a cent per pound. If they were good for nothing at that time, they are good for less than nothing to-day, after four years. Why, then, spend money to maintain seamen on board those ships? Evidently, they are worth less to-day, and why, then, should we risk the lives of those seamen, of our children, as the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Demers) says? In a short speech which I delivered last year on the contribution of thirty-five millions, I said that the Government had not only to send dreadnoughts over to England, but that they also wranted seamen to man those ships. I see, now, by this Order in Council, that the Gov-
ernment intends to train twelve hundred seamen. This shows that my prevision was well founded. If it is not the intention to continue the policy of the late Administration, I fail to see why it would be necessary to train seamen in order to send them over to England.
Our opponents said, in 1911, that our law was not made for Canada, that this country had positively no use for it; but that it was made with a view to sending our children over to England and having them disembowelled in the seas of China and elsewhere. What they said was awful and spread terror in every heart. In the province of Quebec we lost at least fifteen seats on account of that question.
The hon. Postmaster General knows very well that he won his election because he was against the navy. When he scoured the province together with his leader, Mr. Armand Lavergne, entreating the electors to vote against the Government because they had passed the naval law, the electors believed in what he said as they believed also in what was said by all those who got elected, like he did, by this means.
I say that the Minister of Marine has not the majority in this House to ask us to vote those millions for the purpose of training those seamen, because the people had declared themselves against this policy in 1911.
The Prime Minister told us to-night that we, the Liberals, had talked against the armaments, against the purchase of rifles in 1896. Why not use the same kind of reasoning, said he.
Our friends the Ministerialists-the Nationalists of 1911-denied their present leader and told their electors that, in fact, Borden's policy was worse than Laurier's policy, because the former would send our money over to England, whereas we, the Liberals, would keep our money and build a fleet with it.
This question was discussed for such a long time in the House, that I shall deal with it no longer, and shall now say what I think about another matter. In 1911 we spent, for the militia, six millions and a half, and -we are going to spend fourteen millions and a half in 1914-15 for the sanae purpose. I say it is now time that we should be careful. We have too many obligations to meet, too much expenditure devolving upon us to continue that way without going to our ruin. I say that we are not to-day in a position to organize a navy, owing to engagements already entered

into. As for me and as for my electors, I say that this kind of policy is no more in keeping with our views or with the views of the people, and I do not say so out of any fear of not being supported again by my own constituents on the navy question which I approved in 1910, but because the Government refused to follow that policy and preferred to ask $35,000,000 for dreadnoughts which they would send over to England. I claim that, for many years to come, this House, Liberals and Conservatives as well, should leave this naval policy aside and completely so, say for ten or fifteen years, in order to deal with our own business. For my part, I declare here to-night, that if my electors ask me to be their candidate for another term, my platform will be this:	'No navy and no contribution for many years to come, because we have not the means to face such an emergency, and I am sure they will approve this platform as they approved it in the past.

(Translation.) I am not
in raptures with the military and naval expenditures. However, I wish to show that the hon. member for Laprairie is mistaken when he says that the Government is asking $2,460,000 for the navy this year. As a matter of justice to the country and to truth at the same time, let the hon. member look at the Estimates and he will find that the $2,460,000 are not merely for the naval service, but for the service of the whole department, as it was previous to the law of 1910, including, for instance, the protection of fisheries, $375,000; the purchase of new steamers, $230,000; the hydrographical survey, $390,000; the radiotelegraphic service, $370,000, etc. The naval service itself takes but $200,000, or just about that sum, and this is to maintain the Niobe and the Bainbow, and to pay the crews of those two ships.

(Translation.) Let the
hon. member look at the Estimates for 1914-15 and he will find that I am right.
(Translation.) This is for all the services, including the hydrographical survey and others, such as the tidal service, which existed a long time before the naval law was adopted.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to a case of very great bravery on the part of Captain Murdock of the Steamship Dufferin of Sherbrooke, N.S. I have been trying for some time to get this matter before my hon. friend, but as his estimates were not before the House I have not had an opportunity. The incident to which I refer happened in connection with the wreck of the City of Sidney on the Sambro ledges of Halifax harbour. The Dufferin commanded by Captain Murdock was with several other vessels carrying on the work of salvage. A small boat containing two men capsized, and its occupants were thrown into the sea. With great courage a man named William Snow went to the rescue, and succeeded in getting both men into his boat, but before he could get back to the ship his boat also capsized and the three men were thrown into the water. A number of boats were around and quite a number of men looking on, but none of them went to the rescue. The water was very rough and a high sea running. Captain Murdock seeing the men

were in great danger asked, one of the fishermen to lend him a boat. He and a young chap by the name of Herbert Evans sprang into it and started out to rescue the three drowning men. The account of their attempt is given in the Halifax press, and perhaps the best way would be for me to read it:
Around lay the flotilla of boats, with fishermen and others, who had evidently decided that they were unable to aid them. Captain Murdock, of the Dufferin, who was on board the Sydney, threw lifebelts to the men. There was no lifeboat at hand, but a dory with two fishermen in it was near the ship.
Captain Murdock called out to them to give him the boat. They climbed aboard the City of Sydney, while Captain Murdock embarked on his perilous row for life. He had prepared to undertake the rescue single-handed, when from the crowd along the wrecked steamer's rail a young lad, Herbert Evans, a deck hand on the Cabot, climbed down the side and jumped into the dory's stern.
The attempt to reach the men seemed utterly hopeless. The little boat would be lifted on the crest of the incoming combers, and then sink from sight in the hollows. At last the capsized dory was reached. Wm. Snow was quickly hauled on board. Robert Snow, exhausted, had sunk, but Burns was clinging to the bow.
Evans grasped his collar, but when a sea tore the dories apart, Burns was wrenched from his grasp and sank.
It was a thrilling rescue in such a sea, and there was intense excitement among the spectators as a sheet of foam rose above the breaking surf, and It seemed the boat would be lost. Oil had been poured on the water enabling the rescuers to come alongside the ship.
August Burns, who from the bow of the Sydney had watched the death of his brother, boarded the dory and rowed William to the Dufferin.
Men from the steamer Cabot, a quarter of a mile away, jumped into a lifeboat, but were too far away to reach the scene in time.
Both the drowned men leave widows and families.
You will see from this report that the men who are deserving of some recognition are Captain Murdock of the steamship Dufferin, William Snow, who first went to the rescue, and Herbert Evans, a young deck hand of the Cabot. Any one who has seen a storm on the Sambro Ledges will realize the courage displayed by these men. I am bringing this matter to the notice of the minister in order that it may be looked into by the life-saving branch of his department, with a view to suitably recognizing the bravery displayed by these three men, if that has not already been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have no recollection of this matter having been brought to the attention of the department before, but I think my hon. friend from Guysborough
has taken a very proper course in bringing it to my attention now. I will have the facts of the case looked into with a view to recognizing the bravery of 11 p.m. these men who went to the rescue. It is sometimes difficult for us to decide whether a case is one calling for recognition by the department or whether if might not be better dealt with by the Koyal Humane Society of Canada, which recognizes acts of bravery of this sort and attempts to save life generally. It is perhaps a question where this case would fall, but it seems to me that the Department of Marine and Fisheries might very well make some recognition of the bravery of these men, and I will ask the deputy minister to bring it to the attention of the life-saving department with that end in view.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I entirely concur in the appreciation expressed by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) of the great courage which these men displayed in an endeavour to save the lives of those who were in danger of being drowned. I know Captain Murdock very well, and all who know him appreciate him as just the man who would undertake so brave an act. The circumstances to which my hon. friend from Guysborough alludes were brought to my attention by a gentleman in Halifax, who sent me the same press clipping, or a similar one, to that which the hon. member for Guysborough has read, and asked whether any steps could be taken to bring the matter to the attention of the Royal Humane Society of Canada. I had very great pleasure in forwarding the account of the rescue, together with the letter of my correspondent, to that society, and received shortly afterwards an acknowledgment of its receipt. I do not know whether they propose taking any action, but the circumstances have already been brought to their attention. It is a case well worthy of recognition from some source.

There is another matter to which I would like to refer for just a moment in case I might not have another opportunity. I have been asked by the relatives of Joseph LeBlanc, who died on board the steamship Canada, to make some inquiries into the circumstances surrounding his death and burial. I do not do it with the desire of criticising the department, unduly although I think some of its officers in Montreal must have been slightly at fault in this matter. This sailor belonged

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think that any of the officers of the Department of
12 m. Marine and Fisheries, or the Department of the Naval Service, are in any way culpable in connection with this matter. The facts of the case are that Joseph Leblanc, who was a native of Port Felix, Nova Scotia, joined the Canada on April 11, 1913, as an ablebodied seaman at $25 per month. On the 28th of July, a little more than three months afterwards, he was sent to the Montreal General Hospital during a visit of the Canada to that city suffering from emphyema complicated with bronchial pneumonia and he died on the 27th of August. The doctor communicated with the captain of the ship which at that time was in Halifax. The telegrams that passed between the doctor and the captain of the ship were as follows:
Montreal, 22nd Aug., 1913. Commanding Officer Canada,
Dock Yard, Halifax.
Leblanc died in hospital yesterday.
(Sgd) Dr. Ower.
Immediately on receipt of this, on the same day, a telegram was sent to Mrs. Benjamin Richards, Port Felix. Leblanc was an unmarried man and he belonged to East Port Felix. The telegram read:
22nd August, 1913.
Mrs. Benjamin Richards,
East Port Felix.
Joseph Leblanc died yesterday Montreal General Hospital; communicate Dr. Ower re burial.
(Sgd) J. Bond.
On August 23, Captain Stuart of the Canada, having caused the despatch of the
22nd to be sent to Mrs. Richards, wired Dr. Ower at Montreal, as follows:
Unless you receive instructions from Leblanc's relations will you ask agent Marine and Fisheries to bury body.
On the 27th of August Dr. Ower wired to the captain of the Canada that Leblanc's body had been buried by the Sailors' Catholic Club of Montreal. No word had been received from Mrs. Richards in answer to the telegram that had been sent her by the captain of the Canada on the 22nd inst., but on the 27th inst., six days after Leblanc had died, the captain of the Canada received this telegram from Mrs. Richards: August 27, 1913.
The Captain Canada,
Shelburne, Nova Scotia.
If Government will forward J. Leblanc's body Mulgrave free of charge it will be met there, otherwise please have buried Montreal.
Mrs. Richards.

The fact seems to be that when the captain of the Canada was informed by the doctor of the hospital of Leblanc's death, lie at once communicated with Mrs. Richards on the 22nd of August, hut he received no reply from Mrs. Richards until the 27th, and Leblanc had been buried in Montreal in the meantime, and of course it was impossible to send the remains to Nova Scotia Positive instructions were given to Captain Stuart to send all telegrams sent and received concerning the matter and to give us full information. All communications from me to Mrs. Richards were by telegram through his cousin on hoard, J. Bond. On receipt of wire from

Commanding Officer.
Liverpool, May 5, 1914.
These are the facts, and they certainly show that no blame can be attached to Captain Stuart. I may say that all the expenses of the funeral were paid by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The deceased was buried in a lot in the Catholic cemetery which is set apart for sailors. My hon. friend Mir. Sinclair has referred to the fact that perhaps something should be done in the way of assistance for a child which the hon. member says Leblanc adopted. Leblanc had only been a few months in the service of the Marine and Fisheries Department as a sailor on board thle Canada, and our information is that this child who was living with him was a nephew, and that the father of the child is living and is well able to provide for it.

That does not appear
in the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have had communications about it and that is the^fact.
The record the minister first presented was very incomplete.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman was
courteous enough to notify me that he would bring this matter up when the House was considering these Estimates, and I instructed the deputy minister to get all the information he possibly could about it. When the hon. gentleman's question was answered we gave him all the information we had at that time. At an earlier date in the session my hon. friend asked certain questions, the answer to one of which is as follows:
On 22nd August the commanding officer Canada telegraphed Mrs. Richard the news of her brother's death and asked her to communicate with the hospital concerning the burial, otherwise the agent of Marine and Fisheries Department would arrange it. Ship proceeded to sea on 23rd August, and on arrival at Shelburne on 27th August-

Apparently that is not quite correct. The ship was at Shelburne on the 23rd.
-a wire was received from Mrs. Richard as follows: 'If Government will forward Joseph Leblanc's body free of charge to Mulgrave, we will meet it there; otherwise please have buried Montreal. Advise answer.' A letter from Mrs. Richard dated 25th August, asking for the body to be forwarded free of charge, was also received by the Prime Minister.
That letter was dated the 25th of August. It was not received at the Prime Minister's office for eome days afterwards. Immediately Ujpotn its receipt, inquiry was made at the hospital and it was found that Le Blanc had been buried for some days previous to the receipt of the letter. I am quite sure-, the officials of the department, in a case of that sort, would do everything right and proper, if the matter were called to their attention. In this case, no word having been received from the sister until six days or more after Mr. Le Blanc's death and until several days after he was buried, it will be seen how impossible it was to comply with the request of Mrs. Richard.

My information in regard to the matter is altogether different. I was particularly careful to get accurate information from Mrs. Richard. I asked her to get a copy of the telegram she sent from the office of the Western Union at Whitehead, which ehe siaid she sent on the 23rd of August. She sent me the telegram and it was dated the 23rd of August and not the 27th. I have no doubt at all that the telegram was received on the 23rd of August, either by a marine official or some other person in Montreal, and that it was transmitted in some way later on, so that the captain received it on the 27th at Shelburne, Therefore I thought that some person was at fault because, while this telegram was sent on the 23rd of August, the morning after Mrs. Richard received the news of her brother's death, no acknowledgment was received. The relatives were waiting at Port Felix to get some reply to the telegram, and they did not receive any. They are honest people. I know them well, and I have taken great pains to verify the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: To whom was the telegram sent?
To the captain at Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He was not at Montreal.

That was not Mrs.
Richard's fault.
Then some one else must have received the telegram.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If Mrs. Richard sent that telegram to the captain of the Canada at Montreal on the 23rd of August, it certainly did not reach the captain's hands on that day. The very day he got it he took action with regard to the matter and wired to the hospital again at Montreal. If Mrs. Richard had carried out the directions contained in the captain's telegram of the 22nd, in which he told her to communicate with Dr. Ower at the hospital at Montreal, the matter would no doubt have been attended to and the body of Le Blanc sent down, because the doctor would at once have communicated with the Marine Department at Montreal, and they would have sent the body to Nova Scotia. They would have paid the expense of sending it down and there would have been no trouble at all in regard to the matter. I do not believe, however, there is any culpability attaching to any official of the department, either in the local agency at Montreal or on board the steamer or here at headquarters, because we knew nothing about the matter.

So as to facilitate matters, will my hon. friend allow me to bring to his attention something which properly comes under this item, because we are discussing the fishery protection service? I am sorry to say that there is sadness and bereavement in many homes on the coast of Gaspe to-night after the terrible storm which has been raging for many hours on that coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The same thing is true in Gloucester county, N.1B.

I have received a letter, which only confirms what I read in the press of this evening, from one of my old electors from the county of Gaspe, namely, Mr. Elias J. LeMarquand, of Newport point, Gaspe, Que. He is a wealthy merchant of that place and writes as follows:
Dear Mr. Lemieux,-The weather bureau is supposed, as far as I understand, to order signals up when a storm is on the way from the 1st April. The many thousands of fishermen depending on these signals put out their fishing nets last evening and also left their boats afloat to take advantage of the present good fishing, with the result that during the night a howling snow storm set in as severe as the worst experienced in March. From the severity of the storm it must have originated thousands of miles away. The snow is fully six inches deep with telephone communication completely crippled so that no news of the most appalling loss on the coast can be ascertained. In this place alone, ten boats have been washed

ashore and wrecked and the loss of hundreds of nets will not be known till the storm is over. The loss to the coast is simply inestimable at this early or commencing stage of the fishing where thousands of fishermen have fitted out for the fishing on which they and their families depend for a living.
a little further on he adds:
The present value of fish is the highest yet [DOT]ever known. This fact has induced thousands of young men to take to the fishing and this disaster will not only swell up the losses but completely discourage them.
I understand that my correspondent wrote some years ago to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries asking him that outlying fishing places not within sight of the storm signals be notified of coming storms. My correspondent says in regard to that point:
A few months later I received a most indifferent reply; many complaints of the same nature must have followed mine as a 'phone box was added to the service.
Tours truly,
(Sgd) Elias J. LeMarquand.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not remember receiving such a letter.

I am inclined to believe that my hon. friend has given the matter his usual attention. The Government has been very generous by the further Supplementary Estimates which have been placed before us to-day. I see that an amount of $50,000 has been inserted in them to provide for the relief of sufferers from the recent Empress of Ireland disaster. I suppose there is no comparison between the two cases as regards the magnitude of the disaster; but I am told that there are at least twenty to twenty-five fishermen who have lost their lives in this storm. I do not know if my hon. friend has ascertained the number. Perhaps he would think of doing something to alleviate the losses which, in many cases along the coast, will be irreparable, and I refer to his best judgment to see whether or not something should not be done for the bereaved families.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I would be very much obliged if my hon. friend would send me a copy of that letter.
It will be in 'Hansard.'

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would like to have
inquiry made to see if there is any foundation for the charge that there has been negligence on the part of the Signal Service. The storm to which my hon. friend refers not only caused a great deal of destruction and loss of life on the Gaspe coast, but I judge that in the county of Gloucester

there has been a loss of life nearly, if not quite, as great as that on the Gaspe coast. I can only say in regard to the suggestion made by my hon. friend that I will take the matter up with my colleagues and consider it.

I feel it my duty, as representing the county of Rimouski, to read an *article thait appeared in Le Progree du Golfe on February 27 last, suggesting certain ameliorations for. navigation in that county. First, the writer of this article says there should be a light on Mechins wharf. I think that light was put on this spring. He suggests further on that a range light should be placed at Matane, and I think that will be very useful. I have been corresponding with the department about it for a couple of years, but I have net yet succeeded in obtaining it. I think it would be useful, particularly to the sailors who use that wharf. The article reads as follows:
Memorandum on the Navigation of the St.
Lawrence.
Is the navigation of our great river St. Lawrence a subject worthy of the particular attention of this Government? That is a question which should he of interest, not only to those who are entrusted with the management of public affairs, but to all those, as well, who are concerned with the welfare of our seamen, fishermen and others.
To be brief in the expression of what we have to say in this connection, we shall content ourselves with inquiring from the hon. Minister of Marine and from the hon. member for Rimouski how it is that, despite the orders given last year for the putting up of a light at the Mechins wharf, nothing as yet has been done for the protection of people frequenting that harbour, which provides a natural refuge for coasting vessels?
How is it that we never can succeed in obtaining a light inside the port of Matane, in line with the light outside and pointing to the entrance of the port?
Many a time have poor mariners been obliged to spend nights on the sand banks at the entrance of the harbour, with the waves beating furiously On them.
It will not be out of place to state here that a fog whistle has been put up at Ste. Ffilicitfi to prevent ships from coming. too close to the shore in misty weather. A few particulars may be, given. The former Administration was careful to have that fog whistle set up in a place where smuggling was going on, within a curve, the terminal points of which would be, to write in a way to be understood, Cape Chates and the gas buoy of the Matane shoals. The site which would have been, and still is, the most convenient as a fog alarm station, is from the first designated by nature: I mean the Cap 8, la Beleine, in the parish of Ste. FOlicitA about seven miles lower down than the present site.
Since the putting in of that siren, our seagoing vessels have on several occasions struck a submerged rock situated a little lower down.

Through the medium of certain newspapers the notion has been spread that it was a wreck; a story concocted to throw the credulous off the track, and with the object of saving one's skin in an inquiry. The funniest of it all is that steamship owners take it seriously.
Does not the stranding of the ss. Kensington, .at Matane, as well as of others whose keels sweep the bottom every summer, plainly show that it is urgent to improve that part of the river St. Lawrence?
Let the Government put a light and build an alarm station at Cap k la Baleine: they will thereby have done really good service to navigation. That point would also furnish the highest and best site for a Marconi station.
Cap a. la Beleine, once Cap Chatte, is passed, is as important as Bic. Heretofore very little attention has been paid to that fine cape. However, there is a great depth of water at that point, so much so, that it would be possible for a ship to get close enough to shore to render conversation possible with people on the shore.
I want to give that information, because I believe it will help to make navigation safer.
I heard the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) yesterday suggest that pilots should be taken off the boats at one place and taken on at another. As Rimouski county is the place where these pilots are taken on and put off the boats, I feel it my duty to say that I do not see how his suggestion could be very easily carried out without putting the country to double the expense. If I had a suggestion to make, I think the following would be of some use: boats coming down the St. Lawrence all make for the place called Father Point, where there is a boat to receive the pilots that are leaving their boats; and the boats coming up are also making for the same point. Consequently, I am greatly surprised that no accidents have happened so far. These boats running to meet each other in opposite directions, coming to the same point in foggy weather, might certainly have caused accidents before this. But the possibility of accidents might be avoided by giving orders to the boats coming down the St. Lawrence, after leaving their pilots at Father Point, to go out a little further. The channel is thirty-five miles wide there so that there is ample room, and when these boats have left their pilots they should go a few miles away from the route' of the other boats coming up. I think if such an order was given, and the order boats coming up the St. Lawrence, which always beep as close to the shore as they can, follow the same course, I think any possibility of an accident of that kind would be avoided.
Fisheries Protection Service-to provide for new vessels, $230,000.
How many vessels are you going to build?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Three, I think. I do not say we will build them all. We want a small vessel for use on the Great Lakes, the estimated cost of which is $30,000; one new vessel for the Atlantic coast, at an estimated cost of $175,000; and the remainder is to pay the balance of expenditure on the two new vessels on the West coast built in 1913-14.
Will my hon. friend say that the vessels will be built in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Without any doubt whatever. All vessels built for the Government will be built in Canada. I have already announced that as the policy of the department.
Hydrographic Surveys, including the survey of Hudson Bay, $390,000.

How far have
you proceeded with the survey, on Hudson bay especially?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Of this amount it is estimated we will spend $110,000 in Hudson bay this year, the same as last year, in connection with the hydrographic survey at the approach of the Nelson river, and on patrol work investigating the straits in the autumn. $25,000 will be expended in surveys in James bay; $25,000 for Lake Ontario; $25,000 for Lake Superior; $45,000 on the Atlantic coast for the continuation of the survey of the St. Lawrence river outside of Father Point, and $100,000 for the Pacific coast for survey work in the vicinity of the Queen Charlotte islands.
Radio-telegraph service-to provide for the building and maintenance of wireless stations, $370,000.

In view of the inestimable service rendered the other day by the Marconi wireless on board of the Lady Evelyn, the Eureka and other vessels around the place where the disaster occurred, may I suggest to my hon. friend that he should have the Marconi system on board every ship, no matter how small, in the service of his department, and that he should induce as many of the officers of his vessels as possible to become thoroughly familiar with the operation of the wireless system. We are coming to realize more and more that the Marconi system is one of the greatest devices for the safety of human

life and it is most important that all our sailors should have some knowledge of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Everybody will agree with what my hon. friend says as to the advantages resulting from having vessels equipped with the Marconi system. We had a practical illustration of that in the case of the Titanic. There is no doubt that if it had not been for the Marconi system, not nearly so many people would have been saved. It is altogether probable that every person on board the Cobequid, which went ashore last winter on the coast of Nova Scotia at the entrance to the Bay of Fundy, would have perished from cold and exposure if the vessel had not made its condition known by wireless, with the result that vessels made their way to the wrecked steamer. Another striking illustration is afforded in the case of the recent terrible disaster on the St. Lawrence. I think that this country is in the van so far as wireless service is concerned. We have a chain of wireless stations extending from the gulf of St. Lawrence up the St. Lawrence to the Great Lakes, and we have a chain also on the Pacific coast extending to Prince Rupert. These have proved time and again of very great value as aids to navigation. The hon. gentleman suggests that every boat in the Government service, no matter how small, should be equipped with the Marconi system. That is a matter foT consideration. Of course such equipment is attended with considerable expense, but that is not a matter to be considered at all if human life is thereby saved. The Bill which was introduced last session providing for equipping passenger steamers under certain circumstances with wireless, was a most advanced measure; I think no country in the world is ahead of us so far as legislation in that respect is concerned. Of course we can by legislation compel every boat to be equipped with wireless, but in the case of boats which do not carry passengers, very considerable expense would be entailed. In order to make the service efficient, two wireless, operators are necessary, one being on duty all the time and it will be seen that the expense of installation of wireless would be a great burden on small vessels belonging to private individuals. So far as the Government is concerned, that element would not, of course, stand in the way to as great an extent as it would in the case of private individuals. We will, so far as we think it necessary, equip our ,boats with wireless; a good many have it already. I shall bear in mind the suggestion of my hon. friend with regard to the matter.

Control of the northern waters of Canada, $50,000.

What steamers are employed in that work?
(Mr. HAZEN:	The Mary Sachs .and the

Are they on the Pacific or on the Atlantic?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are on the Arctic.
By way of the Atlantic or of the Pacific?

speechtext:
The Pacific.
To assist in the establishment, maintenance and inspection of cold storage for bait, the conservation and development of deep sea fisheries, and to provide for better transportation facilities for fresh fish, $150,000.

When this matter was under discussion on a previous occasion, the hon. minister said that the express rates at the present time were but one-third of what they were when the late Government was in power. I looked the matter up and I discovered that the rates for through express and through freight from the Maritime provinces to Montreal are exactly what they were in 1910.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think I made a statement showing exactly how the matter stands; it is on ' Hansard.'

The express rates are
the same; the only difference is that the local rates have been very largely increased. The rate on fresh fish from ports in the Maritime provinces to towns along the line of the Intercolonial railway have been very largely increased by the present Administration. There is not much use in assisting the transportation of fish by putting a little money into one pocket and taking it out of the other. The old policy of assisting the express rate to the extent of paying one-third of the rates on through packages from the Maritime provinces to Montreal is still continued by the present Administration. As I say, local rates have been increased, and instead of making the conditions better, as the minister .said at the time we had the former discussion, the Department of Railways and Canals made conditions a great deal worse than they were prior to the change of government in 1911. I had expected that the minister would straighten this out, and tell the House and the country the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I made an error in the statement I made in the House when the Estimates were up before, but I corrected it the next day, and the correction appears in 'Hansard.' Practically the whole of this item is for the transportation of fresh fish. To encourage rapid development of the fresh fish trade, the department pays one-third of the ordinary express charges on shipments of fresh fish from the Atlantic coast to points in Quebec and Ontario, and from the Pacific coast as far as Manitoba. A cold storage freight service is also operated from the Maritime provinces two days each week. We guarantee that the earnings on these cold storage cars shall be two-thirds of those of a minimum carload of 20,000 libs. During the past summer an additional service was inaugurated whereby a cold storage express car leaves Mulgrave on Saturday of each week, shipments from Halifax being included in it at Truro. We guarantee that the earnings on this car will be at least equal to the earnings on 10,000 lbs., plus the cost of icing the car. Tip to the present time the shipments have been greater than 10,000 lbs. except on six occasions, so that the cost to the department of this service has so far been practically restricted to that of icing the cars. Up to the end of December, the department's expense on this service has been $26,288.38 from the East, and $38,986.03 from the West. It is expected that this year there will be not only a much larger call on the vote on account of the additional amount of fish that will be shipped, but it is the intention to have a through express cold storage service to Toronto. That accounts for the increase over last year.
Mr. BeWlTT FOSTER: I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a matter of very great importance to the western counties of Nova Scotia, particularly the counties of Kings and Annapolis. For the past seven or eight years the fishermen of those two counties on the bay of Fundy have found it extremely difficult at certain seasons of the year to get bait. So great has the difficulty been that at times they have had to go to Grand Manan and other places to secure it. Inasmuch as the department is providing cold storage cars for the transportation of fish, it occurred to me that the minister might consider the establishment of a cold storage plant for bait at Hall's harbour practically 'halfway between Digby and Cape Blomidon. If this matter were taken up
by the department I am sure that the prominent persons interested in this business down there would be not only willing to devote their time to the management of the business,, but would be willing to help in any way they possibly could.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have power to help
in the establishment of these cold storage plants for bait to the extent of one-half of the cost, providing the cost does not exceed $4,000. We will assist either private individuals or companies in this way if it is demonstrated that a suitable place has been selected, and that the bait will be satisfactory to the fishermen. If there are iany private individuals or companies in the district to which my hon. friend has referred, we shall be glad to assist to one-half the cost if we are satisfied that it will meet the requirements of the fishermen.

Where do you intend
to build that dredge?

He was an engineer and
was killed by the bursting of an emery wheel. When a workman is killed in the discharge of his duty, toy the law of the province of Quetoec his family is entitled to $2,000, and we have fixed on that amount

My hon. friend from

speechtext:
We will have it looked
into at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is a matter of very great importance.
