speechtext:
We are receiving daily
inquiries at the department about the fisheries of Hudson bay, and* we are sending a party up there to investigate.
You bad a man up there last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We had a mam up there who was a professor in a university.

You had a man who
knew nothing about fish or fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The man we sent up there was a gentleman who is-
1 a.m. Mr. SINCLAIR:	I refer to
Mr. Tanner, of Piotou.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We did not send Mr. Tanner; we sent a scientific-

I will show you his
report.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That gentleman was not
sent by our department.

I do not know what
department he was sent by, but he was sent by this Government to investigate something in regard to the fisheries and he recommended that, as the Esquimaux up there are engaged in the fisheries and as they are good Canadians, they should

share in the fishing bounty. If the minister is going to employ anybody to go to Hudson bay to tell us about the fisheries I would suggest that he send somebody who knows something about the question and can give us intelligible information.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The gentleman to whom
my hon. friend refers was not sent by my department t-o Hudson bay or anywhere else; he was sent up there by the Department of Customs.
Has the minister received any communications from the lobster fishermen of Nova Scotia, in particular the island of Cape Breton, as to an extension of the present lobster fishing season?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have received not only from the lobster fishermen of Nova Scotia but also from the lobster fishermen of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island some communications asking that there should be an extension of the season. I received similar requests last year and I declined to accede to any of them. The regulations have been fixed after consideration and I have taken the position, and I intend to continue to take it, that these regulations ought to be observed. Practically there has never been a season in which the lobster fishermen have not asked for an extension of the time. They give some reason every year in support of their request for an extension but the conclusion I came to was that if these regulations were going to be of any use, in protecting the lobster fishery they ought to be observed. Last year I refused the request for an extension and in doing that I had the approval of the officers of the department. My belief is that, these regulations being made for the protection of the fisheries, it is in the interest of the fishermen and of the country generally that the regulations should he observed. The result will be that there will be more fish for the fishermen to catch in future years. That is the policy I have pursued and that is the policy that I am pursuing this year.

That seems to be a very stringent rule, notwithstanding the 'fact that "the officers of the minister's department approve its enforcement, because there are conditions existing which call for some relaxation of the regulations. There was a condition existing along the southern coast of Cape Breton which would certainly have led the officers of the department, if

they had known anything about it, to have advised the minister ,to extend the time. It is all very well to say that we have these regulations and that we must stand by them but does not the (minister see that occasions might arise when these rules should be relaxed? The season began on the 15th April this year, but it was well on into May before any traps were set out because the ice was on the shore until about the 1st of June, and I think that in a case of that kind the minister should take into consideration the protests that come from that part of the country in reference to the season. I am willing to grant that there should be rules and that where ever possible these rules should be adhered to, but I do think that when the drift ice stays on the coast of Nova Scotia until about the 1st of June these rules should be relaxed and that in the present year the season for lobster fishing should be extended. There is a situation which has scarcely ever been known to exist and if the Government do not relax the rules the results will be serious to the lobster fishermen of Cape Breton.

I wish to impress upon the minister the importance of this matter. I have read a great many letters from my own constituency and adjoining ones urging that something be done to relieve the situation amongst the lobster fishermen. One reason that makes it harder than usual is that this is the first year in which the latter part of the season has been curtailed about ten days. In addition to that, work was commenced very late in the spring and this has made it particularly difficult for the lobster fishermen. I think this is a case to which the minister ought to give his consideration and I believe that he ought to give the lobster fishermen the same time that they formerly had especially on the south coast of Nova Scotia. I do not think the same trouble exists on the north shore. I am informed that the lobster fishery is good on the coast of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island but it has been poor on the southern shore of Nova Scotia owing to the fact that there is a lot of ice on the coa,st and to the other fact that the minister has cut ten days off the end of the season. These two circumstances make the situation very urgent this year. I sent the minister a letter the other day written by a
small packer on the coast of Richmond in which he complains very bitterly and says that if the rule is enforced the small packers will come out very badly and that they will not be able to pay their bills let alone make any money. The rule has been relaxed before. It has been done frequently in years past and there is no good reason why it should not be done again because these regulations must not be regarded like the laws of the Medes and Persians as not being susceptible of change when circumstances warrant it. If the minister will send to his officer on the southern shore and ask them for a statement of the facts, I am sure that he will be impressed with the information that he will receive from them. He ehoiuld not sit dm his office and allow himself to be influenced by some person in an upper room of the Eastern block who does not know and is not in touch with the exact situation on the coast of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Everybody admits that the lobster fishery, unless it is protected, will pass out of existence. Lobsters have been getting fewer and smaller year after year and unless the lobster fishing industry is to give out altogether it must be given much better protection than it now enjoys. The regulations have been good and the laws have been good but influences have been brought to bear that fishery officers and ministers have not been able to resist. The result has been that year after year the lobster industry has been falling off and the lobsters have been getting smaller and fewer.
If the industry is worth saving, and I think it is, we have to enforce the law, and that is what I have been trying to do. It is a difficult thing for a minister to do, considering the pressure that is brought to bear on him by political friends and opponents alike. I declined last year to extend the season for lobsters in any case, and so far I have refused this year. If we persevere in this for a few years I believe the result will be a better catch of lobsters, and the fishermen will reap the benefit. Of course there is always a plausible reason given for extending the time, and for years in the past the department went on extending the time until the regulations were more honoured in the breach than in the observance. At times I have thought it would be better instead of close seasons and open seasons by a matter of regulation, that the season

should be fixed by statute. That would be easier for the minister, because now I have to put my back against the wall and resist all the pressurie brought to bear on me from my own province as well as from others.

Does not the fact that
the law is made by regulation show that it was intended to be relaxed?

The lobster season along the coast of Cape Breton and Victoria which commences in the middle of April now and ends on the 16th of July, whereas formerly it used to- toe from the first of May to the last of July. I understand the minister is trying to protect the lobsters by extending the time back to the middle of April, but if he extends it back to Christmas and the first of January of course the lobsters would be absolutely immune, because the ice' would protect them. There is an old saying that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath, and possibly it would he true	to say that the lobsters
are made for man and not man for the lobsters. If the minister could arrange with the polar currents and the Esquimaux so that these ice floes would not be sent down to prevent lobster fishing during the time the fishermen are allowed to take lobsters, it would be a good thing for the fishermen. The minister will, however, see that there is no use of our trying to deal with the icebergs, and so we will have to deal with the minister, and he will have to recognize that he must give way to some extent. I understand that this year, until about the last of May, there was not a lobster caught anywhere along the coast of Victoria county because the water was packed with drift ice. The people there depend for their living on catching lobsters, and while I agree with the minister that there should be every possible protection for the lobsters, yet I submit there must be a season of reasonable length when lobsters can be caught. If the people of Victoria and Cape Breton have no opportunity of fishing this year within the regular season, they certainly should be given some opportunity to catch lobsters. If the ice keeps them from fishing when the minister says they can fish, then they should be given some time to prosecute their calling when they would not be prevented from doing so by climatic conditions. The regulations have been changed thousands of times before, and I think in such urgent circumstances the minister

should extend the time again. I ask the minister not to absolutely make up his mind until he enters into a mutual reciprocity with the drift ice, so that the drift ice will pay attention to his regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The season in the district referred to is from the 15th of April to the 16th of July, and during a great portion of that time there would be no ice.

There was ice for six
weeks of the season this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That regulation was
recommended by the shellfish commisision and concurred in by the Advisory Fisheries Board and by the officers of my department.
Was there a man from Cape Breton on that board?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There was one from Nova Scotia, one from New Brunswick, and one from Prince Edward Island.

I would like to call my hon. friend's attention to an article in the Montreal Daily Herald of to-night in regard to the Montreal harbour? It is headed: 'Politics and the harbour of Montreal: A bit of history connected with Captain Demers' retirement as harbourmaster.' The first paragraph reads as follows:
Captain Bourassa has been appointed harbourmaster for the port of Montreal, with Captain Symonds as his assistant. "The present harbour master, Captain Demers, is again reappointed to his former position with the Dominion Government as wreck commissioner.
The article seems to indicate that there has been a good deal of politics mixed up with this, and that the arrangement is a bad one. How did it happen?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is nothing of that sort in it at all. I can assure my hon. friend Captain Demers was for a number of years wreck commissioner of Canada, and was a very capable and competent officer, so far as I am aware. His record was an excellent one. The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, about a year and a half ago, the commissioners being Mr. Stephens, Mr. Ballantyne and Mr. Geoffrion, advertised for a harbourmaster in the press. They had a large number of applicants, among whom was Captain Demers, because the salary they were offering was larger than the salary being paid to the wreck commissioner.

Was Captain Roper one of the applicants?

.Mr. HAZEN : Yes. There were forty or fifty applicants, and the commissioners selected Captain Demers.
When did he become an applicant?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He waa an applicant when they advertised. Captain Demers was selected and was appointed. Captain Lindsay was appointed his successor in the department as wreck commissioner. After the report was received from the commission appointed to investigate pilotage matters, it was necessary, in order to carry out that report, to appoint a superintendent of pilots who would have supervision over the Montreal and the Quebec pilots. It was an office of great responsibility, and, looking around for a suitable man, for the position, I considered that Captain Lindsay, who had been wreck commissioner and who had had command of a transatlantic liner, was the best man available; I appointed him, and that left the position of wreck commissioner vacant. When it became vacant, Captain Demers had a friend of his give me to understand that, if the position were offered to him, he would accept it, as the position of harbour commissioner in Montreal was not congenial to him. I was very glad to find right at hand a man who had had experience as wreck commissioner and who had filled the position with credit to himself in the department. I therefore offered the position to Captain Demers and he accepted it. I understand that the harbour commissioners have since then appointed Captain Bour-assa, the assistant harbour commissioner, to be harbour commissioner in Captain Demers' place.
Will my hon. friend read the article which is on the front page of the Montreal Daily Herald ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Will my hon. friend tell me in what year this position of harbourmaster was advertised ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It was during the time that Mr. Geoffrion, Mr. Ballantyne and Mr. Stephens were commissioners. I think they ceased to be commissioners on the 1st of January, 1913. Therefore it would be m January and February of 1913, because the new harbour-master went on duty at the opening of navigation in 1913.
When the fishery items were before the House on a previous occasion, the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) 327
criticised quite severely what is known as the Monthly Bulletin issued by the Fishery Department, which gives certain seafish statistics. That bulletin is prepared and made up by an official in the department, namely, Mr. Cowie, who was appointed some time before I took office as Minister of Marine and Fisheries. In justice to Mr. Cowie, I want to read to the House the following statement which he had prepared with regard to the criticism that was made upon that bulletin at the time the fishery items were under discussion :
The undersigned being responsible (or the fisheries statistical work of the department, has the following observations to make on the discussion and criticism of the department's monthly bulletin of sea fisheries statistics, which took place on Friday, the 3rd of April last:
It may be stated at the outset that, in order to economize space and paper during the slack season, the statistics of those counties in which small quantities, or one or two kinds only, are landed, are not tabulated, but are shown in a compact form on the first page of the bulletin. If fishing has not taken place at all in a county during the month the fact is carefully noted also on the first page. A casual glance, therefore, at the first page of any issue of the bulletin should have prevented Mr. Sinclair from falling into the error of stating that some counties were omitted entirely from the bulletin.
Mr. Kyte condemned the bulletin on the ground that the February issue shows for Richmond county a catch of 6,000 lbs. of smelts, valued at $120, or 2c per pound; while for Antigonish and Guysborough counties the price is given as 5c per pound. Typographical errors occur at times, and are corrected in succeeding bulletins,-the catch of smelts for Richmond county in the February bulletin was one of such. The officer's return shows 2,000 lbs. valued at $120, or 6c per pound, which conforms to the price in the neighbouring counties. The error was duly corrected in the March bulletin. The figures for Cape Breton county represent a catch of cod, and not one of smelts as was supposed by Mr. Kyte.
Mr. Sinclair proceeeds to prove that the quantities given in the bulletin are 'merely ridiculous,' by comparing the shipment of fish over the Intercolonial railway from Canso, during January, 1913, with the quantity shown as having been caught and landed in Guysborough in the same month. He values the January shipment at $60,000, which at ljc per pound equals 4,000,000 pounds. One of Mr. Whitman's telegrams, on which he bases his argument, dated January 24, the usual closing time for the haddock season, tells of another stormy week, indicating that the preceding week had also been stormy, and that the week's landings were 150,000 pounds. By allowing an equal quantity for the previous stormy week, Mr. Sinclair's figures leave the huge catch of
3,700,000	lbs. to be caught and brought to land by Canso fishermen in one short week of one of the stormiest months of the year,-obviously the thing is simply an impossibility. Mr. Sinclair should know that the quantity shipped from Canso in January, 1913, bears no relation to
That statement is not correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Well, my hon. friend will have an opportunity to correct it later.

I think it hardly fair that an official should make statements
like this at a time when they cannot be discussed and dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman made a very severe criticism of the work of this official, and it is only fair play to this official that he should have the opportunity of placing his statement on ' Hansard 9
I think the minister has chosen a very curious time to do it, at this hour of the morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is the only opportunity I have had since it occurred. (Reading):
A record of the work performed and the amount of travelling done by every overseer in the service is sent to the department, weekly, and this shows that Overseer Dillon, of Guys-borough, not only visited Canso, but all the other fishing stations of his district as well, at the end of December and again at the end of January. In order to corroborate this record and to make sure as to whether or not the overseer got his figures from the merchants, the inspector of fisheries for the district was requested to visit the fishing sections of the country to investigate the matter, and report upon the accuracy of the Guysborough figures in the bulletin for January, 1914.
His report, W'hich is hereto attached, proves that Mr. Sinclair's information is only fragmentary, and that his assumptions are grossly erroneous. It is accompanied by a statement from each of the fish merchants exactly similar to that supplied by them to the overseer, and completely corroborates the figures contained in the bulletin.
Mr. Sinclair ends by stating that the whole work of collecting the information and publishing the bulletin costs not more than $1,200 annually, and asks how* such important work can be done on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts for that paltry sum. The explanation is simple: the undersigned having a sufficient grasp of the *whole business of fishing, took advantage of the existence of a great staff of officers who were travelling practically every inch of the coast, and so arranged things that the work of securing the required statistical information is accomplished by these officers in the course of their travels, without really adding much to their official burdens. The cost might easily have mounted to five or six thousand dollars, but by the exercise of economy coupled with efficient management, the expense is what it is.
It is submitted that the foregoing makes it clear that the adverse statements made in the course of the criticism were totally inaccurate, quite uncalled for, and altogether unfair.
It is not claimed that perfection has been reached in the matter of collecting statistics under the present system; but, notwithstanding assertions to the contrary, the fact remains that the fisheries statistics of Canada are to-day far more reliable and intelligible than at any time since such records have been kept.
Now, there is a communication attached to that, signed by Mr. Hoc-kin, inspector of fisheries, and dated Pictou, May 4, 1914, which reads:

Having reference to file 55.6 letter April 25.
I went to Canso on the 30th ultimo and with Mr. Dillon called upon the fish buyers there, who kindly gave me a duplicate of the reports they had furnished to overseer Dillon showing the quantity of fish caught and landed in Canso during the month of January, and I enclose a schedule giving the names of fish buyers from whom the statements were received and the quantity stated by them.
I was also given in some instances the actual catch of individual fishermen whose names are included in the report and enclose a statement giving the reported catch-the fish buyers figures and the proportion caught in January and December.
I may say that the reports as given will include 90 per cent of all the fish caught in January in the county of Guysborough. The overseer had received statements from the merchants when he made up his report and he has not understated the quantity caught and landed in Guysborough for the month of January.
I think there is one instance in which the fish should not have been included, viz: that of Messrs. A. and R. Loggie, of Mulgrave, who say that the fish reported by them were bought from fishermen at Petit de Gras, Isle Madame Richmond county.
I am Sir,
Tour obedient servant,
R. Hockin,
Inspector of Fisheries.
P.S.-I may add that Mr. \V. G. Matthews from his records stated that there were only seven days in January that fish were caught and landed.
Annexed to that is a statement showing quantity of fish caught and landed in Guysborough county during the month of January, 1914, showing a total of haddock, 6,947 cwt.; cod,761 cwt.; hake, 87 cwt.; and pollock, 5 cwt. There is also a statement showing reported individual catch of fishermen who landed fish at Canso, and the fish buyer's statement of quantities caught in December, 1913, and January, 1914.
I feel in fairness to the official whose duty it is to make up this bulletin, and who has been so severely criticised, that his statement ought to be on ' Hansard.'

I regret very much that the minister did not do me the courtesy to tell me this morning that he was going to bring this matter up. If he had done so I would have been better prepared with the figures to show that the statements of his officers -are altogether misleading. I was very careful in collecting my information at the time and I gave the minister the name of the gentleman who furnished me with the information, who is one of the most reliable gentlemen in Nova Scotia, and I have no doubt whatever that his information is absolutely correct. I do not think it is very dignified for the minister to 327J	j..
shelter himself behind an official. It indicates a lack of courage.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not sheltering myself.

The minister ought to be responsible for the bulletin he issues. It is undignified for him to present a statement reflecting upon an hon. member, drawn up by a subordinate officer, -and read it to the House. He brings this matter forward and reads a statement made by this official when he does not know whether the statement is correct or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
pardon me? The hon. gentleman referred to Mr. Cowie and took the opportunity, as I recall, to reflect on his competency. I take full responsibility upon myself for anything that occurs in my department; the minister has to take full responsibility for any matter that he may have anything to do with. But everybody knows I do not make up these statistics. If they are not correct and it is brought to my attention, my duty would be to get officers who would see that they are correct. Mr. Cowie makes out a strong case to show that he was correct, and that my hon. friend's criticism was unfair.

I still say that the minister has taken a very undignified position when he puts forward Mr. Cowie in this way. If the minister had given me an opportunity to furnish him with the exact facts, which I have, but have not here at the present time, I could have shown him very clearly that the statements made in the Fishery Bulletin were altogether inaccurate. I was able to point out, -when I brought the matter up, the names of the fishermen, and the quantity each caught. I went very carefully about it so that there could be no mistake, and I was able to show that in one week there was as much fish landed at Canso alone as in the whole county.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is quite clear that the
hon. gentleman cannot be convinced.

It is quite clear that the official statistics must be inaccurate. The minister does not dare to contradict the. statements made in the correspondence which I have presented, because he knows that they are drue. They were furnished to me by a merchant in Canso who knows what he is talking about. In one week the quantity of fish caught at Canso alone was as large as the amount credited to the whole county of Guysborough in a month.

The county of Guysborough has a coastline of 120 miles, on which there are a large number of fishing stations. My hon. friend will not say that his fishery officer travels over that entire district and gets correct information, 'because he does not do it, and I can prove to my hon. friend that he does not do it. He sits in his office and guesses at the amount of fish that is caught along the coast. It would be a month's work for a man to travel along the coast of my constituency, and consult each fisherman .and get even an approach to correct information. I say that it is 'absolutely impossible to get correct information under such a system as we now have. What answer does my hon. friend make to the assertion that he is spending $1,200 in getting information of that kind which $12,000 or even $120,000 would not begin to pay for and obtain upon a correct basis? Are we to understand that these officers travel the coast for nothing? The idea that information of that kind can be obtained all along the coast of the Maritime provinces, compiled at Ottawa and given out to the public through the expenditure of $1,200 is simply absurd. I knew that the statistics -that were being sent out through the country were an injury to the fisheries, not a benefit, and in order to give the minister an idea of the condition that branch of the department was in I took the trouble of collecting this information for the particular month Tn question, and did it with great care and exactness. We have the statement read by the minister and made by one of his officials that that information is not correct. Does he know whether it is correct or not? How does he know that the facts sent to me by a reputable merchant of Canso are not correct? My hon. friend's correspondent does not pretend to say that the proper officer went to the individual fishermen I have named and found that any part of the information which I have given rwas incorrect. I say that it is an undignified procedure for the minister to read the statement of Mr. Cowie, a sub-officer, and place it before the committee as the answer of the Government. If he has any facts that he wishes to lay before the committee as correct information, we shall he very glad to hear them, but I submit that it is not a proper course for the minister to allow an official 
who has been subjected to criticism to write a document of that kind and to read it to the committee as if it were the truth, when I am able to prove to the minister, if he will give me an opportunity of doing so, that it is not true.

The hon. minister, in the
statement which he read to the committee, referred to a criticism I made on the occasion to which the hon. member for Guysborough has referred. The assertion I made as to the incorrectness of the statement as to the value of the smelts caught in my county remains as I made it. Mr. Cowie now admits that there was a typographical error.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A typographical error that had been corrected before the criticism was made in this House.

I have not the papers before me to verify the statement made by Mr. Cowie, but I do say to the hon. minister that it is unfortunate that he did not advise him to revise his report before it was read in the House, containing, as it does, such discourteous language in respect of the hon. member for Guysborough. So far as the statement I made is concerned, I stand by it; the statement as to the quantity and prices of smelts caught in the county of Richmond is absolutely incorrect. I say further that the information which the minister purports to give with regard to the quantity of fish caught in the county of Richmond is a pure guess and nothing more. He has no source of information that would enable him to give correct information to the people interested in this subject, and unless he revises the system by which he obtains his information the $1,200 spent for this purpose will be absolutely wasted.
I wish to convey to the minister the information that he must not bring documents into this House at this hour to insult members, written by his officials for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Allow me to tell my hon. friend that it makes absolutely no difference to me what he tells me, and that I decline to be lectured and browbeaten by him.

I wish to tell the hon. minister that my opinion is as valuable to me as his opinions are to him. This is not

the first time that he read papers prepared by his officials, and the next day swallowed them in toto. If to-morrow or the next day the minister is brought face to face with the fact that this statement which he has read is an absolute tissue of falsehood, he will say: I read the statement prepared for me in the department; I am not responsible. The minister comes here with a statement containing coarse language, a production or an essay by a gentleman in his office who has nothing to do from one end of the year to the other but write such letters. I do not propose to lecture the minister or anybody else, but I want the minister to understand that his avoirdupois or altitude is not going to make the slightest difference to me. I submit that if any member in this House makes a statement that does not agree with what an officer would consider to be right, that officer has the right to protection. He has the right to take the matter up privately with the member, to set forth the facts and to prove that the member was mistaken. It is then up to the member to say in the House that he did misrepresent the officer in question, and if the member does not do so, the minister is within his rights in saying: I am aware that my officer has brought this matter up with the member; that he has or ought to have convinced the member that he was wrong; that the member has not explained the matter, and that as the officer has not an opportunity of coming here and defending himself, the minister will do so for him. But the minister comes here with an essay for which the country has paid the equivalent of many months' salary, prepared to blackguard a member of this House and to tell him that his statements are absurd and absolutely false. That is the kind of literature the minister has been putting on ' Hansard ' to-night. So far as we in Nova Scotia are concerned we shall try to defend ourselves and see that no Cowie is going to cowe anybody on this side of the House. Mr. Oowie will find that he will experience a day of reckoning if he thinks that he is at liberty to browbeat and bulldoze hon. gentlemen of this House as long as he has a minister to read his essays at two o'clock in the morning, when there is very little opportunity of criticism.
Progress reported.
